Nothing is deleted. A rotation leaves a dead staged key where it is, and the timed step activates it once its delay has elapsed, as it activates any staged key.

docs.title: Linked identities
docs.text: A linked identity says that a user of this tenant is a given subject at a named upstream provider. Whoever presents that subject at that provider is that user, and nobody else: it is what keeps a person from being created again every time they arrive by another door, and the one way a subject an upstream provider names becomes a person of this tenant at all. Nothing infers one. A row is written by a sign-in through the provider, or by an operator, and by nothing else.

docs.title: What one holds
docs.text:
Field What it holds Provider The upstream provider, named as the federation knows it: the entity ID of an upstream SAML identity provider, or the identity_provider of a trusted issuer Subject The value that provider gives the person, compared byte for byte. It is not the sub this provider issues Claims The last snapshot of what the provider said of the person, empty when it said nothing Linked at, last seen at When the link was written, and when it was last written again

The pair names one person of the tenant. The store holds one row per provider and subject, and linking a pair to a second person is refused, naming the person it already names. Linking it again to the same person is what a second run of an import does: the snapshot is replaced and the date it was last seen moves, the row keeps its person.

It is sealed. The provider, the subject and the snapshot are personal data, sealed under the data key of the tenant like every column of a person. A lookup matches two blind indexes beside them, keyed tags of the provider and of the subject, and the uniqueness of the pair is held on those tags. The tag of the provider is the one of the model on a column with few distinct values: it says which rows share a provider, which is the price of the uniqueness of the pair. Personal data says what that means.

docs.title: Federation writes them
docs.text:
At the first sign-in through an upstream identity provider, the person and their linked identity are created together, in one unit, all of it kept or none of it. The snapshot holds the claims the provider said, by the names of OIDC Core §5.1, the address, and the telephone number when it said one. At the next sign-ins, nothing is created: the snapshot is refreshed, and what the provider fills is written again for a person it created.

A person is found by their link and never by their address. An address is given again to somebody else when its holder leaves; a subject is not. So an address that another person of the tenant holds, as a mailbox or as a username, refuses a first sign-in rather than linking that person on its own.

docs.title: An operator writes one by hand
docs.text:
For a person who exists already and is to sign in through a provider, or be named by the assertions of a trusted issuer:

bin/console beffroi:user:link alice 'https://idp.example.org/saml/metadata' 'the-subject-it-gives-alice'
Argument What it says username The user of this tenant provider The upstream provider, as the configuration that trusts it names it subject The subject that provider gives this user, compared byte for byte

The command prints the username, the provider, the subject, the identifier of the row and the slug of the tenant. Run again, it refreshes the link with an empty snapshot. A person linked that way signs in through the provider under the link, with none of the rules of a first sign-in: the provider did not create them, so nothing it fills is written of them, and only the snapshot of the link is refreshed.

No command removes a link.

docs.title: What reads them
docs.text:
Reader What it asks Signing in through an organisation The person a SAML assertion names: the link of that provider and that subject, created with the person at the first sign-in The JWT bearer grant, RFC 7523 §3 The user an assertion of a trusted issuer is about: the link of the identity_provider that issuer is declared with and of the subject of the assertion. An assertion about somebody no link resolves, or about a disabled user, is refused as an assertion of an unknown issuer is, and no user is ever created there

The person reads their links in the archive they ask for: one line per link, with the provider, the subject, the snapshot and the two dates.

docs.title: Personal data
docs.text:
Personal data is sealed in its column with a data key of the tenant, itself wrapped by the master key of that tenant in the key management service, so a database alone reads nothing. The lookups that must still work match a blind index, a keyed tag of the value, rather than a readable column.

The data keys can be wrapped by another key management client while the provider serves sign-ins, and destroying them is the one operation that cannot be undone. The same rule holds past the database: what the provider writes to a transport leaves sealed too.

docs.title: What is sealed
docs.text:
Every class of the model that a row holds says, field by field, what it holds of a person: a personal datum sealed under the data key of its table, a blind index of such a datum, or a field a dump gives away together with the sentence that says why that gives nothing away. The suite of the bundle walks the schema against those declarations, and refuses a column no declaration names, a declaration no column carries, and a field sealed under the key of another table than its own.

Family What it seals user The username, the email address, the profile, the phone number, the postal address, and the source that created the person, which says which organisation they are of linked_identity The provider, the subject it gives the person, and the snapshot of what it said passkey_credential The name a person gave a passkey push_subscription The endpoint of a browser web push reaches, and the name a person gave it authentication_session Where a session was opened from and last seen from claim_change What a claim said before a person changed it, what it says after, and where the change came from journal Where each act came from personal_archive The archive a person asked for interaction The login_hint and the id_token_hint of an authorization request pushed_authorization_request The parameters a client pushed device_authorization_request Where a device authorization request came from backchannel_authentication_request The binding message of a backchannel request, and where it came from client What a registered client wrote of itself, what the registration policy wrote on it, and its secret disclosure What a client was given of a person: the scopes, the claims and the authorization details saml_service_provider, saml_upstream_identity_provider The metadata accepted for a SAML peer, whose contacts name people

Each family is the name of its table without the beffroi_ prefix. What stays readable is named as plainly, each field with the sentence that says why it gives nothing away. Among them: the subject, a stable pseudonym that names a person without saying anything about them; the tenant; dates, states and counts; digests and envelopes, which do not open; what a browser, an authenticator or a client publishes anyway, such as the public key of a passkey; identifiers drawn at random; the identifier of a client, and what a request asked of the protocol, such as its scopes; what a session proved, which every token issued from it carries; the names of the groups of the tenant; and the name of an act or of a claim, never its value.

A sealed column is binary in the database, whatever length its mapping states: that length is the one the model checks of the value in clear. An option of the mapping that describes the stored value, such as jsonb, does not apply to a sealed column, which holds a ciphertext no query of the database reads into.

A ciphertext is bound to its tenant, not to its row

The authenticated data of every sealed value name the tenant, so a value of one tenant does not open for another, wherever it is found. They do not name the table, the column or the row: within one tenant and one family, a value moved into another row of the same column opens there.

docs.title: Blind indexes
docs.text:
A sealed column holds a different ciphertext for every write of the same value, so WHERE username = ? matches nothing. The columns that are looked up carry a sibling instead: a keyed tag of the value under the index key of the tenant, sixty-four hexadecimal characters, written in the same statement as the value it indexes, which is what a lookup matches and what a unique constraint holds.

Column Read as What matches on it The username of a person Byte for byte A login, the console naming a person, the uniqueness of a username in the tenant The email address of a person The whole address in lower case, its local part included A sign-in through an upstream provider, the first one or a later one that brings another address, which refuses an address another person holds The provider of a linked identity Byte for byte Every lookup of a linked identity, beside the subject, and the uniqueness of a pair The subject of a linked identity Byte for byte The sign-in through a provider, and an assertion of a trusted issuer

A tag says which rows share a value and never what the value is. That is the one thing a column gives up by carrying one, which is why only these four do: a username, an address and a subject are high-entropy and looked up by equality. The provider is not: a tenant federates from a handful of them, so its column says which rows share one and the largest group is guessable. It carries a tag because a linked identity is looked up, and held unique, by the pair. gender, locale, zoneinfo and birthdate carry none.

The columns derive their tags under subkeys named after themselves, so a username that happens to be an address does not share the tag of that address. A deployment whose projection of the username or of the address changed derives those tags again for every person of the tenant, in pages of a hundred, a second run writing nothing; the tags of the linked identities are not re-derived by it:

bin/console beffroi:user:reindex

docs.title: The data keys of a tenant
docs.text:
Scope What it covers Its life <slug>.<family>, one per family of the table above Every sealed value of that family Minted at the first write of the family. After thirty days, the next write mints another, and the older keys stay to open what they sealed <slug>.blind_index Every blind index of the tenant Minted at the first lookup or write that needs it, never replaced: every tag already written was derived under it

A data key is 32 bytes, AES-256-GCM, held wrapped in the table beffroi_data_key by the master key the configuration names for the tenant, beffroi.keys.key_id resolved for its slug, the one its own keys are sealed under. A process opens each data key once and keeps it, so the key management service is asked once per key and not once per value. Nothing in the ordinary life of a tenant removes a data key: a new key is minted beside the ones there, and a rewrap changes what protects a key and not the key.

bin/console beffroi:data-keys:list

It lists the keys of the tenant by scope, each with its reference, when it was minted, the master key that wraps it, the key management client that opens it and whether it is the current key of its scope or a retired one. It never opens a key. A tenant that holds none has sealed nothing yet, and the command says which families there are.

docs.title: Wrapping them with another client
docs.text:
bin/console beffroi:data-keys:rewrap --to=second --dry-run
bin/console beffroi:data-keys:rewrap --to=second
Option What it says --to The key management client that wraps the data keys the tenant holds, a name of key_management.clients --from Move only the keys that client wraps; all of them when it is left out --dry-run List what would move, and write nothing

The master key is not asked for: it is the one the configuration resolves for the slug of the tenant, so an operator cannot type the master key of another tenant. No sealed value is read and none is rewritten, every ciphertext going on referring to the same data key, the index key included. The provider serves while the keys move: a read resolves the client and the master key from the row of the data key it names, whatever wrapped it. The command moves the keys the tenant holds when it runs; a key minted afterwards, the first of a family or the next one after thirty days, is wrapped by the client beffroi.keys.kms names. The act tenant.data_keys_rewrapped goes to the journal, and its event carries the client the keys were taken from when --from named one, the client and the master key that wrap them afterwards, how many keys moved, and how many scopes the tenant holds. One tenant at a time, by hand: nothing schedules it.

The keys of the tenant itself, its signing and encryption keys, are sealed apart, one file each, and no command rewraps them: a key sealed by another service is replaced by a rotation.

docs.title: Destroying them
docs.text:
bin/console beffroi:data-keys:destroy example

The command erases every data key of the tenant, the index key included, and the slug has to be typed back: without it, or with another one, it says how many keys over which scopes it would erase, and erases nothing. There is no --force. Afterwards every column the keys sealed holds a ciphertext nothing opens, by anybody, and the rows are still there: what is gone is the means of reading them. The act tenant.data_keys_destroyed goes to the journal, and its event carries how many keys over how many scopes were erased, which is what cannot be counted afterwards. It cannot be undone.

docs.title: Past the database
docs.text:
What leaves the process on a transport leaves sealed. The body of every message the provider writes to a transport, an event, a command or a notification, is a JWE to the MESSAGE-SEAL key of the tenant, under ECDH-ES+A256KW and A256GCM, its protected header naming the tenant, so a body moved to the queue of another tenant does not open there. The serializer that seals it is the default one of every transport, the failure transport included, so a broker, the table of a transport and a backup of either hold nothing readable. What stays in the clear on a message is what makes a failed one readable: the class of the message, its stamps and the slug of the tenant it was written under, nothing of a person among them.

The journal of the acts, what a client was given at each of them, what a record used to say and the archive a person asks for are sealed where they sit like every other column of a person.

docs.title: How long it is kept
docs.text:
What Kept for Forgotten by An act of the journal, and what a client was given at it beffroi.journal.retention days, 180 by default A daily step A change of a claim beffroi.history.retention days, 180 by default A daily step The archive a person asked for Seven days from the moment it was asked for, a figure in the code An hourly step

The archive is the one file in which all of it stands in clear at once, so it is held by rules rather than by settings: it is sealed at rest in a family of its own, it expires a week after it was asked for, whether it was built or not, and it leaves under a passphrase of the person's choosing when they ask for one, sixteen characters at the least.

Your data, on the account pages

docs.title: The ports of the core
docs.text:
The core asks the outside for what it cannot do itself: storage, randomness, a hasher, the key management service, the ceremonies of WebAuthn. Each of these is a port, an interface of Beffroi\Core\Port, and each port has one to five methods, so a caller sees what it calls and nothing more. When two callers need disjoint halves of a store, the store has two ports: a person's page reads CanPageCredentialsInterface, where a login reads CredentialRepositoryInterface.

Where a port says what its implementations throw, it says it in its contract, as @throws: JwsSignerInterface throws when the tenant has no active key or when the key management service does not answer, and GeoLocatorInterface never throws at all, an address nothing knows being no place.

Beside its ports, the core reads two PSR interfaces it is handed: a clock (PSR-20), which its use cases read the time from, and an event dispatcher (PSR-14), which the bundle binds to its event bus (events).

docs.title: Where the implementations live
docs.text:
Most ports have one implementation, which the bundle aliases the interface to; a name in the tables below is that implementation, in the bridge of the core (Beffroi\Core\Bridge) or in the bundle. Where several implementations of one interface are read as one list, a port, an interface of the model or an interface of the bridge, a tag feeds that list, every service carrying the tag being in it:

docs.title: What else the bridge of the core ships
docs.text: The bridge of the core holds fourteen stores in memory, for tests and for whoever wires the core without the bundle: InMemoryUserRepository, InMemoryCredentialRepository, InMemoryAuthenticationSessionRepository, InMemoryTenantKeyRepository and their siblings; the journal has none. It holds three implementations that answer nothing, NullBreachedPasswords, which asks no list, NullGeoLocator, which finds no place, and NullUserAgentParser, which reads no device, and two sources fixed for tests, FixedUuidGenerator and FixedRandomness. The protocol has ports of its own, which the ports of the protocol list.

docs.title: Tenants
docs.text: A tenant is the unit of isolation: it owns an issuer, a set of keys, a population of people, the clients that may ask about them and the SAML peers it trusts. Nothing crosses from one tenant to another, and a subject identifier is only meaningful inside the one that minted it. A deployment serves one tenant today, the one its configuration declares.

docs.title: What the configuration says
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    tenant:
        issuer: '%env(BEFFROI_ISSUER)%'
        slug: default
        name: 'Example'
        look:
            logo_uri: 'https://www.example.com/logo.svg'
            primary_color: '#1b4b8f'
            primary_content_color: '#ffffff'
        self_served_claims: [name, given_name, family_name, locale, zoneinfo]
Option Default What it decides issuer required The issuer identifier (OIDC Discovery 1.0 §3): an absolute https URL with no query, no fragment and no trailing slash, plain HTTP on a loopback host only. Every endpoint is served under it, the SAML metadata included slug default The stable name of the tenant, from which its identifier is derived. Renaming it is creating another tenant name the host of the issuer What the pages call it look none The logo and the two colours every page shows. The logo is loaded by the browser of the visitor, never by the provider, and the two colours are declared together or not at all self_served_claims none The claims of OIDC Core §5.1 the people of this tenant may change of themselves on the page of their account. A tenant whose directory owns the data opens none authentication_classes the default policy The acr vocabulary of the tenant, below

docs.title: Its row
docs.text:
The configuration declares the tenant, and a row of the database holds what the rest of the model points at. One command makes the row say what the configuration says:

bin/console beffroi:tenant:synchronize

It reports what it did, created, renamed or left alone, and is safe to run at every deployment. What a command decides with a date, the floor of its logins below, is written on the row and nowhere else.

docs.title: The classes it answers with
docs.text:
A session never stores an acr: it records what was proven, and satisfies every class whose predicate holds on those proofs. The predicates are the provider's, one class each, and a tenant names its classes on them.

Predicate What it requires Its class in the default policy phishing_resistant_hardware A passkey bound to its authenticator phrh (OpenID Connect EAP ACR Values 1.0) phishing_resistant A passkey, synced or bound phr (OpenID Connect EAP ACR Values 1.0) two_factors Two methods of different kinds, knowledge, possession or inherence (RFC 8176 §2), or one that counts as several 2 single_factor One method, whatever it is 1

A tenant that names nothing answers with that default policy, strongest first. One that names its own maps each class name to a predicate:

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    tenant:
        authentication_classes:
            gold: phishing_resistant
            silver: two_factors
            bronze: single_factor

A name no wired predicate carries refuses the start, naming the ones that are wired, and phr or phrh on a predicate that is not their meaning is refused too: OIDC Core §2 forbids using a registered name in another sense. What the discovery document announces in acr_values_supported is the classes of this policy the tenant can actually prove.

docs.title: The floor of its logins
docs.text:
A tenant may require more of every login than a single factor, and name the predicate every login of its people has to satisfy:

bin/console beffroi:tenant:login-floor phishing_resistant

A floor asks for more, never for something else. It is a predicate, and a predicate only ever holds on more proofs, so it can say "a passkey at least" and cannot say "a password and nothing else": the switch to do it wrong is not expressible. A tenant that names no floor keeps single_factor, which every login satisfies.

What the floor forbids leaves the model. The command asks before it runs, then forgets every credential of the tenant that proves nothing the floor reads, its secret and its row: under phishing_resistant, every password, one-time code and backup code goes, and nothing dormant is left to leak. The act stays in the journal of each person, a credential revoked earlier stays where it was, and lowering the floor afterwards gives nobody back what was forgotten.

Everything reads it.

  • The core refuses a login under the floor wherever a login ends, so no second copy of the rule can drift. A password the floor reads nothing of is refused before anybody is named, at the cost of nothing.
  • The login page offers only the logins the tenant admits: a tenant that signs its people in by passkey shows no password field and no username, the passkey naming its own user.
  • A step-up offers no kind of credential the floor forbids, and the page of the second factor offers an enrolment only where a code is admitted.
  • The length a password has to reach follows it: fifteen characters where a password signs somebody in alone, eight where a second factor goes with it (NIST SP 800-63B §3.1.1.2). A password already stored is left as it is, since a hash says nothing of the length behind it.
  • A login through an upstream identity provider is held to it as well.

A person created after the floor was raised has nothing to sign in with yet. An enrolment ticket gives them their first passkey without a password ever existing.

docs.title: The domains it federates
docs.text: A tenant whose SAML service provider declares upstream identity providers federates their domains: its people of those domains sign in at their organisation's identity provider and through nothing else, and its login page asks for the address first.

docs.title: Users
docs.text: title: Users description: A person of a tenant: the username, the subject clients know them by, the claims of their profile, and the source that created them.

docs.title: Users
docs.text: A user belongs to a tenant, is named by a username unique within it, and is known to clients by a subject identifier that never changes, even when the username or the address does. The standard claims of OIDC Core §5.1 are held beside the identity, each one a field of its own in the model rather than an entry in a bag of strings, and the person names the source that created them. Their credentials, their linked identities and their group memberships hang off the user.

docs.title: What a user holds
docs.text:
Field What it holds Subject The sub of OIDC Core §2: 1 to 255 printable ASCII characters, no space. Unique within the tenant, never changed and never given to anybody else Username What the person types to name themselves: 1 to 255 bytes once the whitespace around it is trimmed, unique within the tenant and matched exactly, case included Email address Optional, a valid address, with a flag that says whether it was verified. An absent address cannot be verified Phone number Optional, with a flag of its own that says whether it was verified Address The structured claim of OIDC Core §5.1.1. An address with no member is no address, and is not held Profile The thirteen other claims of OIDC Core §5.1, below Source Local, or the upstream provider that created the person and the claims it holds of them Dates When the record was created, when it last changed, and when the account was disabled, if it was

The subject stays readable in the database, a stable pseudonym that names a person without saying anything about them; every other field of the person that says something about them is sealed under the data key of the tenant. Personal data says how.

docs.title: The subject clients know them by
docs.text:
The subject is drawn when the user is created, a random UUID (version 4, RFC 9562 §5.4) that says nothing of when the account was opened. An import brings its own instead, so that the clients of the provider it came from find the same person under the same sub:

bin/console beffroi:user:create alice --subject 248289761001

Nothing changes it afterwards: a new username or a new address leaves it as it was. It is the sub a client receives, unless that client is registered for a pairwise identifier (OIDC Core §8.1), in which case it receives one derived for its sector, and the pairwise subjects page says how. The pages of the account show neither.

docs.title: Creating one
docs.text:
bin/console beffroi:user:create alice --email alice@example.com
Argument or option What it says username What the user types to name themselves, unique in the tenant --email Their address, unverified --email-verified The address was verified by whoever provisions the user --subject The sub of an identity being imported, drawn otherwise

A username or a subject the tenant already holds is refused, and so is an address or a subject that is not well formed. The command prints the username, the subject, the email address with its state, the identifier of the row and the slug of the tenant. It gives the user no credential: a password is beffroi:user:set-password, and a first passkey on a tenant that holds no password is an enrolment ticket.

A person is also created by an upstream identity provider, at their first sign-in through their organisation. That person is named by their address, which is their username, the address is verified, and the source says which provider created them.

docs.title: The claims of the profile
docs.text:
Claim What it holds name, given_name, family_name, middle_name, nickname, preferred_username Names profile, picture, website Three URLs gender A free string, OIDC Core §5.1 naming two values and allowing others birthdate YYYY-MM-DD, or YYYY alone, 0000 standing for a year nobody knows. A value of another shape is refused, wherever it comes from; the shape is what is checked, four digits and two pairs of two, and not whether that month and that day exist zoneinfo The clock of the person, a name of the zoneinfo database locale The language the person reads email, email_verified The address and its flag phone_number, phone_number_verified The number and its flag address The six members of OIDC Core §5.1.1: formatted, street_address, locality, region, postal_code, country

A claim that is not set is absent. The provider holds nothing under that name, and a client is never sent the claim with a null value: it is sent no claim at all. A flag goes with its value, so email_verified is sent only beside an address and phone_number_verified only beside a number, and an address with no member is no address. updated_at, the instant the record last changed, always has a value. Which claims a client receives, by scope or by name, is scopes and claims.

docs.title: Describing a user from the console
docs.text:
bin/console beffroi:user:profile alice --given-name Alice --family-name Liddell --locale fr-FR

It writes the whole profile. What the command does not say is cleared, so a run says every claim the person is to keep. A run that says nothing is refused rather than taken for a request to clear everything, and a value left empty says nothing. The command prints the name, the given name, the family name, the phone number and the postal address it wrote; reading a user without writing is beffroi:user:show.

Claim Option name, given_name, family_name, middle_name --name, --given-name, --family-name, --middle-name nickname, preferred_username --nickname, --preferred-username profile, picture, website --profile-url, --picture, --website (--profile is an option of the console itself) gender, birthdate, zoneinfo, locale --gender, --birthdate, --zoneinfo, --locale phone_number, phone_number_verified --phone-number, --phone-number-verified address --address for formatted, --street-address, --locality, --region, --postal-code, --country

The email address is not among them: it is given when the user is created, and rewritten afterwards only by the upstream provider that created the person. No command renames a user either.

docs.title: What a person says of themselves
docs.text:
A person changes, on the page of their account, the claims their tenant opens in tenant.self_served_claims, and no other: a tenant that opens none serves a page that only reads. Fourteen claims can be opened: name, given_name, family_name, middle_name, nickname, preferred_username, birthdate, gender, locale, zoneinfo, profile, picture, website and phone_number, and a name none of them answers refuses the start. The rule is applied by the use case that writes, for every caller, and not only by the page that shows the form.

  • A closed set is closed on the server. Described by the person, zoneinfo takes a name of the zoneinfo database this PHP carries and locale one of the locales its ICU data holds, written as a BCP 47 tag, and anything else is refused; a PHP whose ICU holds no data closes no set for locale. beffroi:user:profile holds neither claim to these sets.
  • A new number is not a verified one. A person who writes a telephone number takes back its verification, since what was proved was proved of the number that is gone.
  • What it said before is kept. Each change writes what the claim said and what it says now, sealed, kept for beffroi.history.retention days, 180 by default, and read at /account/profile/changes. The act, person.described_themselves, goes to the journal of the person, which keeps the act and never the value. Saying again what a claim already says writes the act and no change.

Choosing a language on a page writes the locale claim of a signed-in person, and that claim alone.

docs.title: The source that created a person
docs.text:
A person names the source that created them. Local, for a person the console, a fixture or an import created; or an upstream provider, for a person created at their first sign-in through their organisation, with the claims of their profile that provider fills.

What a source holds, a manual description does not change. beffroi:user:profile refuses a held claim said otherwise, naming the provider, before anything is written; it keeps a held claim it is not told about rather than clearing it, and it accepts one said with the value it already has, so a provisioning script can run again. The page of the account offers the person no field for a held claim, and the use case behind it refuses one posted by hand. A choice of language on a page leaves a held locale as the provider wrote it.

What the provider stops saying is released. At every sign-in through it, the source holds the address, the telephone number when the provider said one, and those of the claims it fills that it said at that sign-in, and nothing else: a claim it no longer says is left with the value it wrote last, and from then on the person, or the console, may change it.

The username follows the address. A person a provider created is named by their address, and when the provider sends another one, the username becomes that address in the same unit as the rest of the sign-in.

beffroi:user:show prints the source beside the identity: local, or the name of the provider followed by the claims it holds. The source is sealed with the rest of the person, since the provider that created somebody says which organisation they are of.

docs.title: Reading a user
docs.text:
bin/console beffroi:user:show alice

It prints the username, the subject, whether the account is enabled, when it was created, the email address with its state and the source, then the name, the given name, the family name, the phone number and the postal address. Below them, one line per credential with its kind, identifier, name and dates, revoked ones included, and one line per group with the source of the membership and the date it was added. It writes nothing. The console commands list what else reads a person: beffroi:user:sessions, beffroi:user:journal and beffroi:user:applications.

docs.title: A disabled user
docs.text:
An account carries the date it was disabled, and a disabled person is refused at these places:

  • every login, by password, by passkey or by code, after the credential was checked, so that the refusal costs what a wrong credential costs and says nothing of the state of the account;
  • a sign-in through an upstream provider, before anything the provider said is written;
  • an enrolment ticket, which is not issued for them and no longer opens anything once they are;
  • an assertion of a trusted issuer at the token endpoint (RFC 7523 §3) that names them;
  • an access token that names them, at UserInfo, at introspection, and presented to the token exchange (RFC 8693).

Nothing else reads the state of the account: a session already open goes on serving the browser that holds it, and a refresh token goes on being exchanged at the token endpoint. beffroi:user:show says disabled since and the date. No command or page of the bundle disables or enables an account.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text: A person holds credentials, not a password: a password, passkeys and a TOTP with its backup codes can exist at the same time. Each kind is a class of its own, which names itself and declares what it can do by the interfaces it implements, so a credential that can be revoked and one that completes a password are told apart by their type and never by a match on a string.

docs.title: The kinds
docs.text:
Kind Per person Proves Taken out of use Page password One pwd Replaced, never revoked, or forgotten by the floor of the tenant Passwords passkey Several hwk or swk, and user Revoked, or forgotten by the floor of the tenant Passkeys totp One active otp, a code or a backup code alike Revoked, or forgotten by the floor of the tenant TOTP

Backup codes are not a kind: they are held by the TOTP credential they stand in for, ten of them, and a renewal replaces the set.

Every credential holds its identifier, the person and the tenant it belongs to, when it was created and when it was last used, and each kind keeps what makes it that kind in a table of its own: a hash for a password, a public key and its counters for a passkey, a sealed secret and hashed codes for a TOTP. The provider holds nothing a credential could be presented with: a hash does not open, a passkey's private key never leaves the authenticator, and the secret of a TOTP is an envelope only the key management service of the tenant opens.

docs.title: What a kind declares
docs.text:
Interface What it says Kinds ProvingCredentialInterface What one authentication with it may prove, as amr values (RFC 8176 §2), nothing for a revoked one password, passkey, totp RevocableCredentialInterface It can be taken out of use and keep its row passkey, totp SecondFactorCredentialInterface It completes a password rather than replacing it: while one is active, a password alone signs nobody in totp NameableCredentialInterface Its holder names it, and renames it passkey ExternallyIdentifiedCredentialInterface A party presents it by an identifier of its own before anything is verified, unique in the tenant passkey, by its credential ID

What a person can still prove, and so which class a step-up may reach for them, is read credential by credential from ProvingCredentialInterface, never from a kind.

docs.title: What the floor of the tenant admits
docs.text:
The floor of the logins of a tenant admits a credential when it reads at least one of the methods that credential proves. A credential it does not admit is not offered at the login, cannot be enrolled, and is forgotten, row and secret, when the floor is raised.

Floor Password Passkey TOTP and backup codes single_factor Admitted Admitted Admitted two_factors Admitted Admitted Admitted phishing_resistant Not admitted Admitted Not admitted phishing_resistant_hardware Not admitted A passkey bound to its authenticator only Not admitted

A person whose address is of a domain an upstream identity provider answers for is posed no local credential at all, whatever the floor, and a credential they held before their domain was federated signs them in no more.

docs.title: Revoked and forgotten
docs.text:
A revoked credential keeps its row. It never authenticates again, it stays listed with the date it was revoked in beffroi:user:show and in the archive of the person, and a revoked passkey on the page of the passkeys too, where a revoked TOTP leaves the page of the second factor. The first revocation wins: revoking it again changes nothing and announces nothing. A person revokes their own on the pages of their account, and an operator any of them:

bin/console beffroi:user:revoke-credential alice 0199f1c2-7b3a-7c4d-9e5f-1a2b3c4d5e6f

The identifier is the one beffroi:user:show lists. A password is refused there, a password being replaced and never revoked. What happens to the sessions a credential opened is the caller's: revoking a passkey or a TOTP leaves them as they are.

A forgotten credential keeps nothing. Raising the floor of a tenant forgets every credential the floor does not admit, its row and its secret, and a credential revoked earlier, which proves nothing any more, is left where it was. The act, credential.forgotten, stays in the journal of the person, and it is the only trace left.

docs.title: Where a person reads them
docs.text: The pages of the account show the password with the date its hash was last written, which a rehash moves as a new password does, each passkey with its name, its dates and its state, and the authenticator application with its dates and the number of backup codes left. The archive a person asks for lists every credential with its kind, its identifier, its name, its credential ID when it has one, and its dates, and never a hash, a secret or a public key.

docs.title: Adding a kind
docs.text: A kind is a class that extends Credential, or RevocableCredential when it can be revoked, names itself in kind() and implements the interfaces of what it can do, with a table of its own in the Doctrine mapping: the store reads the kinds from the entities mapped under Credential and names none of them. For it to sign anybody in, the firewall needs a login that proves it, a class tagged beffroi.login, which security describes.

docs.title: Backup codes
docs.text: Backup codes are what a person types on the code page when their authenticator application is out of reach. They are not a credential of their own: the TOTP holds them, ten of them, and they prove what a code of the application proves, otp. Each one is accepted once, stored as a hash, and shown once, on the page that drew it.

docs.title: What a code is
docs.text:
Property Value Length Ten characters, written in two groups of five joined by a hyphen Alphabet The alphabet of RFC 4648 §6, the capital letters and the digits 2 to 7 Entropy Fifty bits: one byte drawn from the randomness of the deployment per character, its low five bits picking one of the thirty-two At rest A hash, made by the password hasher as a password is, argon2id, and the instant it was spent

What the person types is compared in capitals, with the spaces and the hyphens taken out, so a code copied with its hyphen, typed without it or in lower case is the same code.

docs.title: Shown once
docs.text: A set is drawn when the TOTP is set up, and each time the person asks for another. Each time, the codes are the response to the form that asked, one numbered list with a button that copies it where the browser lets the page write to the clipboard, and they are stored hashed: nothing shows them again, the pages of the account included. Drawing them at the set-up costs no hash until the first code of the application has confirmed it, so an enrolment abandoned leaves nothing.

docs.title: Spending one
docs.text:
On the code page, anything other than six digits is read as a backup code. It is held to the limit of the codes of the application, five per person in a sliding window of one minute, and it is verified against every unspent code of the set without stopping at the first that matches, the first that matched being the one spent. A code spent is refused afterwards, as a code nobody issued is, and the page says that a backup code was refused and works only once.

A code accepted writes the act backup_code.used to the journal of the person, not totp.used: what the two prove is the same, what they say of the account is not, a spent code being one the person no longer has.

docs.title: Drawing another set
docs.text:
On the page of the second factor, a person who holds a TOTP draws another set with a proof made in the last five minutes. The ten new codes replace the whole set at that instant: the ones they had stop working, spent or not, which is what somebody who lost their list needs. It is not an enrolment: the application and what it proves are untouched, nothing is scanned again and no code is asked for. The act backup_codes.renewed goes to the journal of the person and says when, which is what somebody reading an old list on paper needs to know.

No set is drawn for a revoked TOTP, and none for a person of a domain an upstream identity provider answers for.

docs.title: When the last one is used
docs.text: Nothing else happens: the TOTP stays active, the application goes on signing the person in, and the page of the second factor counts what is left, down to No backup code left. A person who reaches it draws another set there. Removing the application on that page, revoking the TOTP from the console or raising the floor of the tenant to one that reads no otp takes every code of the set with it.

docs.title: Passkeys
docs.text:
A passkey is a discoverable WebAuthn credential (W3C Web Authentication Level 3), enrolled from the pages of the account or from an enrolment ticket, and used on its own, with no password in the way. A person holds as many as they enrol, each with a name they gave it. The provider holds the public key, the counters and the flags of a passkey, and never anything it could sign with: the private key does not leave the authenticator.

A passkey proves the possession of a key, and it is what lets a client ask for a phishing-resistant authentication: under the default policy of a tenant, a session a passkey opened answers phr, or phrh for a passkey bound to its authenticator (the classes it answers with).

docs.title: The relying party
docs.text: Parameter Value Relying party identifier The host of the issuer (WebAuthn Level 3 §5.4.2) Origin accepted The origin of the issuer, scheme and port included, so plain HTTP on a loopback host only, as for the issuer Algorithms ES256 and RS256, COSE -7 and -257 (RFC 9053 §2.1, RFC 8812 §2), in that order of preference Challenge 32 random bytes, drawn for each ceremony (§13.4.3 asks 16 at the least) Resident key Required: a passkey is a discoverable credential (§5.4.6) User verification Preferred and never required, so that a security key with no PIN enrols and signs in Attestation None asked (§5.4.7)

docs.title: Enrolling one
docs.text:
On the page of their passkeys, /account/passkeys, a person adds one in a click: the page asks for creation options, the browser creates the passkey, and the page posts it back, named New passkey in the language of the page, a name they correct in its line afterwards. The options are kept in the session of that browser until the passkey comes back, and the page asks for a proof made in the last five minutes before it lets a passkey be added.

  • The user is named by a handle and not by an identifier. The user handle of §5.4.3 is 64 random bytes, drawn for the first passkey of a person and shared by all of their passkeys, never the subject and never the address (§14.6.1). The user entity carries the username as its name, and the name claim, or the username, as what the authenticator shows.
  • Every passkey the person holds is excluded, revoked or not, so an authenticator does not enrol twice.
  • What comes back is checked against the options: the challenge, the origin and the relying party, then the record. A credential ID the tenant already holds is refused (§7.1, step 26), so are options drawn for another person, a record without its backup flags and a credential of another type than public-key.
  • An attestation an authenticator sends anyway is verified, in the formats packed, fido-u2f, android-key, tpm and apple. none is what is asked, and any other format is a refusal and never a pass. The attestation is not kept, and no policy reads it afterwards.
  • The floor of the tenant is asked once the passkey is known. What a passkey proves is read from the flags of its creation, so a tenant whose floor is phishing_resistant_hardware refuses a synced passkey once the ceremony has answered, and admits one bound to its authenticator.

A passkey enrolled writes the act credential.enrolled to the journal of the person.

docs.title: Signing in with one
docs.text:
The login page asks the browser for a discoverable credential: no username and no list of allowed passkeys, so the page says nothing of who holds one. The options are drawn for that browser and kept in its session until the assertion comes back.

The assertion is verified against the passkey of the tenant its credential ID names, the signature first. Then, so that a refusal costs what a wrong signature costs, the provider refuses a passkey of another tenant, an assertion whose backup eligibility is not the one of the enrolment, a revoked passkey, a person of a federated domain and a disabled person.

What the assertion proves When hwk Always, for a passkey bound to its authenticator swk Always, for a synced passkey user The authenticator tested the presence of the user, the UP flag of its authenticator data (§6.1) mfa The authenticator verified the user, with a PIN or a biometric it does not name, the UV flag (§6.1)

Under a floor of two_factors, a passkey proves two factors only when the authenticator verified the user: a security key without a PIN proves the possession of a key, one factor, and that login is refused.

The counters are read, not trusted. The sign count and the backup state of the assertion replace the stored ones (§7.2, step 26). When either count is not zero, a count that did not grow is told, by the event passkey.used that announces the login, and not refused, a synced passkey keeping its count at zero.

docs.title: Synced or bound
docs.text: Whether a passkey may be synced to other devices is the backup eligibility flag its authenticator set when it was created, which WebAuthn Level 3 §6.1.3 forbids to change. The flag recorded at the enrolment is the one the provider reads for the rest of the life of that passkey: it decides whether a login with it proves swk or hwk, and so, under the default policy, whether the session answers phr or phrh. An assertion that carries another flag is refused, as a revoked passkey is, rather than rewriting the record.

docs.title: A first passkey from a ticket
docs.text:
A person created on a tenant that signs its people in by passkey has nothing to sign in with, and no password to be given. An administrator issues them a ticket instead:

bin/console beffroi:user:enrolment-ticket alice

The command prints a link, /enrol/{ticket}/{value} under the issuer, once, with the instant it opens until, and the row keeps a hash of what the link carries, so a store read by somebody else opens nothing. Whoever issued it hands it over.

  • It opens one enrolment, once. The page asks the browser for a passkey, and the ticket is spent only when the passkey is in the rows: a ceremony that could not finish leaves the person their link.
  • For seventy-two hours, which covers a weekend between the day it is issued and the day somebody starts. What is not used in three days is issued again.
  • One at a time. Issuing a ticket forgets the unspent ones of that person, so a link forgotten in a mailbox stops opening anything the day another is issued. A disabled account gets none.
  • It proves no login. Once the passkey is posed, the browser is sent to the account, which sends it to sign in with that passkey: the session comes from the passkey, never from possession of the link.

A link that opens nothing, an identifier nobody issued, a wrong value, a ticket spent, out of time or of a disabled person, is answered by the same page with the status 404, and each of them costs one hash, so neither the answer nor its time says which it was. An identifier that is not a UUID is no ticket at all, and is answered 404 without a hash. The passkey the ticket poses is enrolled under the same rules as any other, the floor of the tenant included. The page needs a browser that can hold a passkey, and says so to one that cannot. Issuing a ticket is an act of the journal of that person, enrolment_ticket.issued.

docs.title: Renaming and revoking
docs.text:
A person renames a passkey in its line on the page of their passkeys, 1 to 255 characters once the whitespace around it is trimmed, and the event credential.renamed carries the name it had. A revoked passkey is a record of what was: its line offers no field to rename it.

Revoking one is asked for a proof made in the last five minutes, since it is the gesture that can leave somebody with no way in at all. The passkey never authenticates again and its line stays, listed as revoked with its date; the sessions it opened are left as they are. An operator revokes one with beffroi:user:revoke-credential, which credentials describes.

docs.title: Not for the people of an organisation
docs.text: A person whose address is of a domain an upstream identity provider answers for signs in there, and is posed no passkey here: the pages of the account offer them no form, an enrolment, a ticket's included, is refused, and a passkey they held before their domain was federated is refused at the login.

docs.title: The FIDO metadata
docs.text:
The metadata of the FIDO Alliance say, authenticator by authenticator, what it is and whether it was found compromised. Two commands store them under beffroi.webauthn.metadata_storage, var/webauthn of the project by default, and nothing refreshes them on its own:

bin/console beffroi:webauthn:mds-refresh
bin/console beffroi:webauthn:mds-import vendor-statement.json
Command What it stores beffroi:webauthn:mds-refresh The Metadata BLOB of https://mds.fidoalliance.org/, or of each --url given, verified before anything is kept: one signature, made by the first certificate of its chain, the chain leading to the root it pins, GlobalSign Root CA - R3 shipped with the bundle unless --root names another, as a PEM or DER file or an https URL. No redirect is followed, and a refused blob keeps nothing beffroi:webauthn:mds-import Metadata statements a manufacturer publishes for keys the service does not list, or that the FIDO conformance tools ship, one authenticator per file, unsigned and trusted as the file is

What reads them is a ceremony whose options ask for an attestation: an authenticator its status reports name as compromised is refused, a full attestation is checked up to the root its statement names, and an AAGUID the metadata do not know is refused on a full attestation and passed on a self attestation. The enrolment of the provider asks for no attestation, so a deployment that never ran either command enrols passkeys all the same.

docs.title: Passwords
docs.text: A person holds one password at most. It proves pwd (RFC 8176 §2), it is replaced and never revoked, and it is stored as a hash that names the algorithm that produced it, so several algorithms coexist and a hash made by an older one is replaced the next time the person signs in. What a password has to be is a rule of the core and not an option: an option to lower it would be the option to do it wrong.

docs.title: Setting one
docs.text:
An operator writes the password of a person, asked twice on the terminal without being shown:

bin/console beffroi:user:set-password alice

With --password-stdin, the command reads the password from the standard input, up to the end of its first line, for a provisioning script. A password is never an argument nor an option, which a shell would keep in its history, and a command run without a terminal and without --password-stdin is refused. The command replaces a password the person already holds, and ends none of their sessions.

A person replaces their own on the password page of their account: they type the one in use, which is verified, then the one they want, twice. A password that is not the one in use is refused, and so is the one they already hold; every other browser signed in as them is signed out, and the one they asked from stays. Typing the wrong password there costs nothing against the attempts of the login, since only somebody signed in as that person can try.

Both refuse what the rules below refuse, and both refuse to pose a password at all where the floor of the tenant reads nothing a password proves.

docs.title: What a password has to be
docs.text:
A prospective password is refused rather than warned about when it is too short, longer than 4096 bytes, too easy to guess, or held by a list of compromised values. Nothing else is asked of it: it is never refused for holding no digit, no capital or no symbol, the composition rules NIST SP 800-63B §3.1.1.2 asks a verifier not to impose.

How short is too short is two numbers, as NIST SP 800-63B §3.1.1.2 makes it, and the floor of the logins of the tenant decides which one applies:

The floor of the tenant The length a password has to reach single_factor, a password being the whole of a login fifteen characters two_factors, a second factor going with it eight characters

A floor that reads nothing a password proves, phishing_resistant or phishing_resistant_hardware, holds no password at all. The length is counted in characters, each code point one, and the page, the console and the core read the same number. A password already stored is left as it is when the floor moves from one of those two to the other, since a hash says nothing of the length behind it; a floor that holds no password forgets it, row and hash. Both numbers are in the code and not in a configuration.

How easy to guess is an estimate of the search space, counted over the bytes of the password. The pool is the sum of the alphabets the password draws from, ten for the digits, twenty-six for the lower-case letters, twenty-six for the capitals, thirty-three for the other printable characters, thirty-three for the control characters and 128 for the bytes beyond ASCII. Each distinct byte is worth the base-2 logarithm of that pool, and each byte written again the logarithm of the number of distinct ones. Under sixty bits, the password is refused. The length and the estimate are two rules and neither absorbs the other: the estimate is what refuses passwordpassword, or one letter typed sixteen times, which no length catches.

Held by a list of compromised values is the rule §3.1.1.2 puts first, and the next section.

docs.title: The list of compromised passwords
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    passwords:
        breached:
            endpoint: 'https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/'
            timeout: 2.0
Option Default What it decides endpoint empty A range endpoint in the shape of Pwned Passwords, to which the first five hexadecimal characters of the SHA-1 of a password are appended. Empty, nobody is asked timeout 2.0 How long one request to the list may take, in seconds, the whole exchange; 0.1 at the least

The list is asked by range. The first five hexadecimal characters of the SHA-1 of the password go out, the thirty-five that are left are compared locally against every suffix the range answers, the answer is asked padded so that its length says nothing of the range either, and no API key is needed. Nothing of the person who typed it goes with the request.

An unknown is a refusal. A list that does not answer in time, answers a status other than 200, or answers a body that is not a range is not a clean answer: nothing is written, and whoever posed the password is told to pose it again. A password the list counts is refused, and how many times it counts it is not said.

A deployment that names no endpoint asks nobody and poses passwords on the rules of the core alone, no password and no prefix of one ever leaving it. On the page of the account, the list is asked last, after the password in use was verified and found different from the one posed, so a person who mistyped is answered without anything leaving.

docs.title: A password already in use
docs.text:
A password that passed every rule the day it was written turns up in a list published a month later. So, after a login verified the password, a login that goes on to a code included, the SHA-1 of what was typed is handed to a lane that no sign-in waits on, when the deployment names a list and the password was not looked up in the last thirty days. What the lane learns is written on the password: found, with the date, or not found. A list that could not be asked writes nothing: the lane tries again, the password stays due, and the next login asks again.

What the list was found to hold is read on the password page of the account rather than in the one request that noticed it. Every later login that serves no authorization request of OpenID Connect sends the person there before the page that was waiting for it, whatever that login used, a password, a code or a passkey, and the single sign-on of a SAML service provider included, until the password is replaced; once it is, the browser goes on to the page that was waiting. A new password carries no mark. A login that answers an authorization request of OpenID Connect is not diverted.

docs.title: How it is stored
docs.text:
A hash is a document of three members: the name of its algorithm, the encoded hash, and the parameters an imported format keeps apart from the digest. A name nothing wired accounts for makes a row this deployment cannot read, refused where the row is read rather than taken for an algorithm nobody chose.

Algorithm What the bundle does with it argon2id Makes every new hash, with the parameter set of RFC 9106 §4: 64 MiB of memory and four lanes, and the four passes PHP takes by default, one more than that set asks. The hasher refuses parameters below these argon2i, bcrypt Verifies a hash of them, then stores the password again as argon2id at the next successful login pbkdf2-sha256, pbkdf2-sha512 Reads the hash back and names it. No hasher the bundle wires verifies one

A hash that is not of the algorithm and the parameters the hasher makes, another algorithm or other parameters, is replaced at the next successful login, and the act password.rehashed goes to the journal of the person: the password did not change, its hash did.

No command takes a hash: a password is set from its value, and a person who has none is given a passkey by an enrolment ticket or signs in through their organisation. An algorithm is a class implementing PasswordAlgorithmInterface, tagged beffroi.password_algorithm; a hasher of algorithms is a class implementing AlgorithmPasswordHasherInterface, tagged beffroi.password_hasher. The registry hands each hash to the hasher that supports its algorithm, and every new hash to the hasher that supports the first algorithm wired.

docs.title: The order of a login
docs.text:
The login page and the use case of the core play one order, written once:

  1. A tenant whose floor reads nothing a password proves refuses every password, before anybody is named and without paying a hash, the answer depending on nobody's account.
  2. The person is named by the username typed. A username nobody holds is refused.
  3. The attempt is counted against that person: five in a sliding window of one minute, the sixth refused. A username nobody holds is counted nowhere, so a limiter cannot be filled with what an attacker types.
  4. The hash is verified. A refusal reached before this step, an unknown username, too many attempts or a person who holds no password, still pays the verification of a hash the hasher made of a value nobody knows, so the time of the answer does not say whether the account exists.
  5. A disabled account, and a person of a federated domain, are refused after the password, as a wrong password is.
  6. The count of attempts is emptied, the password dated as used and stored again when its hash is not the one the hasher makes, and the act password.used written. A person who holds an active TOTP is then held at the code page rather than signed in: authentication sessions say what follows.

Every refusal of these steps is announced with the request it came from, and the person is told the same thing whatever the reason. A form without its token, or with an empty field, is refused by the login page before any of them: it is not an attempt on an account, and costs the person it names nothing.

docs.title: A person of an organisation
docs.text: A person whose address is of a domain an upstream identity provider answers for has no password here. One is neither set for them, by the console or on the page of their account, nor accepted from them, and a password they held before their domain was federated is refused at the login and can no longer be replaced.

docs.title: Totp
docs.text: title: TOTP description: A time-based one-time password as the second factor of a password, RFC 6238: its parameters, its enrolment, the code page, replay and revocation.

docs.title: TOTP
docs.text: A TOTP (RFC 6238, on the HOTP construction of RFC 4226) is the second factor of a password: a person sets up an authenticator application from the pages of their account, and from then on a password alone signs them in no more, the code page asking for the code the application shows. A person holds one active TOTP, which carries no name, since nothing tells one authenticator application from another, and ten backup codes go with it. What it proves is otp (RFC 8176 §2), a code of the application or a backup code alike.

docs.title: The parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Value Period Thirty seconds (RFC 6238 §5.2) Digits Six Algorithm HMAC-SHA-1 (RFC 6238 §5.1) Secret 160 bits, the length RFC 4226 §4 recommends, drawn from the randomness of the deployment Window The current time step and one on each side (RFC 6238 §5.2)

They are the parameters every authenticator application implements, and none of them is an option. The secret is stored sealed by the key management service of the tenant, an envelope that opens for that tenant and for that use only, and the code is computed in memory when one is checked.

docs.title: Setting one up
docs.text:
On the page of the second factor, /account/two-factor, a person who holds none is offered to set one up, where the floor of the tenant admits a one-time code. The enrolment is the two steps it is:

  1. The secret is handed to the application. The page shows the provisioning URI as a QR code, an SVG the bundle draws and embeds, with no image loaded from anywhere, and the same secret in base32, in groups of four, for an application in front of no camera. The URI is the Key Uri Format: the name of the tenant as the issuer and the username as the account, a colon in either shown as a space.
  2. The first code confirms it. A code the application computes for the current step, or one on each side, creates the credential, its secret sealed and its backup codes hashed, and the step of that code is recorded as accepted, so the code that enrolled the application signs nobody in. The response is the page of the ten backup codes, shown this once.

What the first step drew, the secret, the URI and the backup codes, is kept in the session of that browser for ten minutes, sealed by the key management service of the tenant, and nowhere else: an enrolment abandoned leaves nothing behind, and a code that does not match shows the same QR code again, so the application is not scanned twice. Both steps ask for a proof made in the last five minutes.

A person who holds an active TOTP is refused a second one, and removes the first before setting up another. A tenant whose floor reads no otp, phishing_resistant or phishing_resistant_hardware, sets up none, and nor does a person of a domain an upstream identity provider answers for. A TOTP set up writes the act credential.enrolled to the journal of the person.

docs.title: The code page
docs.text:
A password verified for a person who holds an active TOTP opens nothing: the login is held in the session of the browser for five minutes, and the browser is sent to the code page, /login/code, which asks for the code the application shows, or one of the backup codes.

What was typed is read without the spaces somebody puts between the digits. Six digits are a code of the application; anything else is read as a backup code.

Rule What it refuses The login is held for five minutes A code typed later. The password is asked again, before any code is read Five codes per person in a sliding window of one minute, counted with the user codes they get wrong on the device page The sixth, before the secret is even opened. An attempt is counted once the secret is open, so a key management service that does not answer costs the person nothing A code is accepted once, and the accepted step only moves forward A code already accepted, and the code of an earlier step after a later one was accepted (RFC 6238 §5.2), whatever the drift The window A code of no step of the window A disabled account Its code, after the code was checked, so the refusal costs what a wrong code costs A person of a federated domain Any code, before it is read

A code accepted writes the act totp.used, or backup_code.used for a backup code, and once the form token of the page holds, the session opens on pwd and otp, both dated when the code was accepted. Every refusal of a code is written as a refused login with its reason, and the page never says that reason: it says that the code, or the backup code, was refused, by the shape of what was typed, and too many codes tried is the one reason it names. A post with no code, or from a browser with no login waiting, is refused before any of it and writes nothing. When the key management service does not open the secret, the page answers 503 with a Retry-After of ten seconds, and nothing is counted.

docs.title: Removing it
docs.text: On the page of the second factor, a person removes the application with a proof made in the last five minutes: the TOTP is revoked, its row stays, its backup codes stop working with it, and the password alone signs them in again where the floor of the tenant is single_factor; under two_factors, a password alone is under the floor and opens nothing. The sessions it completed are left as they are. An operator revokes it with beffroi:user:revoke-credential, and raising the floor of the tenant to one that reads no otp forgets it, row and secret.

docs.title: A Symfony relying party
docs.text: The client of reference for this provider is Symfony's own oidc_login authenticator, which Symfony 8.2 adds with an oidc user provider: what Beffroi emits is played against it, with no patch of the authenticator. That makes a Symfony application the shortest path to a sign-in you can watch end to end, and it takes two halves: a client declared on the provider, and a firewall in the application.

docs.title: On the provider
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    clients:
        my-application:
            client_name: 'My application'
            secret: '%env(MY_APPLICATION_SECRET)%'
            redirect_uris: ['https://app.example.com/oidc/callback']
            post_logout_redirect_uris: ['https://app.example.com/']
            token_endpoint_auth_method: client_secret_basic

/oidc/callback is the path oidc_login is called back on unless told otherwise, and / the one it sends a browser to after a logout; both are compared exactly. What the declaration leaves out takes the defaults this application needs: the scopes openid profile email, the authorization code grant and its renewal by a refresh token, access tokens in the at+jwt shape (RFC 9068), and a consent asked of each person the first time. The secret is at least 32 visible ASCII characters, generated.

Your first client

docs.title: In the application
docs.text:
The authenticator needs the HTTP client of Symfony to reach the provider, and web-token/jwt-library to verify what it signed:

composer require symfony/security-bundle symfony/http-client web-token/jwt-library
config/packages/security.yaml
security:
    providers:
        oidc:
            oidc: ~

    firewalls:
        main:
            lazy: true
            oidc_login:
                provider_uri: '%env(OIDC_PROVIDER_URI)%'
                client_id: '%env(OIDC_CLIENT_ID)%'
                client_authentication:
                    client_secret_basic: '%env(OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET)%'
                scope: ['openid', 'profile', 'email']
                refresh_access_token: true
                enable_end_session: true
            logout: true

    access_control:
        - { path: ^/profile, roles: ROLE_USER }

The routes of the firewall, the callback and the logout among them, are declared by one route loader, which the application imports:

config/routes/security.yaml
_security:
    resource: security.route_loader
    type: service
.env.local
OIDC_PROVIDER_URI=https://op.example.com
OIDC_CLIENT_ID=my-application
OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=

OIDC_PROVIDER_URI is the issuer, exactly as the provider announces it: the authenticator reads everything else from its discovery document. A visit to /profile without a session sends the browser to the authorization endpoint of the provider, which signs the person in, asks for their consent the first time, and sends the browser back to /oidc/callback with a code. The user of the firewall is an OidcUser built from the claims UserInfo answers with, holding ROLE_USER.

docs.title: What the two sides agree on without being told
docs.text:
oidc_login Beffroi Sends PKCE with S256 unless told otherwise Refuses an authorization request without it, and never takes plain Accepts an ID token signed with RS256 unless id_token_signature.algorithms names others Signs with RS256, the first algorithm it is wired with, unless the client registers another id_token_signed_response_alg Reads the claims from UserInfo unless user_data_source says otherwise Answers UserInfo with the claims of the scopes the person agreed to (OIDC Core §5.3) Renews the access token with the refresh token, with refresh_access_token Issues a refresh token to a confidential client registered for the refresh token grant, offline_access asked for or not, and to a public one that asks for offline_access Sends the scopes of scope Takes the scopes the client registered and refuses any other with invalid_scope

The refresh token of this client stands. A confidential client is told from a copy of its token by its own authentication, so Beffroi answers a renewal with a new access token and no new refresh token, and the one the application holds works until it expires, thirty days after it was issued by default. Only the refresh token of a public client bound to no key or certificate is rotated at every use (RFC 9700 §4.13.2): its successor comes with the response, and the rotated token presented again revokes its whole family. For such a client, two requests of one browser renewing the same token at once would be that replay; a session handler that locks the session keeps them apart, and the default one of Symfony does.

docs.title: Signing out
docs.text:
enable_end_session is RP-Initiated Logout 1.0: the /logout of the firewall sends the browser to the end session endpoint of the provider, with the ID token as id_token_hint and the absolute URL of post_logout_redirect_path, / unless told otherwise, as post_logout_redirect_uri. The provider ends its session, which revokes what was issued under it, and sends the browser back to that URL. It has to be one of the post_logout_redirect_uris of the client: any other is refused with invalid_request, and no error of that endpoint is a redirection.

The back channel tells the application when the session of the provider ends anywhere else: at the end session endpoint through another client, from the account of the person, by the console. The provider posts a logout token to the client (Back-Channel Logout 1.0 §2.5), and the firewall ends the local session it opened under it.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    clients:
        my-application:
            # ...
            backchannel_logout_uri: 'https://app.example.com/oidc/backchannel-logout'
            backchannel_logout_session_required: true
config/packages/security.yaml
security:
    firewalls:
        main:
            oidc_login:
                # ...
                backchannel_logout:
                    enabled: true
                    cache: cache.app

/oidc/backchannel-logout is the path the route loader declares for it, POST only. The pool cache names remembers the ended sessions, for a day unless lifetime says otherwise, and has to be shared by every server of the application. The logout token is posted by the worker of the provider, so the application answers that URI where the worker can reach it, over HTTPS, or over plain HTTP on a loopback host.

docs.title: A resource server
docs.text:
An access_token firewall checks the access token a request carries, in one of two ways.

An at+jwt, verified where it arrivesAny token, described by the provider config/packages/security.yaml
security:
    firewalls:
        api:
            pattern: ^/api/
            stateless: true
            access_token:
                token_handler:
                    oidc:
                        discovery:
                            base_uri: '%env(OIDC_PROVIDER_URI)%'
                            cache:
                                id: cache.app
                        issuers: ['%env(OIDC_PROVIDER_URI)%']
                        audience: '%env(OIDC_CLIENT_ID)%'
                        enforce_at_jwt_type: true

The discovery document and the keys of the JWK Set it names are kept in the pool discovery.cache.id names, and the token is accepted from the issuers issuers lists. Beffroi signs every access token with RS256, which is what the handler accepts unless told otherwise, and types it at+jwt (RFC 9068 §2.1), which enforce_at_jwt_type holds it to.

The aud of the token is the client it was issued to, unless the client asked for a resource (RFC 8707 §2), in which case it names that resource and the audience of the handler is that identifier. Nothing reaches the provider: a token revoked there is accepted here until it expires, ten minutes after it was issued by default.

config/packages/framework.yaml
framework:
    http_client:
        scoped_clients:
            introspection.client:
                base_uri: '%env(OIDC_INTROSPECTION_URI)%'
                auth_basic: '%env(OIDC_CLIENT_ID)%:%env(OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET)%'
config/packages/security.yaml
security:
    firewalls:
        api:
            pattern: ^/api/
            stateless: true
            access_token:
                token_handler:
                    oauth2:
                        http_client: introspection.client
                        issuer: '%env(OIDC_PROVIDER_URI)%'
                        audience: '%env(OIDC_CLIENT_ID)%'

OIDC_INTROSPECTION_URI is the issuer followed by /introspect. The provider describes a token to the client it was issued to and to nobody else (RFC 7662 §2.2), so the resource server asks with the credentials of that client, and an opaque access token, access_token_format: opaque on the client, is read this way only. A token whose session has ended, or whose grant was taken back, is described as inactive from then on; a cache on the handler keeps an active answer for up to sixty seconds, never past the exp of the token.

Beffroi reads both halves of HTTP Basic credentials form-urlencoded, as RFC 6749 §2.3.1 writes them and as oidc_login sends them, while the scoped client sends auth_basic as it is given. A secret drawn in base64url reads the same both ways; one holding a +, a % or a colon is encoded in the variable the scoped client reads.

Either way, what a route needs is a scope, which Symfony reads from the scope of the token or of the answer:

config/packages/security.yaml
security:
    access_control:
        - { path: ^/api/invoices, roles: 'OAUTH2_SCOPE(invoices.read)' }

A token without it is refused with 403 and the insufficient_scope challenge of RFC 6750 §3.1. A scope that stands for no claim, invoices.read here, exists on the provider once a client registers it in its scope, and the application asks for it in its own.

docs.title: The reference relying party
docs.text:
beffroi-auth/oidc-demo is this page grown into everything the provider serves: a Symfony application on oidc_login, a resource server that checks the same access token several ways, an API Platform API behind the introspection endpoint where every operation names the scope it needs, and a forge where a client is composed option by option out of what the provider announces and registered on the spot, from one that puts the whole authorization request in the URL of a browser to one that pushes it signed, reads a signed response, holds a bound token and opens an encrypted ID token.

From a working copy of the monorepo with oidc-demo checked out beside it, castor demo points it at the development stack and starts it on https://localhost:8002, and castor demo --check signs in as the development user, opens /profile and signs out, from the command line.

docs.title: What it needs
docs.text:
What Why PHP 8.4 or later Database PostgreSQL, through Doctrine ORM A key management service To seal the signing keys and the data keys. For development, a local file-backed client is enough; a deployment uses Vault, AWS KMS or another provider symfony/key-management supports TLS The provider serves nothing useful over plain HTTP, and the specifications require HTTPS on every endpoint
