A message broker is not required to start. The writes the protocol does not need the result of are dispatched asynchronously, to transports that default to the database, doctrine://default, where they wait for a worker that consumes them (messenger:consume). A broker takes their place by its DSN in BEFFROI_MESSENGER_DSN.

Nothing is published yet

The beffroi/* packages are not on Packagist at this point, so the commands below describe the installation of the version this documentation follows rather than one you can run today. The pages are written now so that the first release does not ship undocumented.

docs.title: In a Symfony application
docs.text:
composer require beffroi/symfony-bundle

Without Symfony Flex, register the bundle yourself:

config/bundles.php
return [
    // ...
    Beffroi\Bundle\BeffroiBundle::class => ['all' => true],
];

Then import the routes of the bundle under the path your issuer uses. A provider whose issuer is https://op.example.com imports them at the root:

config/routes/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    resource: '@BeffroiBundle/config/routes.php'
    prefix: /

What the configuration cannot do without is the issuer, and the client of symfony/key-management the private keys are sealed with, which the application declares and the bundle names:

config/packages/key_management.yaml
key_management:
    clients:
        op: 'service://beffroi.kms.op'

services:
    beffroi.kms.op:
        class: Symfony\Component\KeyManagement\EncrypterInterface
        factory: ['@key_management.factory', 'fromString']
        arguments: ['%env(BEFFROI_KMS_DSN)%']
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    tenant:
        issuer: '%env(BEFFROI_ISSUER)%'
    keys:
        kms: op
        key_id: '%env(BEFFROI_KMS_KEY_ID)%'
        storage: '%kernel.project_dir%/var/keys'
    clients: []

A name key_management.clients does not hold fails the build of the container. The firewall of the pages, the session cookie and the rest an application writes are on installing the bundle.

The issuer is the exact string the provider announces as iss and the prefix every endpoint is served under. It is not a cosmetic setting: a client compares it byte by byte, and it never changes for a tenant. Every token the tenant issued names it, so a configuration that names another issuer for the same tenant is refused rather than served: another issuer is another tenant, under another slug.

The whole configuration tree

docs.title: As an application of its own
docs.text:
If you have no application to host it, do not write one. beffroi/op is the Symfony skeleton, the bundle and FrankenPHP already assembled, and it is the deployment the project supports.

The standalone application

docs.title: Then
docs.text:
1. The tenant and its keys, without which nothing can be signed.
  2. Your first client, so something can ask for a token.
  3. A Symfony relying party, to see a sign-in end to end.

docs.title: The tenant and its keys
docs.text: A provider that cannot sign cannot answer. Two things happen before the first request: the tenant of the configuration gets its row, and it gets a key.

docs.title: The schema
docs.text:
The bundle ships its Doctrine migrations, and registers their path with doctrine/doctrine-migrations-bundle when the application has it, which provides the command:

bin/console doctrine:migrations:migrate

docs.title: The tenant
docs.text:
The tenant is declared in the configuration, not created by a command: the issuer is a property of the deployment. The command writes the row that matches what the configuration says.

bin/console beffroi:tenant:synchronize

It writes what the configuration says of the tenant, its name, its look, the claims its people may change of themselves and the classes it answers with, and prints the tenant it synchronised. Run it on every deployment. The issuer is the one thing it never changes: every token a tenant issued names it, so a configuration that gives a tenant another issuer is refused, by this command and by the provider, which serves nothing while its row and its configuration disagree. Another issuer is another tenant, under another slug.

docs.title: Its first keys
docs.text:
bin/console beffroi:keys:generate --algorithm=MESSAGE-SEAL
bin/console beffroi:keys:generate
bin/console beffroi:keys:list

The key the messages are sealed to comes first. Nothing the provider writes to a transport leaves the process in clear, and drawing any other key announces its own staging on a transport: on a tenant that does not hold a MESSAGE-SEAL key yet, that announcement has nothing to be sealed to, and the command fails. Then comes the signing key of the default algorithm, and then a key for each further algorithm the deployment serves, SAML-SIGNING among them for a tenant that speaks SAML.

beffroi:keys:generate draws a key, seals it with the configured key management service and makes it the active key of its algorithm at once. That is the right command for an empty deployment and the wrong one for a live deployment, where beffroi:keys:rotate replaces a key without an outage: it stages the new key, publishes it in the JWK Set immediately, and lets it take over once the staging delay has elapsed, so a client that cached the key set still verifies what it receives.

Check that the keys in use can actually be opened:

bin/console beffroi:keys:list --check

That opens the keys in use, and the ones about to be, with the key management service, and fails on one it cannot open or one that has worked past its age with nothing staged behind it. It is worth running in a deployment pipeline: a key the provider cannot open is an outage at the first token request, not at the next rotation.

A key works for an age, ninety days unless the configuration says otherwise, counted from the moment it became active, and a year for the SAML signing key, whose family has figures of its own. Reaching it is not an outage either: a timed step stages a successor without anybody asking for one. That is what --check reports of an active key, in one of three answers: it has not worked past its age, it has and a successor is staged behind it, or it has and nothing is staged. The last one fails the run, because a planning that has stopped looks exactly like that from outside.

docs.title: A user
docs.text:
bin/console beffroi:user:create alice --email alice@example.com
bin/console beffroi:user:set-password alice

The subject the clients will know Alice by is generated and stable. You pass --subject only when you are importing an identity that already has one somewhere else.

Keys, in full

docs.title: The standalone application
docs.text: title: The standalone application description: beffroi/op on your machine and as a deployment of its own: the development stack, the production image, and the first start in the order it has to happen.

docs.title: The standalone application
docs.text:
beffroi/op is a provider you deploy rather than a provider you assemble: a Symfony skeleton on the bundle, served by FrankenPHP in worker mode, with PostgreSQL for the model and RabbitMQ for the writes the protocol does not wait on. It is the deployment the project supports, and the development stack the conformance plans run against is this application.

It is the apps/op directory of the monorepo, beffroi-auth/beffroi. Its composer.json resolves the beffroi/* packages through path repositories to ../../src/*, so the application is built from a working copy of the monorepo: beffroi-auth/op is a read-only mirror of that one directory, and installs nothing on its own.

docs.title: What it adds to the bundle
docs.text:
The bundle brings, with the packages under it, the protocols, the identity model, the pages and the commands. The application brings what a deployment decides, and nothing else.

What Where it lives The layout of the pages and their stylesheet, Tailwind and DaisyUI, built by the standalone Tailwind binary it pins templates/, assets/styles/app.css The theme a visitor reads the pages in, light, dark or the one of their system, chosen by a form posted to /theme src/Theme/ Its own page of what the provider holds of a person, at /account/profile, which says under the field that was refused why it was src/Controller/, src/Form/ The root of the issuer, /, which sends a browser to the home of the account config/routes/home.yaml The firewall of the interaction pages, with the four logins of the bundle: a password, a passkey, a code, and an upstream SAML identity provider config/packages/security.yaml The headers a deployment answers with, and the name and attributes of the session cookie config/packages/nelmio_security.yaml, nelmio_cors.yaml, framework.yaml The transports of Messenger, on RabbitMQ config/packages/messenger.yaml FrankenPHP and Caddy, with the host that asks for a client certificate frankenphp/ One type of authorization detail, invoice_payment (RFC 9396 §2), the bundle wiring none src/AuthorizationDetails/

docs.title: On your machine
docs.text:
The development stack runs the application in Docker beside PostgreSQL and RabbitMQ. It is driven from the root of the monorepo by Castor, 0.23 or later, and asks the machine for Docker Compose and Composer besides. The two composer install below run on the machine and not in a container, so it also needs PHP 8.4 or later with the extensions the locked packages require, intl, dom, zip and amqp among them.

git clone git@github.com:beffroi-auth/beffroi.git && cd beffroi
composer install && (cd apps/op && composer install)
castor start
castor provision

castor start brings up the provider on https://op.localhost, the host that asks for a client certificate on https://mtls.op.localhost, PostgreSQL and RabbitMQ. On a machine with an mkcert authority, the stack serves a certificate mkcert issues there for its names, which a browser that trusts mkcert accepts; on any other, Caddy issues one from its internal authority. On a stack that names no key management service yet, the worker is created and left stopped, because it refuses to start without one.

castor provision is what a first start needs, in order, and it can be run again at will:

  1. it writes into apps/op/.env.local what is missing there: the key management service, a sodium key generated in place unless --kms file, --kms vault or --kms aws names another backend, the secrets of the clients the stack declares, and the password of the development user;
  2. it plays the migrations;
  3. it writes the row of the tenant with beffroi:tenant:synchronize;
  4. it draws the keys of the tenant, the key messages are sealed to first, or checks with the key management service that the keys already there still open;
  5. it creates the user alice with a verified email address, describes her with the claims of the profile, phone and address scopes, and sets her password;
  6. it issues the client certificate of the stack, on the machine, under var/mtls/;
  7. it starts the worker.

It ends by printing where the discovery document and the JWK Set are, the key management service, the username, password and subject of alice, and the secrets of the clients. https://op.localhost/ sends a browser to the home of the account, which asks it to sign in.

The clients of the stack are declared for the development environment only: the clients of the OpenID conformance suite, and those of the demonstrations of the repository, among them oidc-demo. castor stop takes the stack down, castor logs follows its logs and castor console runs a console command in the container that serves it.

docs.title: As a deployment of its own
docs.text:
The production image is built from the root of the monorepo, which is the build context its Dockerfile expects:

docker build --file apps/op/Dockerfile --target frankenphp_prod .

The build copies apps/op/ of the working copy as it stands, installs the application without its development dependencies, compiles .env for production with composer dump-env prod, builds the stylesheet and compiles the assets. composer dump-env compiles a .env.local too when one is there, and the one the development stack writes holds its key management service, the secrets of its clients and the password of its user: the image is built from a checkout that holds no .env.local. What changes from one machine to the next is then read from the environment when the container starts: the issuer, the database, the broker, the key management service.

The environment the application reads

docs.title: The first start, in order
docs.text:
The order is the one of castor provision, and two of its constraints hold for every deployment: the tenant has a row before it has a key, and its first key is the one messages are sealed to.

  1. The schema. The container that serves HTTP waits for the database and plays the migrations before FrankenPHP starts, every time it starts.

  2. The tenant and its keys, in a container of the image:

    bin/console beffroi:tenant:synchronize
bin/console beffroi:keys:generate --algorithm=MESSAGE-SEAL
bin/console beffroi:keys:generate

    Drawing a key announces it on a transport, and what goes on a transport is sealed to the key the tenant keeps for its messages. That key is therefore the first one: a tenant that does not hold it yet has beffroi:keys:generate fail on the message it cannot seal. The second command draws the key of the default signature algorithm, RS256, which the access tokens are signed with, and the ID tokens of a client that names no other algorithm.

  3. The keys of what this application turns on. Its configuration turns on web push and the SAML identity provider, each with a key of its own:

    bin/console beffroi:keys:generate --algorithm=VAPID
bin/console beffroi:keys:generate --algorithm=SAML-SIGNING

    The discovery document announces every algorithm the bundle is wired with, and a key is drawn for each one a client uses: a client that registers ES256 for what the provider signs for it needs the key of ES256, and one that encrypts to the provider with ECDH-ES+A256KW the key of that algorithm. The development stack draws both.

  4. A person who can sign in:

    bin/console beffroi:user:create alice --email alice@example.com
bin/console beffroi:user:set-password alice

  5. The worker, once the steps above are done: the same image, running bin/console messenger:consume on the schedule and the four lanes of the provider.

The image, the processes and the worker

docs.title: Then
docs.text:
1. The tenant and its keys, for what each of those commands does.
  2. Your first client: outside development the application declares none.
  3. A Symfony relying party, to see a sign-in end to end.

docs.title: Your first client
docs.text: A client is an application the provider answers. It has an identifier, a way of authenticating itself, and the exact addresses it may be sent back to.

docs.title: Declaring one
docs.text:
Clients a deployment knows in advance are declared in the configuration. The key is the client_id.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    clients:
        my-application:
            client_name: 'My application'
            secret: '%env(MY_APPLICATION_SECRET)%'
            redirect_uris: ['https://app.example.com/oidc/callback']
            post_logout_redirect_uris: ['https://app.example.com/']
            token_endpoint_auth_method: client_secret_basic
            scope: 'openid profile email offline_access'
Field What it means client_name What a person reads on the consent page. It is the name of a stranger until you set it secret Never written in the file. An environment variable, and only for a confidential client redirect_uris The addresses the browser may be sent back to, compared exactly. One entry per address, no pattern post_logout_redirect_uris Where the browser may be sent after a logout, compared the same way token_endpoint_auth_method The one method this client authenticates with. A client authenticates with the method it registered and no other, RFC 6749 §2.3.1 scope The ceiling of what this client may ask for. Asking for more is refused, asking for less is normal

docs.title: A public client
docs.text:
A client that cannot keep a secret does not get one: no secret, and token_endpoint_auth_method: none. PKCE is what protects it, and a public client cannot be exempted from it.

beffroi:
    clients:
        my-desktop-application:
            client_name: 'My desktop application'
            redirect_uris: ['http://127.0.0.1/oidc/callback']
            token_endpoint_auth_method: none
            scope: 'openid profile offline_access'

A native application receives its code on the loopback interface, named by its IP literal, 127.0.0.1 or [::1], and never by a name (RFC 8252 §8.3), on whatever port it opened: for a public client, a loopback redirect URI is the one comparison that ignores the port (RFC 8252 §7.3). A custom URI scheme is refused (RFC 8252 §7.1), so a mobile application registers an https URI it claims (RFC 8252 §7.2).

docs.title: What the provider refuses
docs.text:
• A redirect URI that is not in the list, even by one character, even by a trailing slash. The one difference accepted is the port of a loopback URI registered by a public client, above.
  • An authorization request with code_challenge_method=plain, always, and one without code_challenge, unless the client is a confidential one registered with requires_pkce: false. A public client cannot be.
  • A client authenticating with a method other than the one it registered.
  • A scope the client was not granted.

docs.title: Reading what exists
docs.text:
bin/console beffroi:client:list
bin/console beffroi:client:show my-application

The listing covers every client of the tenant, the ones the configuration declared and the ones that registered themselves, each saying which it is. A client that registered itself can be deleted with beffroi:client:delete; one the configuration declares cannot, because the configuration would put it back.

Clients, in full and client authentication

docs.title: Migration
docs.text:
This section holds one page per version that asks something of you, with the changes listed and the way to make them.

There is nothing here yet: no version of Beffroi is released, so no version has to be migrated from. The first page will appear with the first release that changes a public interface.

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text:
• Until 1.0, a minor version may change the public API. What changes is listed here, with the reason and the replacement, before the version is published.
  • A migration page describes the version it belongs to, read from the version selector at the top of the page. It never describes a version you are not reading.
  • A database change ships as a Doctrine migration, never as a sentence telling you to run some SQL.
  • A removal is announced before it happens. A deprecation in one minor version, the removal in the next major one.

docs.title: Coming from another provider
docs.text:
Three things exist, and one does not.

  • The subjects can be kept. beffroi:user:create --subject creates a person under the sub the clients already know them by, so an application that stored it finds the same person.
  • The old provider can stay where it is, upstream. An identity provider that speaks SAML 2.0 is declared upstream of the tenant: the people of its domains sign in there, and each is created here at their first sign-in, with the claims and the groups its declaration maps.
  • A person who exists here can be tied to it by hand, with beffroi:user:link, and then signs in under that link.
  • A password hash cannot be imported. No command takes one: a password is set from its value, and a person without one poses a passkey from an enrolment ticket or signs in through their organisation. Importing the people of a directory as they are is what SCIM will serve.

docs.title: Index
docs.text: title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect description: What beffroi/oidc implements: clients, authorization requests, grants, tokens, discovery, logout.

docs.title: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect
docs.text: beffroi/oidc is the protocol, in pure PHP, on top of the identity core. It knows no HTTP: it reads values, applies the rules of the specifications, and returns what the answer must contain. Turning that into a request and a response is the job of the bundle.

docs.title: The shape of a sign-in
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant B as Browser
    participant C as Client
    participant P as Beffroi
    C->>P: Authorization request (PAR, or in the URL)
    P->>B: Login page, then consent
    B->>P: Credentials, then the answer
    P->>C: Redirect with the code, and iss
    C->>P: Token request, with the PKCE verifier
    P->>C: Access token, ID token, refresh token
    C->>P: UserInfo, with the access token

Every step of that exchange has a page below, and each page cites the section of the specification it describes.

docs.title: What is served
docs.text:
• Clients

    What a client is, where it came from, what it registered, and how it authenticates.

  • Authorization requests

    What is read, what is refused, PKCE, and the iss that goes back in every response.

  • Grants

    Authorization code, refresh token, client credentials, device code, CIBA, token exchange, JWT bearer.

  • Tokens

    Access tokens as at+jwt or as references, ID tokens, refresh tokens, and what is encrypted.

  • Discovery and JWKS

    The document the provider publishes, derived from what is wired rather than from a list kept beside it.

  • Logout

    RP-initiated, front-channel and back-channel, and what each one can promise.

docs.title: Hardening a client can ask for
docs.text: The provider does not need a different deployment to serve a demanding client. The same endpoints accept pushed authorization requests, signed request objects, signed and encrypted responses, and tokens bound to a key with DPoP or to a certificate with mutual TLS. A client that asks for none of it keeps working, and the FAPI 2.0 profiles are what prove the strict end of that range.

docs.title: One source of truth
docs.text: What the provider announces is derived from what it is wired with. The discovery document reads the grants that are tagged, the client authentication methods that are registered and the algorithms that are available, so there is no list to keep in agreement with the code. Enabling a grant announces it; removing it stops announcing it. Discovery and JWKS says what that produces.

docs.title: Authorization details
docs.text: title: Authorization details description: Asking for what a scope cannot say, RFC 9396: the types a deployment wires, how a request is judged, what the person reads and what the token carries.

docs.title: Authorization details
docs.text: A scope says what kind of thing a client may do; authorization_details says what it may do, to what, and how much (RFC 9396 §2): pay this invoice, up to this amount, from this account. It is a JSON array of objects, each naming its type in type, and it is the one thing an authorization carries that a person has to be able to read before agreeing to it, rather than recognise.

docs.title: A type is a class of the deployment
docs.text:
The bundle wires no type. A type says what a client may do to what in the words of one domain, so no type is universal, and a deployment that serves rich authorization requests wires the one its domain needs. A provider wired with none refuses every authorization_details of a request that reads one, and announces nothing. The requests that read one are an authorization request, a pushed request and a token request of the authorization_code or refresh_token grant; every other request ignores it, as it ignores any parameter it does not read.

A type implements Beffroi\Oidc\Domain\AuthorizationDetails\AuthorizationDetailTypeInterface, names itself, and validates its own members: it is the only place that knows what a detail of its kind means. It returns the detail it accepted, building the members it keeps in an order of its own, so that two requests asking for the same thing in a different order produce the same detail, and the parameters the consent page renders it with. A detail it refuses, it refuses by throwing Beffroi\Oidc\Exception\InvalidArgumentException.

src/AuthorizationDetails/AccountAccessType.php
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace App\AuthorizationDetails;

use Beffroi\Oidc\Domain\AuthorizationDetails\AuthorizationDetail;
use Beffroi\Oidc\Domain\AuthorizationDetails\AuthorizationDetailTypeInterface;
use Beffroi\Oidc\Exception\InvalidArgumentException;
use Symfony\Component\DependencyInjection\Attribute\AutoconfigureTag;

#[AutoconfigureTag('beffroi.oidc.authorization_detail_type')]
final readonly class AccountAccessType implements AuthorizationDetailTypeInterface
{
    public function type(): string
    {
        return 'account_access';
    }

    public function of(array $members): AuthorizationDetail
    {
        $account = $members['account'] ?? null;
        if (! is_string($account) || preg_match('/^[A-Za-z0-9-]{1,64}$/D', $account) !== 1) {
            throw new InvalidArgumentException('A detail of the type "account_access" names its account in "account".');
        }
        $actions = $members['actions'] ?? null;
        if (! is_array($actions) || ! array_is_list($actions) || $actions === []) {
            throw new InvalidArgumentException('A detail of the type "account_access" lists its actions in "actions".');
        }
        foreach ($actions as $action) {
            if (! in_array($action, ['read', 'write'], true)) {
                throw new InvalidArgumentException('The actions of a detail of the type "account_access" are read and write.');
            }
        }
        $actions = array_values(array_unique($actions));
        sort($actions);

        return new AuthorizationDetail(
            'account_access',
            ['account' => $account, 'actions' => $actions],
            ['account' => $account, 'actions' => implode(', ', $actions)],
        );
    }
}

The third argument is what the page says of the detail: the parameters of the message authorization_details.<type> of the beffroi domain, which the deployment writes in its own catalogue (translations):

translations/beffroi+intl-icu.en.xlf
<trans-unit id="authorization_details.account_access" resname="authorization_details.account_access">
    <source>authorization_details.account_access</source>
    <target>Account {account}: {actions}</target>
</trans-unit>

What is wired is what a client may register, what a request may name and what the discovery document announces in authorization_details_types_supported (RFC 9396 §10). Two classes that answer for one type are a wiring the provider refuses to read. The standalone application wires one type, invoice_payment, whose detail names an invoice, the actions asked of it among read and pay, the locations where it is used and the most that may be moved.

docs.title: Registering the types
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    clients:
        billing:
            # ...
            authorization_details_types: ['account_access']

authorization_details_types is the closed list of the types a client may ask for, among the ones wired, and a client that registers none asks for none. A name nothing serves is refused when the client is read, the refusal listing the types that are wired. A client that registers itself may send the member as well.

docs.title: Asking
docs.text:
authorization_details is read at the authorization endpoint and at the pushed authorization request endpoint, as the JSON of the array, URL-encoded, and in a request object as the array itself:

[
    {
        "type": "account_access",
        "account": "acct-4711",
        "actions": ["read"]
    }
]

Each element is an object naming its type, of a type the provider serves and the client registered, holding what that type accepts. A malformed array, an element that is not an object, an object that names no type, a member whose name is a number, a type nobody serves, a type the client did not register and a detail its type refuses are one refusal, invalid_authorization_details (RFC 9396 §5), at the redirect URI of an authorization request and in JSON at the pushed request endpoint. The description names neither the type nor what the client registered. A detail asked for twice counts once.

The device authorization endpoint and the backchannel authentication endpoint read no authorization_details, and ignore one they are sent.

docs.title: What the person reads
docs.text: The consent page shows, under the scopes, "the client also asks to be allowed to:" and one line per detail, the message of its type rendered with the parameters the type chose. A consent covers a detail when it holds an identical one, the same type with the same members: RFC 9396 §7 leaves the comparison to whoever defines the type, and equality is the one answer that can never grant more than was agreed to. A request that changes anything in a detail asks again, and a request that asks for no detail is covered by a consent that holds its scopes. A new agreement adds its details to the ones the consent already held. The page of the account that lists the applications a person allowed renders the details the same way.

docs.title: What the token carries
docs.text:
The code carries the details agreed to, and the token endpoint serves them:

  • the token response lists in authorization_details the ones it granted, as each type built them, and leaves the member out when it granted none (RFC 9396 §7);
  • a self-contained access token carries them in its authorization_details claim, and the introspection of an access token, of either shape, describes them in the same member (RFC 9396 §9);
  • a token request may ask, in authorization_details, for a subset of the details of the authorization it spends, for authorization_code and refresh_token: the access token of that response carries the subset, and the refresh token stays bound to every detail agreed to, so a later refresh may ask for one the narrowed token did not carry. A detail the authorization does not carry is invalid_authorization_details.

Consent and access tokens

docs.title: Authorization request
docs.text:
The authorization endpoint, /authorize, reads a request in the query of a GET or in the form of a POST (OIDC Core §3.1.2.1). It finds the client, compares the redirect URI exactly, requires PKCE with S256, and hands what is left to an interaction, which decides whether a person has to be shown a page at all. Every answer that reaches the client, a code or a refusal, carries iss (RFC 9207 §2), and state when the request carried one.

GET /authorize?response_type=code
    &client_id=billing
    &redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fbilling.example.com%2Foidc%2Fcallback
    &scope=openid%20profile%20email
    &state=af0ifjsldkj
    &nonce=n-0S6_WzA2Mj
    &code_challenge=E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM
    &code_challenge_method=S256 HTTP/1.1
Host: op.example.com

docs.title: How a request is read
docs.text:
Every parameter is read the same way at every endpoint of the provider (RFC 6749 §3.1): it is one string, a parameter sent empty is a parameter not sent, a parameter the provider does not read is ignored, and nothing is converted into anything else. A parameter the provider reads, sent twice in a query or in a body of Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded, is refused with invalid_request, with one exception, resource, which RFC 8707 §2 lets a client send once per resource.

Two kinds of request take their parameters from elsewhere than the query or the form:

  • A pushed request names, in request_uri, a reference the client received from the pushed authorization request endpoint. The parameters are the ones it pushed, and every other parameter the browser carried but client_id is dropped.
  • A request object carries the request in a JWT, by value in request or by reference in request_uri (request objects). The parameters are the claims of the object, and every other parameter the browser carried but client_id is dropped as well.

Both are resolved before anything else is read, and what either refuses is refused on a page, since what names the destination is what could not be read.

docs.title: The parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Required What it has to be The error of a refusal client_id Yes A client of the tenant A page redirect_uri Yes One of the redirect URIs of the client, byte for byte A page state No Printable ASCII (RFC 6749 appendix A.5), sent back as it came A page response_type Yes code unsupported_response_type response_mode No A mode the provider answers in (response modes) unsupported_response_mode scope Yes Scope tokens separated by spaces, every one registered by the client, openid among them invalid_scope code_challenge Yes, unless the client is exempted 43 to 128 unreserved characters (RFC 7636 §4.2) invalid_request code_challenge_method With a challenge S256 invalid_request nonce No Text with no control character, carried into the ID token invalid_request prompt No none, login, consent and select_account, separated by spaces, none alone invalid_request max_age No A number of seconds, 0 or more invalid_request login_hint No Text with no control character invalid_request ui_locales No Language tags separated by spaces (RFC 5646) invalid_request acr_values No Values of visible ASCII separated by spaces invalid_request display No page, popup, touch or wap invalid_request id_token_hint No An ID token this provider signed, for this client invalid_request claims No A claims request (OIDC Core §5.5) invalid_request dpop_jkt No The JWK thumbprint of the key the code is reserved for, a SHA-256 in base64url (RFC 9449 §10) invalid_request resource No, repeatable An absolute URI without a fragment, registered by the client invalid_target authorization_details No A JSON array of details of types the client registered invalid_authorization_details

A required parameter that is missing is invalid_request, wherever its line says the refusal goes. What prompt, max_age, login_hint, acr_values and id_token_hint ask of the login is on the page about interactions, and claims on scopes and claims. ui_locales chooses the language of the pages (translations). display is checked and kept, and no page of the bundle reads it.

docs.title: The order of the checks
docs.text:
A request is judged in two stages, because the specification decides when a refusal may go back to the client (RFC 6749 §4.1.2.1, RFC 9700 §4.1): nothing goes back to a redirect URI that has not been checked yet. Each stage stops at its first refusal.

  1. Before anything is read. A form posted from another site without the session cookie is posted again, then the pushed request or the request object is resolved.
  2. The first stage, refused on a page. client_id, and the client it names. A client registered with require_pushed_authorization_requests is refused a request that was not pushed, and one registered with require_signed_request_object a request that no request object carried, both before the redirect URI is read, so that nothing of the request goes back to the browser it came from. Then redirect_uri, state, and the response mode the answer will travel in.
  3. The second stage, refused at the redirect URI. response_type, response_mode, then prompt, max_age, login_hint, ui_locales, acr_values, display, the form of id_token_hint, claims, then scope, the PKCE pair, nonce, dpop_jkt, resource and authorization_details.
  4. The interaction, refused at the redirect URI too. The id_token_hint is verified, an essential acr the provider cannot prove is refused with unmet_authentication_requirements, and the login and the consent the request needs are asked for (interactions).

docs.title: PKCE
docs.text:
A request carries a code_challenge and code_challenge_method=S256, the one method the provider is wired with and announces in code_challenge_methods_supported (RFC 7636 §4.3). plain is wired nowhere and announced nowhere, and a challenge sent without a method is refused rather than read as plain, which is what RFC 7636 §4.3 would make of it.

A confidential client registered with requires_pkce: false may send neither parameter; a challenge it does send is held to the same rules, and the code exchange then verifies it. A public client cannot be registered so. The token endpoint compares BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier)) with the challenge in constant time (authorization code).

docs.title: The redirect URI
docs.text: redirect_uri is required, and compared byte for byte with the redirect URIs the client registered (RFC 6749 §3.1.2.3): a trailing slash, the case of a letter or a parameter of the query make another URI. The one exception is the loopback redirection of a public native client, whose port may differ (RFC 8252 §7.3), which clients describes. The answer goes to the URI the request named, the parameters added to the query it already has, and the token request repeats that URI exactly.

docs.title: The answer
docs.text:
When nothing more is needed, the browser goes back with a code, the state of the request when it carried one, and the iss of the tenant:

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://billing.example.com/oidc/callback?code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA0g2Wn7KcHtdUYvSYn4Ls8&state=af0ifjsldkj&iss=https%3A%2F%2Fop.example.com

That is the query mode, the default for code; the response mode of the request decides how the answer travels, and a refusal travels the same way. The code is worth one exchange and lives 60 seconds by default (tokens.authorization_code_ttl, 600 at most). A token request spends it as soon as it finds it, whatever the checks that follow decide, the client the code was issued to, the redirect URI and the verifier among them (authorization code).

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
On a page. A refusal of the first stage, of a pushed request or of a request object is never sent to the redirect URI: the person reads a page, with status 400, that asks them to start again from the application, and beneath it the error and the error_description for whoever develops the application. The page is the bundle's error.html.twig, which an application overrides like the others (pages).

At the redirect URI. Every other refusal goes back to the client, in the mode of the request, with error, error_description, state and iss:

Error When invalid_request A parameter missing, repeated or malformed, a challenge missing or not S256, an id_token_hint that is not an ID token of this provider for this client invalid_scope A scope the client did not register, a malformed list, a list without openid unsupported_response_type Anything but code unsupported_response_mode A mode the provider does not answer in invalid_target A resource that is not an absolute URI, or that the client did not register invalid_authorization_details A detail of a type the provider does not serve or the client did not register, or that its type refuses login_required, consent_required A page was needed and the request said prompt=none unmet_authentication_requirements An essential acr that cannot be met (OIDC Core §5.5.1.1) access_denied The person refused on the consent page

A request whose person signs in through an upstream identity provider has more answers, all sent back the same way (signing in through an organisation): access_denied when that provider authenticated nobody, with no consent page shown, or login_required when it declined to ask the person under prompt=none; and login_required, or account_selection_required for prompt=select_account, when it did not authenticate the person again as the request asked, whatever its prompt.

docs.title: A request posted from another site
docs.text:
A browser does not send a session cookie set SameSite=Lax with a POST that another site makes it send (RFC 6265bis), so a request a client posts to /authorize arrives without the session the browser holds. Answered as it came, it would ask a signed-in person to sign in again, and the cookie of the new session would replace the one they held.

So a POST of a form to /authorize that the browser says came from another site (Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site), that carries no session cookie, and whose every field a browser posts back unchanged, is answered with a page of the provider's own origin that posts the same form again, pair by pair and in its order. The second post is made from the provider's origin, carries the cookie and is not posted again; it is read, judged and refused exactly as the first would have been. Nothing is decided on that page, and nothing of the request is spent by the first post, a pushed reference included. The page submits itself where scripts run, and where they do not it says "Your browser came from another site without your session. Use the button below to continue.", in the language the ui_locales of the posted form asks for, or else the browser. A browser that sends no Sec-Fetch-Site is answered as it always was, and a request in the query is never touched.

Beside it, no answer of a page of the interaction plane to such a request, a POST or any method but GET and HEAD from another site without the session cookie, carries a new session cookie: the one the session listener would have written is taken off the response.

Interactions, response modes and pushed authorization requests

docs.title: Client authentication
docs.text: A client authenticates with the one method it registered and with no other (RFC 6749 §2.3.1). The method is read wherever the provider has to know which client is calling: the token endpoint, the introspection and revocation endpoints, the pushed authorization request endpoint, the device authorization endpoint and the backchannel authentication endpoint. A request that presents another method than the registered one is refused exactly as a request that presents a wrong secret is.

docs.title: The methods
docs.text:
The bundle wires seven, in this order:

Method What the request carries What is checked What the client registers client_secret_basic Authorization: Basic, the identifier and the secret form-urlencoded and joined by a colon (RFC 6749 §2.3.1, RFC 7617 §2) The secret, against the hash the provider keeps A secret client_secret_post client_id and client_secret in the body (RFC 6749 §2.3.1) The same A secret private_key_jwt client_assertion, a JWT it signed with a key of its own (RFC 7523 §2.2, OIDC Core §9) The signature against the keys the client publishes, then the claims jwks or jwks_uri client_secret_jwt client_assertion, a JWT signed with its secret under HS256 (OIDC Core §9) The MAC with the secret the provider keeps, then the claims A secret tls_client_auth client_id, and a certificate at the TLS handshake (RFC 8705 §2.1) The one value of RFC 8705 §2.1.2 it registered, read out of the certificate One of the five tls_client_auth_* values self_signed_tls_client_auth client_id, and a certificate at the TLS handshake (RFC 8705 §2.2) That the certificate is one the client publishes jwks or jwks_uri none client_id alone (RFC 6749 §2.1) Nothing: the client names itself Nothing

A client that registers no method takes client_secret_basic, the first one wired for a declared client and the default of RFC 7591 §2 for one that registers itself. What the wiring holds is what a client may register and what the discovery document announces, so a method taken out of the wiring is neither accepted nor announced.

Member of the discovery document What it lists token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported, revocation_endpoint_auth_methods_supported The seven methods, in the order above introspection_endpoint_auth_methods_supported The six that authenticate a client: none is refused there (RFC 7662 §2.1) token_endpoint_auth_signing_alg_values_supported and its two siblings What an assertion may be signed with: RS256, PS256, ES256 and EdDSA for private_key_jwt, HS256 for client_secret_jwt

docs.title: A shared secret
docs.text:
client_secret_basic and client_secret_post present the secret itself, and the provider keeps only a hash of it, made by the password hasher of the core and compared by it. A request whose client is unknown, or registered for another method, pays the same verification against a decoy hash, so the time an answer takes says nothing about which clients exist.

client_secret_basic reads a header made of Basic, whatever its case, then spaces or tabs, then one token (RFC 7235 §2.1). A token that does not decode to an identifier and a secret joined by a colon, an empty one included, is invalid_request; a header of another form is not one the method reads. client_secret_post takes the secret from a body that also names the client in client_id, and a client_secret without one is invalid_request.

client_secret_jwt signs an assertion with the secret, so the provider has to hold the secret to compute the same MAC: it keeps the secret itself, sealed in the row of a client that registered itself. That is the cost of the method: a compromised process of the provider holds what computes the MAC as well.

docs.title: An assertion
docs.text:
private_key_jwt and client_secret_jwt carry the same assertion, in the same two parameters:

POST /token HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code&code=...&redirect_uri=...&code_verifier=...
&client_assertion_type=urn%3Aietf%3Aparams%3Aoauth%3Aclient-assertion-type%3Ajwt-bearer
&client_assertion=eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6IjEifQ...

client_assertion_type is urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer and nothing else, and the two parameters come together or not at all. Which of the two methods reads the assertion is decided by its alg: HS256 is client_secret_jwt, an algorithm the provider signs with is private_key_jwt. The signature is verified first, and nothing the assertion says is believed before it is. Then:

Claim What it has to say iss, sub The client_id, both of them. A client_id in the body, when there is one, names the same client aud One value, and only one: the issuer of the tenant. A client registered for the backchannel grant may name the token endpoint or the backchannel authentication endpoint instead, on either host the provider serves them on (CIBA Core §7.1) exp Present, not past, and no further ahead than the lifetime the provider accepts iat Present, and not in the future jti Present, and never seen before for that client: it is remembered until the exp in the beffroi.client_assertions cache pool, which a deployment of several machines points at a store they share

The key is the client's and nobody else's. A kid in the header names one of the keys the client publishes, a header without one is tried against all of them, and a key that names another alg, or a use other than sig, is not tried. jwk, jku and x5c in the header are ignored (RFC 8725 §3.10).

Keys behind a jwks_uri are read and kept. The URL is read with one GET, no redirect followed, any status but 2xx refused, within a time and a size of its own. The set is kept in the beffroi.client_keys cache pool, filed under its URL, and read again when an assertion names a kid the kept set does not hold, at most once per cooldown: a client that rotates its key is followed at once, and one that signs with a key it never published cannot make the provider call it on every request. A set that cannot be read refuses the authentication, and the reason goes to the audit trail.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    client_authentication:
        assertion_max_lifetime: 300
        assertion_leeway: 30
        jwks_timeout: 3.0
        jwks_max_size: 65536
        jwks_ttl: 86400
        jwks_refetch_cooldown: 300
Option Default What it decides assertion_max_lifetime 300 Seconds ahead of the request the exp of an assertion may be (RFC 7523 §3) assertion_leeway 30 Seconds allowed of the clock of a client, both ways jwks_timeout 3.0 Seconds one read of a jwks_uri is given, connection included jwks_max_size 65536 Bytes a jwks_uri may answer before the read stops jwks_ttl 86400 Seconds a set read from a jwks_uri is kept jwks_refetch_cooldown 300 Seconds between two reads of one jwks_uri when an assertion names an unknown kid

The same six options bound the assertions of the issuers a tenant trusts for the JWT bearer grant, and the reads of the sets they publish.

docs.title: A certificate
docs.text:
tls_client_auth and self_signed_tls_client_auth read the same thing, the certificate of the connection, and the client names itself in client_id. The certificate is the one the TLS listener in front of the provider writes in the SSL_CLIENT_CERT server variable, never a header: a request that carries SSL-Client-Cert, X-SSL-Client-Cert, X-Client-Cert or X-Forwarded-Client-Cert is refused with invalid_request. Only the leaf reaches the provider, so the chain, the validity period and the revocation of the certificate are judged by the listener, which is where a deployment that turns tls_client_auth on says which authorities it accepts.

  • tls_client_auth compares one value read out of the certificate with the one the client registered: its subject distinguished name, written as RFC 4514 writes one and normalised when the client is read, so that openssl x509 -noout -subject -nameopt RFC2253 prints a name it can register as it is; or one entry of its subject alternative name, a DNS name compared without regard to case, a URI compared as text, an IP address compared as the octets it stands for, an email address compared as written.
  • self_signed_tls_client_auth authenticates a certificate the client publishes in its JWK Set, as the first entry of the x5c of a key (RFC 7517 §4.7) or by its x5t#S256 (§4.9). The certificate is compared, not the key inside it, so a certificate reissued on the same key is published before it is presented.

Both bind the tokens of the request to the certificate that authenticated it (RFC 8705 §3.1). A certificate presented beside a secret or an assertion authenticates nothing: the listener asked for it, the request did not choose it. Whether it binds the tokens of such a client is what the client registered in tls_client_certificate_bound_access_tokens. Mutual TLS says how a deployment serves the host that asks for a certificate, and what a bound token is then.

docs.title: A public client
docs.text: none is not an authentication, and it is announced as what it is: the client names itself in client_id and proves nothing, which is what a native or a browser application can do. The introspection endpoint refuses it with invalid_client, describing a token only to a client that proves who it is (RFC 7662 §2.1), and a client that registers it is refused client_credentials and requires_pkce: false. What protects a public client is PKCE and its exact redirect URI, never this method.

docs.title: How a request is read, and refused
docs.text:
The request presents one mechanism or it is refused before anything is verified: credentials in the Authorization header and others in the body are two mechanisms (RFC 6749 §2.3), and so are a secret and an assertion. The two certificate methods read one thing and are one mechanism, the registration of the client saying which of them verifies it. An Authorization header no method reads, of another scheme than Basic or not of its form, is refused when nothing else in the request proves the client, a public client naming itself included; beside a credential of the body or a certificate of the connection that proves the client, it is not read.

What the request does Error Status A credential parameter that is not a single string, Basic credentials that do not decode, half of an assertion, another client_assertion_type, an assertion that is no JWT invalid_request 400 Two mechanisms at once invalid_request 400 A client_id in the body that names another client than the credentials invalid_request 400 An Authorization header no method reads, and nothing else that proves the client, or no credential at all invalid_client 401 An unknown client, a method other than the registered one, a wrong secret, an assertion refused or replayed, keys that cannot be read, a certificate that is not the client's invalid_client, described Client authentication failed. 401

Every refusal of the last line reads the same, so an answer does not say whether a client exists or which method it registered; why it was refused goes to the audit trail, with the client and the method, as a ClientAuthenticationFailed event. A 401 carries WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="<issuer>" when the client used the Authorization header, and no challenge otherwise (RFC 6749 §5.2).

A client that authenticates counts one request against its own load budget, load.client, 1200 requests in 60 seconds by default, here and nowhere else, this being the one place its identifier is proven rather than claimed. A public client counts nothing there, the budget of the address it calls from bounding it. A spent budget is answered 429 with a Retry-After.

Clients, DPoP and mutual TLS

docs.title: Clients
docs.text: A client is an application the provider answers, known by its client_id. It holds the addresses a browser may be sent back to, the one method it authenticates with, the scopes and resources it may ask for, and how it wants the documents written for it. A client comes from one of two places: the configuration of the deployment declares it, or it registered itself at the registration endpoint. Both are read by the same reader under the same rules, so the same members mean the same thing wherever they were written; the source decides what a member left out stands for, who may change the client and how it goes away. A registration is held to two rules more, when it is written: the scopes it names are ones its tenant hands out, and a sector_identifier_uri it names is backed by the document behind it (pairwise subjects).

docs.title: Declaring one
docs.text:
Clients a deployment knows in advance are declared under beffroi.clients, keyed by their client_id.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    clients:
        billing:
            client_name: 'Billing'
            logo_uri: 'https://billing.example.com/logo.svg'
            policy_uri: 'https://billing.example.com/privacy'
            redirect_uris: ['https://billing.example.com/oidc/callback']
            post_logout_redirect_uris: ['https://billing.example.com/']
            token_endpoint_auth_method: private_key_jwt
            jwks_uri: 'https://billing.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json'
            scope: 'openid profile email offline_access invoices.read'
            resources: ['https://api.example.com/']

The declarations are read as a whole, the first time the provider reads a client, and one that does not hold together is refused there with the client and the rule it broke, before anything is served under it: bin/console beffroi:client:list reads them, and is the quickest way to see a mistake. The same refusal reaches a client that registers itself, as the 400 of RFC 7591 §3.2.2.

What a member left out means depends on the source. A declaration takes what an application that signs a person in comes for; a client that registers itself takes what RFC 7591 §2 says it gets.

Member Declared and left out Registered and left out grant_types authorization_code and refresh_token authorization_code scope openid profile email openid, or the default set the policy of the tenant names token_endpoint_auth_method The first method wired, client_secret_basic client_secret_basic access_token_format The first shape wired, jwt jwt, a client that registers itself never naming this member subject_type The first kind wired, public The same

A secret is chosen by the deployment for a declared client, and drawn by the provider for a registered one. A declared secret is at least 32 visible ASCII characters (RFC 6749 appendix A.2), a value to generate and put in an environment variable, never in the file. It is hashed with the password hasher of the core the first time the client is looked up in a process, and kept as a hash, except for a client that authenticates with client_secret_jwt: that method computes a MAC with the secret, so the provider keeps the secret itself. A client registers a secret exactly when the method it registered proves one, and a declaration that carries a secret for any other method is refused.

docs.title: What a client registers
docs.text:
Every member below is spelled the same in the configuration and in a registration request, under the name RFC 7591 §2, OIDC Registration §2 or the specification of its feature gives it, the members marked deployment being this provider's own. secret is written in the configuration alone, and software_id, software_version and software_statement in a registration request alone: the configuration has no such option and refuses it. A member this provider does not read is refused rather than ignored, and a value of the wrong kind is refused rather than converted: a string where a list is expected, or "true" where a boolean is.

The members marked deployment are written by whoever declares a client, or by the registration policy of the tenant. They are exceptions to a rule, or privileges, and a client that registers itself never obtains one: one in the body of its registration request is refused with invalid_client_metadata, and a software statement does not grant one either.

docs.title: Who is asking
docs.text: Member What it decides client_name The name the consent page shows. A client that registers none is shown under its client_id logo_uri The image the consent page shows. The browser of the person loads it from the client, with no referrer, and the provider never fetches it policy_uri, tos_uri, client_uri The pages the consent page links to, in that order contacts Ways to reach the people responsible for the client. No page shows them

docs.title: Where a browser goes
docs.text: Member What it decides redirect_uris Where the answer of the authorization endpoint may go, compared byte for byte with the redirect_uri of a request (RFC 6749 §3.1.2.3) post_logout_redirect_uris Where a browser may be sent after a logout, compared the same way initiate_login_uri Where the provider sends a browser to have this client begin a login (OIDC Core §4), from /initiate-login?client_id=.... HTTPS, on a loopback host as anywhere else

docs.title: What it may ask for
docs.text: Member What it decides grant_types The grants it may use at the token endpoint, among those the provider is wired with response_types code, and nothing else. It is not kept, the grants saying the same thing: a registration that names code without the grant that answers with one is refused scope The closed list of scopes it may ask for, space delimited (RFC 6749 §3.3). A scope outside it is invalid_scope resources Deployment. The resources it may ask an access token for (RFC 8707 §2). See resources authorization_details_types The types of authorization detail it may ask for (RFC 9396 §2), among those the provider is wired with. See authorization details

docs.title: How it proves who it is
docs.text: Member What it decides token_endpoint_auth_method The one method it authenticates with, among those the provider is wired with. See client authentication secret Configuration only: the shared secret of a declared client whose method proves one jwks, jwks_uri Its public keys, inline or behind a URL, one or the other and never both. A symmetric key (kty: oct) is refused tls_client_auth_subject_dn, tls_client_auth_san_dns, tls_client_auth_san_uri, tls_client_auth_san_ip, tls_client_auth_san_email What names it in its certificate (RFC 8705 §2.1.2), exactly one of the five, for tls_client_auth and for no other method

docs.title: How its requests are made
docs.text: Member What it decides requires_pkce Deployment. true by default. false is accepted for a confidential client only, which may then send no code_challenge; a challenge it sends is verified all the same require_pushed_authorization_requests Its authorization requests are only read from a pushed request (RFC 9126 §6) require_signed_request_object Its authorization requests are only read from a request object, whose signature is what request_object_signing_alg says, and its backchannel authentication requests only from an object it signed request_object_signing_alg The one algorithm its request objects are signed with, or none for unsigned objects. Left out, any algorithm the provider verifies, and never an unsigned object request_uris The URLs a request object of this client may be read back from, compared byte for byte, fragment included

docs.title: What it receives
docs.text:
Member What it decides access_token_format Deployment. The shape of its access tokens: jwt or opaque. See access tokens require_sender_constrained_tokens Deployment. A token request that proves neither a certificate nor a key is refused with invalid_request rather than answered with bearer tokens tls_client_certificate_bound_access_tokens Its tokens are bound to the certificate of its connection whichever way it authenticated (RFC 8705 §3.4), and a token request that presents none is refused with invalid_request id_token_signed_response_alg The algorithm its ID tokens and logout tokens are signed with. Left out, RS256, the first algorithm wired id_token_encrypted_response_alg, id_token_encrypted_response_enc Its ID tokens encrypted to one of its keys once signed. The two go together, neither has a default userinfo_signed_response_alg Its UserInfo answer as a signed JWT (application/jwt). Left out, plain JSON userinfo_encrypted_response_alg, userinfo_encrypted_response_enc Its UserInfo answer encrypted to one of its keys authorization_signed_response_alg The algorithm of its signed authorization responses. Left out, RS256 authorization_encrypted_response_alg, authorization_encrypted_response_enc Its signed authorization responses encrypted to one of its keys requires_consent Deployment. true by default. false names a first-party application, which no consent page is shown for

What encryption a client may register, and which of its keys a document is addressed to, is on the page about encryption.

docs.title: Who it sees
docs.text: Member What it decides subject_type public or pairwise, the kind of sub it sees for a person (OIDC Core §8) sector_identifier_uri The sector its pairwise identifiers belong to. See pairwise subjects

docs.title: Logout, backchannel authentication and token exchange
docs.text: Member What it decides backchannel_logout_uri, backchannel_logout_session_required Where a logout token is posted, and whether the client reads its sid (Back-Channel Logout 1.0 §2.2). See logout frontchannel_logout_uri, frontchannel_logout_session_required The page loaded in a frame at a logout, and whether it receives iss and sid (Front-Channel Logout 1.0 §2) backchannel_token_delivery_mode poll or ping, for a client of the backchannel flow (CIBA Core §4). No default. See backchannel authentication backchannel_client_notification_endpoint Where the provider calls a ping client back. Required with ping, refused with another mode or with none token_exchange Deployment. For a client of the token exchange grant: subject_token_types, and may_act_for_a_user. See token exchange may_act Deployment. Who may act for the subject of a token issued to this client (RFC 8693 §4.4)

docs.title: What it says of its software
docs.text: Member What it decides software_id, software_version Registration only: what the software the client is an instance of calls itself, and its version (RFC 7591 §2) software_statement Registration only: read by the registration mode that takes one, never as metadata. See dynamic registration

docs.title: The addresses a client registers
docs.text:
Every URL a client registers, whatever the provider does with it, is held to one rule: an absolute URI, with no fragment and no credentials, whose host is a name of letters, digits, hyphens and dots or an IP address, in HTTPS. Plain HTTP is accepted on a loopback host only, localhost, a name under .localhost, an address of 127.0.0.0/8 or [::1]. A custom scheme is not an address the provider sends anybody to, and is refused.

Three members depart from it, each for its own reason. initiate_login_uri is HTTPS on a loopback host too, OIDC Registration §2 giving it no exception. request_uris may carry a fragment, which OIDC Core §6.2 gives a meaning, and the URL is read back without it. resources are identifiers and never fetched, so a URN is a resource as an HTTPS URL is (RFC 8707 §2). tls_client_auth_san_uri is no address either: it is the text a certificate is compared with, and only has to be non-empty.

A redirect URI matches byte for byte, a trailing slash or a letter in another case included, and a registered query is part of what matches. The one exception is the loopback redirection of a native application (RFC 8252 §7.3), and it belongs to a public client only: a redirect URI registered in plain HTTP on 127.0.0.1 or [::1] matches the same URI on any port, the path and the query compared byte for byte. A public client therefore registers the loopback interface by its address and never by a name: plain HTTP anywhere but on 127.0.0.1 and [::1] is refused for it (RFC 8252 §8.3). A confidential client keeps the port it registered. The same holds for post_logout_redirect_uris.

docs.title: What a registration has to hold
docs.text:
Each rule below is checked where the client is read, so a declaration that breaks one is refused when the declarations are read, and a registration that breaks one is refused with invalid_client_metadata. A registration is refused with invalid_redirect_uri instead for a value of redirect_uris or post_logout_redirect_uris that the rule of every address refuses, and for redirect URIs its grants do not call for, or call for and lack; the rule a public client's loopback addresses follow answers invalid_client_metadata, as every other one does.

  • The client_id is printable ASCII with no space at either end (RFC 6749 appendix A.1). A client of client_credentials or of the token exchange is named where a subject is expected, the sub of its own tokens or the act of an exchanged one, so its identifier is 1 to 255 visible ASCII characters with no space at all (OIDC Core §2).
  • The client_name is not empty, and neither is any of the contacts.
  • A method that proves a shared secret has one, and any other method has none.
  • jwks and jwks_uri are never both there. One of them is, for private_key_jwt, self_signed_tls_client_auth, a request_object_signing_alg naming an algorithm, and any encrypted response. An inline jwks holds a key every encryption the client registered can be addressed to.
  • tls_client_auth comes with exactly one of the five certificate values, and every other method with none.
  • The client is registered for at least one grant. refresh_token comes with a grant that issues one: authorization_code, the device code or the backchannel grant.
  • A client of authorization_code registers at least one redirect URI, and a client of no grant that sends a browser back registers none, and no response_types either.
  • client_credentials is refused to a public client, which proves nothing.
  • The token exchange grant and the token_exchange member come together or not at all, and the token types it names are ones the provider reads.
  • requires_pkce: false is refused to a public client.
  • backchannel_logout_session_required needs a backchannel_logout_uri, and frontchannel_logout_session_required a frontchannel_logout_uri.
  • An encryption names its alg and its enc together. OIDC Registration §2 would default the enc to A128CBC-HS256, which the provider is not wired with, so it takes no default.
  • A pairwise client has a sector: its sector_identifier_uri, its redirect URIs all on one host, or, when it registers no redirect URI, its jwks_uri.
  • Every name is one the provider is wired with: a grant, a method, an algorithm, an access token shape, a delivery mode, a kind of subject, a type of authorization detail. The refusal lists the wired names.

docs.title: Public and confidential
docs.text: A client is public when it registered token_endpoint_auth_method: none: it names itself and proves nothing, as a native or a browser application cannot keep a secret. Everything else is confidential. What protects the code of a public client is PKCE, which is mandatory for it, and the exact redirect URI. Besides the loopback exception above, the difference shows where a rule asks for a client that proves itself: requires_pkce: false and client_credentials are refused to a public client at its registration, the introspection endpoint refuses it, and a refresh token reaches it only when it asks for offline_access (refresh tokens).

docs.title: Reading what exists
docs.text:
bin/console beffroi:client:list
bin/console beffroi:client:show billing
bin/console beffroi:client:delete 3x4mpl3Cl13nt1d3nt1f13rDr4wnByTh3Pr0v1d3rXX

beffroi:client:list prints every client of the tenant with its name and its source, configuration or registration, and for a registered client when it registered and when it was last used. beffroi:client:show prints the same for one client, and for a registered one the members it registered and the ones the registration policy of the tenant wrote on it; for a declared one it points at the configuration, which is the whole of what it is. beffroi:client:delete deletes a client that registered itself, and refuses a declared one, which goes away with its block in the configuration.

A registered client whose stored registration the reader refuses, a row naming a member this version does not read or breaking a rule it holds, is answered as no client at all, and the reason is written to the log as an error.

Client authentication and dynamic registration

docs.title: Consent
docs.text: A consent is what a person agreed to let one client obtain about them: a set of scopes, and the authorization details the client asked for beyond them. It is recorded once per person and client, and a request that asks for no more than it covers is answered without asking again. A person reads their consents and takes any of them back from the pages of their account, and an operator does the same at the console.

docs.title: When a person is asked
docs.text:
The question is asked during an interaction, once the person is signed in:

  • A client registered with requires_consent: false is never asked about, prompt=consent included. It is the first-party application of the deployment, and only a declaration names one: a client that registers itself never obtains the member.
  • Any other client is asked about when no consent of this person is in force for it, when the one in force does not cover every scope of the request, or every authorization detail of it, and whenever the request says prompt=consent.
  • With prompt=none, a request that would have shown the page is answered consent_required at the redirect URI instead (OIDC Core §3.1.2.6).

A consent covers a scope when it holds it, and an authorization detail when it holds an identical one, the same type with the same members: a request that changes anything in a detail asks again. A request that asks for no detail is covered by any consent that holds its scopes.

docs.title: The page
docs.text:
The consent page, /consent, says who is asking and what for, in the language of the interaction:

What it shows Where it comes from "Authorize the client", as its title The client_name of the client, or its client_id when it registered none Its logo The logo_uri of the client, loaded by the browser of the person with no referrer. The provider never fetches it "You are signed in as username." The account of the session Every scope of the request openid, profile, email, address, phone and offline_access in words, any other scope by its name What the request asks for beyond its scopes One line per authorization detail, in the words its type gives Links to the client's pages policy_uri, tos_uri and client_uri, in that order, each only when registered, opened in a new tab with no referrer Two buttons, Allow and Deny

The page lists every scope the request asks for, those already agreed to included, and every authorization detail. A consent records scopes and details, and the claims a request names one by one in its claims parameter are not listed on the page: they are served whatever the consent holds (scopes and claims). Its Content-Security-Policy is the one of the deployment, completed with the origin of the client's logo and the one of the tenant's logo in img-src, and the origin of the redirect URI in form-action, where the answer is carried after an Allow: nothing a client registers makes the page load anything else. The template is consent.html.twig, which an application overrides like every page of the bundle (pages).

Allow records the consent and the interaction goes on, to the code. Deny ends the interaction, and the client receives access_denied at its redirect URI (RFC 6749 §4.1.2.1). A form posted without the token the page was rendered with is refused with a 403 page and decides nothing.

docs.title: What a consent holds
docs.text:
Field What it is The person and the client One consent in force per pair The scopes Every scope agreed to The authorization details Every detail agreed to, each once, none when nothing beyond the scopes was asked When it was given, and when it was taken back A consent taken back stays as a record, and asks again

A new agreement extends, and never takes back. When a person agrees to a request while a consent is in force, the provider records a new consent holding the scopes and the details of both, each once, and takes the previous one back at that instant. A request that asked for less does not narrow what was agreed before, and a request that asked for no detail keeps the details already held. A ConsentGranted event names the new consent and the one it replaced.

The same consent is recorded whichever page asked for it: the consent page of an authorization request, the page where a person approves the code of a device, and the page where they approve a backchannel request. The last two add scopes alone, those flows reading no authorization detail.

docs.title: Taking it back
docs.text:
A person takes a consent back from the page of their account that lists the applications they allowed; an operator does it at the console:

bin/console beffroi:user:applications alice
bin/console beffroi:user:revoke-consent alice billing

beffroi:user:applications lists the consents in force of a person, with what each client holds. beffroi:user:revoke-consent takes back the consent a person gave a client, and says so when there was none. Either way the same thing happens, and what was issued under the consent goes with it:

  • the consent is taken back, so the next authorization request of that client asks again;
  • every grant this person left to this client is revoked, an authorization code, a device code they approved and a backchannel request naming them alike, so no access token that descends from one opens UserInfo or is described as active by the introspection endpoint any more;
  • every refresh token the client holds for this person is revoked, so nothing renews;
  • every opaque access token the client holds for this person is removed, and an unknown token is an invalid one (RFC 6750 §3.1).

A self-contained access token in the hands of a resource server that verifies it offline is still worth something until it expires, ten minutes by default (RFC 9068 §4): nothing the provider does reaches it there. Its introspection says it is inactive from the instant the consent is taken back.

A ConsentRevoked event names the consent, the client, the person, and what went with it, by identifier.

The account pages and interactions

docs.title: Discovery and JWKS
docs.text: Two documents describe the provider to whoever is about to talk to it. The discovery document says what the provider serves and where (OIDC Discovery 1.0 §3, RFC 8414 §2), and the JWK Set publishes the public keys a client verifies what it receives with and encrypts what it sends with (RFC 7517 §5). Both are read from what the provider is wired with: a grant, a client authentication method or an algorithm is announced because it is served, and stops being announced the moment it is not.

docs.title: The discovery document
docs.text:
One document, served at the two places a client looks for it:

Method Path Specification GET /.well-known/openid-configuration OIDC Discovery 1.0 §4 GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server RFC 8414 §3

Both answer 200, application/json, with Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600: a client may keep the document an hour.

The routes are where the issuer says they are. OIDC Discovery 1.0 §4.1 appends the well-known path to the issuer, so the routes of the bundle are mounted under it: a deployment whose issuer is https://op.example.com serves https://op.example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration. Routes mounted anywhere else make every endpoint that locates the others fail at the first request, with an error that names both URLs, rather than publish endpoints a client would not find. RFC 8414 §3 inserts its well-known segment between the host and the path of the issuer instead: the two locations are the same URL under an issuer that is an origin, and under an issuer that carries a path, the route of the bundle answers under that path, which is not where RFC 8414 §3 looks.

Every URL is built from the issuer, never from the Host header of the request that asked.

docs.title: What it publishes
docs.text:
Each specification the provider implements contributes its own members, in the order they are wired, and nothing assembles a list of them beside the wiring. Two capabilities announcing the same member is a fault the provider refuses rather than arbitrates.

Members What decides them issuer, authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint, userinfo_endpoint, jwks_uri The issuer, and the routes under it. Always present scopes_supported openid, the scopes the wired claims stand for, the scopes the clients of the tenant registered, and offline_access where a wired grant issues a refresh token and another spends one. Scopes and claims claims_supported, claims_parameter_supported sub and the claims the provider serves; true response_types_supported ["code"], and nothing else: no implicit flow and no hybrid response_modes_supported The response modes wired, query, form_post, query.jwt and form_post.jwt in the bundle, plus jwt when a signed mode is among them (JARM §2.1). Response modes grant_types_supported The grants the token endpoint is wired with, all seven in the bundle. Grants code_challenge_methods_supported The PKCE methods wired: S256. plain is wired nowhere acr_values_supported The classes of the policy of the tenant that the logins it serves can prove, in the order the policy names them. Tenants subject_types_supported The kinds of sub the provider assigns: public and pairwise. Pairwise subjects token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported, token_endpoint_auth_signing_alg_values_supported The client authentication methods wired, in the order they are tried, and what their assertions may be signed with. Client authentication id_token_signing_alg_values_supported, userinfo_signing_alg_values_supported The signature algorithms the provider is wired with: RS256, PS256, ES256 and EdDSA in the bundle id_token_encryption_*, userinfo_encryption_*, request_object_encryption_* (alg_values_supported, enc_values_supported) The encryption algorithms wired: ECDH-ES+A256KW and RSA-OAEP-256, with A256GCM.
