A deployment that wires no key encryption or no content encryption algorithm announces none of these pairs rather than empty lists request_parameter_supported, request_uri_parameter_supported, require_request_uri_registration true all three: a request_uri is read only from a URL its client registered request_object_signing_alg_values_supported The signature algorithms wired, and none beside them only when a client of the tenant registered request_object_signing_alg: none. Request objects authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported true: every authorization response carries iss (RFC 9207) pushed_authorization_request_endpoint, require_pushed_authorization_requests The endpoint; true only when every client registered for the tenant requires pushed requests. Pushed authorization requests device_authorization_endpoint The endpoint where a device code is asked for (RFC 8628 §4) introspection_endpoint, introspection_endpoint_auth_methods_supported, introspection_endpoint_auth_signing_alg_values_supported, introspection_signing_alg_values_supported The endpoint, the wired methods that authenticate a client (all but none), what their assertions are signed with, and the signature algorithms wired (RFC 9701). Introspection revocation_endpoint, revocation_endpoint_auth_methods_supported, revocation_endpoint_auth_signing_alg_values_supported The endpoint, and the methods of the token endpoint, none included end_session_endpoint, frontchannel_logout_supported, frontchannel_logout_session_supported, backchannel_logout_supported, backchannel_logout_session_supported The endpoint, and true for each logout channel wired, both in the bundle. Logout dpop_signing_alg_values_supported The signature algorithms wired. DPoP tls_client_certificate_bound_access_tokens true when a method that authenticates by certificate is wired, which the bundle does. Mutual TLS

Some members are announced only when what they describe exists, and are absent otherwise rather than empty:

Members Present when registration_endpoint The registration policy of the tenant registers clients. Closed, which is the default, the tenant has no registration endpoint at all. Dynamic registration backchannel_authentication_endpoint, backchannel_token_delivery_modes_supported, backchannel_authentication_request_signing_alg_values_supported, backchannel_user_code_parameter_supported A grant of the backchannel flow is wired; the last one is then false. Backchannel authentication authorization_signing_alg_values_supported, authorization_encryption_alg_values_supported, authorization_encryption_enc_values_supported A signed response mode is wired mtls_endpoint_aliases mutual_tls.origin names the host that asks for a certificate protected_resources A client of the tenant registered resources (RFC 9728 §4). Resources authorization_details_types_supported A type of authorization detail is wired (RFC 9396 §10). Authorization details

The document announces no check_session_iframe: OpenID Connect Session Management 1.0 is not implemented, and logout goes through the front and back channels. Its content changes when the wiring or the registrations of the tenant change, never during a key rotation, which is the JWK Set's business.

docs.title: The JWK Set
docs.text:
GET /jwks, the jwks_uri of the discovery document, answers 200 with application/json and the public keys of the tenant (RFC 7517 §5).

What it holds. Every key of the tenant in service, staged, active or retiring, of an algorithm the tenant publishes for: the keys it signs with and the keys a client encrypts to it with. Each JWK carries its kid, kty, alg and use, and nothing private. The keys the tenant keeps for itself are never in it, whatever their status: the key a browser is handed for web push, the key the tenant seals what leaves the process to, and the SAML keys, whose certificates the SAML metadata publish.

How long a client keeps it. The answer says Cache-Control: public, max-age= followed by keys.jwks_max_age, three hundred seconds by default. A set with no key in it is answered no-store, so that no cache keeps an empty set for that long.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    keys:
        # kms and key_id, as the deployment names them
        jwks_max_age: 300
Option Default What it decides jwks_max_age 300 The max-age of the JWK Set, in seconds. The max-age of the SAML metadata reads it too staging_delay jwks_max_age plus 60 How long a new key is published before it signs, in seconds, for every key but the SAML signing key, which has its own

docs.title: Through a rotation
docs.text:
A rotation asks a client for nothing but to read the set again within its max-age.

  1. A new key is published before it signs, for staging_delay seconds: three hundred and sixty by default, the max-age of the set plus the sixty seconds a copy has to be old before Symfony's oidc_login fetches the set again on a kid it does not know. A client with a warm cache has seen the new key by the time anything is signed with it.
  2. The new key becomes active once that delay has run, and signs from then on; the key it replaces is retiring, and stays in the set.
  3. The retiring key leaves the set once nothing it signed can still be presented: the longest lifetime among the ID token, the at+jwt when a client of the tenant receives that shape, the logout token up to its exp, which is the budget of its delivery, and the signed authorization response when a signed mode is wired. A key a client encrypts to stays as long as a pushed request or a request object encrypted to it may still arrive. The timed step retires it past that date.

An operator can cut the first step short, and a client with a warm cache then meets a kid it does not know yet: a key activated before its delay has run, with beffroi:keys:activate, a key that takes over at once, with beffroi:keys:rotate --now, and a key that replaces a compromised one, with --compromised, after which the compromised key leaves the set at once, with no window. Keys gives the commands that rotate, activate and retire a key, and the timed step that stages a successor once a key has worked its age.

docs.title: Dynamic registration
docs.text: title: Dynamic registration description: A client the provider has never seen, RFC 7591 and RFC 7592: closed by default, the three modes a tenant opens it in, what a registration may and may not ask for, and how a client reads, replaces and deletes itself.

docs.title: Dynamic registration
docs.text: A client may register itself at /register (RFC 7591), and then read, replace and delete its own registration at the URI it was handed (RFC 7592). Registration is closed by default: a tenant opens it by naming a mode, which decides what authorises a registration. A client that registers itself is read by the reader a declared client is read by, under the same rules, and is held besides to what its tenant offers.

docs.title: Opening it
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    client_registration:
        mode: initial_access_token
        default_scope: 'openid profile email'
        keep_a_client_unused_for: 7776000
        keep_a_client_never_used_for: 604800
Option Default What it decides mode none What authorises a registration: initial_access_token, software_statement or open. Left out, or empty, the tenant registers nobody and announces no registration endpoint default_scope none What a client that names no scope is registered with (RFC 7591 §2). Left out, openid alone. It is held to what the tenant hands out like every registered scope, so a scope written here that the tenant does not offer refuses every registration that names no scope exempt_confidential_clients_from_pkce false The confidential clients this policy registers are registered without the PKCE requirement. A public client is never exempted, and a challenge an exempted client sends is verified all the same keep_a_client_unused_for 7776000 Seconds a client that was used may go unused before it is deleted, ninety days keep_a_client_never_used_for 604800 Seconds a client that was never used lives at all, seven days statement_issuers none The authorities whose software statements the tenant accepts, for the software_statement mode statement_max_lifetime 300 Seconds ahead of the request the exp of a software statement may be statement_leeway 30 Seconds allowed of the clock of an authority, both ways sector_identifier_timeout 3.0 Seconds one read of a sector_identifier_uri is given, connection included sector_identifier_max_size 65536 Bytes a sector_identifier_uri may answer before the read stops

Closed is the absence of the endpoint, not a mode that refuses. A tenant that names no mode answers a registration, a POST to /register, with a 404, as it answers a path it does not serve, and its discovery document has no registration_endpoint. A tenant that names a mode announces the endpoint, and its endpoint answers. /register takes a POST and no other method, whether the tenant registers or not. A mode nothing wired serves is a mistake of the deployment: the first registration fails on it, naming the modes that are wired.

docs.title: The three modes
docs.text:
An initial access tokenA software statementOpen

mode: initial_access_token registers a client presented by an initial access token the tenant issued (RFC 7591 §1.2): a credential for the team that integrates, named, worth a number of registrations and no more, expiring, and revocable. It opens no other endpoint, carries no subject and no scope, and says one thing only: that whoever holds it may register a client with this tenant.

POST /register HTTP/1.1
Host: op.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer 0NM8Z6ijkVrFDzEaMPwCLWmTvdFxNsRwBCzu8UxS4pQ

{"client_name": "Billing", "redirect_uris": ["https://billing.example.com/oidc/callback"]}

The token is spent in the request it authorises, before the metadata is read: a token worth one registration registers one, whether the registration that followed was written or refused. A token unknown, spent, expired or revoked is answered exactly as a request that carries none, so that whoever does not hold a token of this tenant learns nothing about the one they presented.

bin/console beffroi:client:token:issue 'Billing team' --registrations=1 --days=30
bin/console beffroi:client:token:list
bin/console beffroi:client:token:revoke 0192f1a4-6c1e-7b8a-9c3d-2e4f5a6b7c8d

beffroi:client:token:issue prints the value once, and the provider keeps its SHA-256 and never the value: a token that was lost is replaced by issuing another. It is worth one registration and thirty days unless the command says otherwise, a day at least. beffroi:client:token:list shows what each token has served of what it is worth, and whether it still authorises anything. beffroi:client:token:revoke takes one back at once, and the clients it registered stay.

mode: software_statement registers a client presented by a statement an authority the tenant pins signed (RFC 7591 §2.3), in the software_statement member of the body. The provider issues nothing: the proof is the authority's, which is what lets a registration cross the boundary of an organisation.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    client_registration:
        mode: software_statement
        statement_issuers:
            'https://authority.example.org':
                jwks: '%env(json:AUTHORITY_JWKS)%'
                signing_algorithms: ['ES256']

An authority is keyed by the iss it signs with, an absolute URI compared byte for byte, and pins its public keys inline and the algorithms it signs with, among those the provider verifies. The key comes from this configuration and never from the statement: a key or a jwks_uri the statement names is never read (RFC 8725 §3.10). A tenant that pins no authority accepts no statement.

The statement is verified before any of it is read as metadata. Its signature is checked against the keys of the authority its iss names, under one of the algorithms pinned for it. Its aud names the issuer of the tenant, once. Its exp is present, not past, and no further ahead than statement_max_lifetime. Its iat is present and not in the future. Its jti is present and never seen before, remembered until the exp, so one statement registers one client. RFC 7591 §2.3 asks none of this of a statement; the provider asks it of every signed thing it takes back. Whatever fails, the answer is the same invalid_software_statement.

What a statement says outranks what the client sent (RFC 7591 §3.1.1): a member both carry is the statement's, so the registration is written with the client_name and the logo_uri the authority signed. A statement is held to what the tenant offers as a body is: one that names a scope, a grant or a method the tenant does not offer is refused with invalid_client_metadata, as a body naming it would be. The claims of RFC 7519 §4.1 of the statement describe the statement and are not metadata. A replacement of the registration reads no statement.

The statement is the credential of this mode, and it travels in the body: a body that is not a JSON object is refused with invalid_client_metadata before anything else is read, and a JSON object that carries no statement is answered 401.

mode: open registers whoever asks, with no credential at all (RFC 7591 §1.3): nothing authorises, so nothing is read and nothing is refused before the metadata is, and everything else, the reader, the policy and the refusals, is the same. A credential presented anyway is read by nothing and spent by nothing.

A client nobody vouched for chooses the name and the logo a person reads on the consent page, and a tenant that names this mode for its real users lets anybody write them. The standalone application writes a client_registration in its development environment alone, where the mode is open unless the environment names another, for the conformance suite to register its clients.

docs.title: The request
docs.text:
POST /register HTTP/1.1
Host: op.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer 0NM8Z6ijkVrFDzEaMPwCLWmTvdFxNsRwBCzu8UxS4pQ

{
    "client_name": "Billing",
    "redirect_uris": ["https://billing.example.com/oidc/callback"],
    "token_endpoint_auth_method": "private_key_jwt",
    "jwks_uri": "https://billing.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json",
    "scope": "openid profile email"
}

The body is one JSON object whose members are the metadata of the client, the members clients lists, read by the same reader under the same rules. A body that is not a JSON object carries no metadata and is refused with invalid_client_metadata: in the initial_access_token mode once the token has been read, and in the software_statement mode before anything, the statement being in the body.

What a client may register is what the specifications define, and what the tenant offers:

  • The members this provider defines for itself are not a client's to send: requires_consent, requires_pkce, access_token_format, resources, token_exchange, may_act and require_sender_constrained_tokens are exceptions and privileges. A body that carries one is refused, and a software statement does not grant one either: a client that registers itself never obtains them.
  • A member nobody reads is refused, client_id and client_secret included: the provider draws both.
  • What a member names is one the provider is wired with: a grant, a method, an algorithm, a mode of delivery, a kind of subject, a type of authorization detail.
  • A scope is one the tenant hands out, the ones its discovery document lists in scopes_supported.
  • A sector_identifier_uri is proven: the provider reads the document behind it once, with one GET, no redirect followed, within sector_identifier_timeout and sector_identifier_max_size, and the document is the JSON array of URIs of OIDC Registration §5 that lists every redirect URI of the client, or its jwks_uri when it registers no redirect URI (CIBA Core §4). A document that cannot be read, or that leaves one out, refuses the registration (pairwise subjects).

What a client leaves out takes the defaults of RFC 7591 §2: the authorization_code grant alone, the code response type that goes with it, and client_secret_basic. A scope left out is the default_scope of the tenant, or openid alone. The registration policy writes beside the registration what it grants, the default scope on a registration that named none and the PKCE exemption on a confidential client when the tenant grants it, and that is read back before what the client sent, until the policy writes the registration again.

docs.title: The answer
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store
Pragma: no-cache

{
    "client_id": "s6Bh3dRkqt3Hm9vBkrnfeR7_xU2ZyQ4lJaN0cP8TwYg",
    "client_id_issued_at": 1793001600,
    "registration_access_token": "Yx9o3Wq1fPz7kL2mN8rT4vB6cD0eF5gH1jK3lM9nQ2s",
    "registration_client_uri": "https://op.example.com/register/s6Bh3dRkqt3Hm9vBkrnfeR7_xU2ZyQ4lJaN0cP8TwYg",
    "client_name": "Billing",
    "redirect_uris": ["https://billing.example.com/oidc/callback"],
    "token_endpoint_auth_method": "private_key_jwt",
    "jwks_uri": "https://billing.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json",
    "scope": "openid profile email"
}

The client_id is drawn by the provider, 256 random bits in base64url, and a client cannot choose it. When the method the client registered proves a secret, client_secret_basic, client_secret_post or client_secret_jwt, the answer also carries a client_secret drawn the same way and client_secret_expires_at at 0, which says the secret does not expire (RFC 7591 §3.2.1). The metadata follow, as the client sent them, a member a statement signed standing in place of the one the client sent.

A secret and a registration access token are said once. The provider keeps a hash of the secret, or the secret sealed for client_secret_jwt, and the SHA-256 of the token, and answers neither again: a read of the registration carries neither.

The registration is written before the answer is sent, so the client leaves with an identifier that exists.

docs.title: Reading, replacing and deleting itself
docs.text:
The registration_client_uri answers the three methods of RFC 7592 §2, with the registration access token as a bearer credential and no other:

Request Answer GET 200, the registration as the provider holds it, without the secret and without the token PUT 200, the registration replaced whole (RFC 7592 §2.2) DELETE 204, and the client is gone Another method 405

A replacement is whole and never a patch: a member the request leaves out is a member the client no longer registers. The replacement is read by the reader, under the policy of the tenant and the rules a registration body is read under, so it names nothing a registration body could not; it is read from the request alone, whatever the mode, with no statement in front of it. The request names the client in client_id, the one the URI answers for; it carries none of client_id_issued_at, client_secret_expires_at, registration_access_token and registration_client_uri, which the provider assigned; and a client_secret it echoes is the one it holds. What the provider assigned stays: the identifier, the date and the token, which is not rotated. The secret is the one thing that may change: a client that registers a method proving a secret where it held none, or one its kept secret does not suit, is handed a new one, said once, and a client that registers a method proving none keeps no secret.

A deleted client is gone at once, with its token: a request that presents it afterwards is answered as a token nobody holds. What the client was issued, consents, grants and refresh tokens, is left where it is and can no longer be spent, since nothing resolves the client it names. The sessions of the people who used it are not touched.

A token that reads no client, a value nobody was handed, one drawn for another client, a client of another tenant or a client that deleted itself, is answered 401 with invalid_token and the same description, so the endpoint tells nobody which clients exist. The credential is read before the body: an unreadable body presented with a token that reads nothing is a 401, not a 400. These endpoints are not announced in the discovery document: a client holds the URI it was handed.

docs.title: The clients nobody uses
docs.text:
A registered client carries the date it was last used, an authorization code issued for it or tokens issued to it at the token endpoint, and the provider deletes the ones nobody uses any more, on a timed step that runs every hour: a client used, but not for keep_a_client_unused_for, and a client never used and registered more than keep_a_client_never_used_for ago. One run deletes a hundred clients at most, and the next run takes the rest; what it deleted is written to the log. A tenant with no registration policy deletes nothing, and a declared client is never deleted: it goes away with its block in the configuration.

Each deletion, by the step, by the client itself or by beffroi:client:delete, emits the same RegisteredClientDeleted event.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
Answer When 404 A registration, at a tenant that registers nobody 401, invalid_token, WWW-Authenticate: Bearer Nothing the request presents authorises it: no token, or one that authorises nothing; no statement in the software_statement mode; no registration access token of this client at its URI 400, invalid_client_metadata A member that does not hold, is not read, is not the client's to send, names what the provider or the tenant does not offer, or a body that is not a JSON object 400, invalid_redirect_uri A value of redirect_uris or post_logout_redirect_uris that is not an address a client may register, or the redirect URIs and the grants disagreeing. Every other address, and the rule the loopback addresses of a public client follow, answer invalid_client_metadata 400, invalid_software_statement A statement the tenant does not accept, whatever the reason

What these endpoints answer themselves, a registration, a read, a replacement, a deletion and their refusals, carries Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store and Pragma: no-cache. The description of a 400 is the sentence of the refusal, in ASCII (RFC 7591 §3.2.2), the same sentence a deployment reads when a declaration of the same member is refused.

Clients and pairwise subjects

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: An error is either redirectable, and goes back to the client at a redirect URI that was validated first, or it is not, and the person sees a page while the client learns nothing (RFC 9700 §4.1). Confusing the two is how an open redirector is born, so which one an error is depends on where it was found, never on its code.

docs.title: Sent back, or shown
docs.text:
The authorization endpoint reads a request in two stages. The first establishes who is asking and where an answer may go: the client, a request it had to push or sign and did not, the redirect URI compared byte for byte, the request object or the pushed request the parameters are read from. A refusal there is a page, since nothing says yet that the redirect URI belongs to the client. Everything after it is sent back to the redirect URI (RFC 6749 §4.1.2.1), in the response mode the request asked for:

Parameter Value error The code error_description What the developer of the client needs to fix the request state The one the request carried, when it carried one iss The issuer, always (RFC 9207 §2)

A request that asked for a signed response mode gets its refusal signed as it would have got its code (JARM §2.1). A request that asked for a response mode the provider does not serve is refused with unsupported_response_mode in the first mode the provider is wired with, query in the bundle, the only one it is sure the client reads.

The end session endpoint never redirects an error (RP-Initiated Logout 1.0 §4): every refusal there is a page. Every other endpoint answers the caller directly, a client or a resource server, and redirects nothing anywhere.

docs.title: The shape of an answer
docs.text:
The endpoints of the protocol answer the JSON of RFC 6749 §5.2, with Cache-Control: no-store and Pragma: no-cache: /token, /par, /introspect, /revoke, /device_authorization and /backchannel_authentication.

{
    "error": "invalid_grant",
    "error_description": "The authorization code is invalid."
}

Two headers come with some refusals: WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="<issuer>" with an invalid_client that answers a client which tried the Authorization header (RFC 7235 §4.1), and DPoP-Nonce with a use_dpop_nonce (RFC 9449 §8).

UserInfo answers with a challenge of RFC 6750 §3, the WWW-Authenticate header naming the scheme that would have worked, and the same JSON as its body. UserInfo lists them.

The registration endpoints answer the errors of RFC 7591 §3.2.2 with a 400, and a 401 carrying a Bearer challenge to a request that presents no credential they act on; /register answers 404 on a tenant that registers no client. Dynamic registration says when.

A page shows the person a sentence for the code, translated, and the error_description under it as it is, for whoever has to fix the client. Its status is the status of the error.

Every error_description is a sentence of the provider, in English and in ASCII without a double quote or a backslash (RFC 6749 §5.2), never a message of an exception and never something the request chose. A refusal that would tell a registered client from an unknown one, or a token that exists from one that does not, reads the same whatever the cause: a client that names itself and does not prove it is told Client authentication failed., a code or a refresh token that grants nothing is told it is invalid, and an access token refused because it was not issued here is told so and nothing more.

docs.title: The error codes
docs.text:
Code Status Where Sent back invalid_request 400 Every endpoint: a parameter missing, repeated or of the wrong shape, a client authentication that cannot be read, a client certificate in a header At the authorization endpoint, after the first stage invalid_client 401 Every endpoint that authenticates a client, and the introspection endpoint for a public client Never invalid_grant 400 /token: what the grant presents, a code, a refresh token, a device code, a backchannel request, a token or an assertion, grants nothing Never unauthorized_client 400 /token, for a grant the client is not registered for; /device_authorization and /backchannel_authentication, for a client not registered for that flow Never unsupported_grant_type 400 /token, for a grant the provider is not wired with Never invalid_scope 400 /authorize, /par, /token, /device_authorization, /backchannel_authentication At the authorization endpoint invalid_target 400 /authorize, /par, /token, for a resource that is malformed or that the client did not register (RFC 8707 §2) At the authorization endpoint invalid_authorization_details 400 /authorize, /par, /token (RFC 9396 §5) At the authorization endpoint unsupported_response_type 400 /authorize, /par: anything but code At the authorization endpoint unsupported_response_mode 400 /authorize, /par At the authorization endpoint, in the default mode access_denied 400 /authorize, when the person refuses on the consent page or the identity provider of their organisation authenticated nobody; /token, when the person denied a device code or a backchannel request At the authorization endpoint login_required 400 /authorize, under prompt=none, when the person is not signed in as the request demands Always consent_required 400 /authorize, under prompt=none, when no consent covers the request Always account_selection_required 400 /authorize, when the request asks for an account to be selected, prompt=select_account, and the identity provider of the organisation, asked to authenticate again, answers for the person it already holds a session of (OIDC Core §3.1.2.6) Always unmet_authentication_requirements 400 /authorize, for an essential acr the provider cannot meet Always invalid_request_object 400 /authorize and /par, for a request object that cannot be read, is not signed as the client registered, or does not verify (RFC 9101 §6.3) Never: a page at the authorization endpoint invalid_request_uri 400 /authorize, for the request_uri of a pushed request that grants nothing, never issued, expired, already used or pushed by another client, all four alike; and for a request_uri the client did not register, or behind which no request object can be read Never: a page authorization_pending, slow_down 400 /token, while a device code or a backchannel request waits for its person (RFC 8628 §3.5, CIBA Core §11) Never expired_token 400 /token, for a device code or a backchannel request past its lifetime Never invalid_binding_message 400 /backchannel_authentication (CIBA Core §13) Never invalid_dpop_proof 400, or 401 at /userinfo /token, /par, /userinfo (RFC 9449 §5, §7.1) Never use_dpop_nonce 400, or 401 at /userinfo The same three, when the provider asks for a nonce (RFC 9449 §8) Never invalid_token 401 /userinfo; the registration endpoints, for an initial or a registration access token they do not act on Never insufficient_scope 403 /userinfo, for a token somebody signed in for whose scopes leave openid out Never unsupported_token_type 400 /revoke, for an at+jwt (RFC 7009 §2.2.1) Never invalid_client_metadata, invalid_redirect_uri, invalid_software_statement 400 The registration endpoints (RFC 7591 §3.2.2) Never

A redirected error reaches the client only once its redirect URI is established: the same code, found in the first stage of an authorization request, is a page.

docs.title: The pages
docs.text:
The interaction plane answers what cannot go back to a client with the error page of the provider, which carries one of the codes above or one of its own:

Code Status When unknown_interaction 400 A page of a sign-in reached with no request of this browser waiting for it interaction_expired 400 The request took too long interaction_completed 400 The request was already answered invalid_csrf_token 403 A form posted without the form token of the page that served it login_required 401 A page of the account reached without a session; the page offers the sign-in no_login_to_begin 404 A third-party initiated login naming no client that can begin one (OIDC Core §4) too_many_requests 429 A budget of load is spent, as below

The sentence of each code tells the person what to do next, which is to start again from the application, or to sign in for login_required. Translations says how those sentences are replaced.

docs.title: Refused for load
docs.text:
Two budgets bound what the provider takes, and both always exist:

  • the budget of an address, counted on every route of the bundle, both planes, before any work is done: before a session is opened, a password hashed, an assertion or a proof verified;
  • the budget of a client, counted where its authentication succeeded, at the endpoints that authenticate a client. A public client proves nothing and is bounded by the budget of its address.

A request past either one is answered 429 (RFC 6585 §4) with Retry-After, the seconds before the window has room again, and Cache-Control: no-store. On the protocol plane the body is JSON with an error_description and no error member, since none of the registered codes says a budget is spent and a client is not meant to act on it but to wait; on the interaction plane it is the page too_many_requests.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    load:
        origin:
            limit: 2400
            interval: 60
        client:
            limit: 1200
            interval: 60
Option Default What it decides origin.limit, origin.interval 2400 requests in 60 seconds What one address may send, whatever it asks for. It is not counted per tenant: it bounds the load on the machine client.limit, client.interval 1200 requests in 60 seconds What one authenticated client of one tenant may ask

A number too low on /token or on /jwks is an outage a deployment inflicts on itself, so a deployment sets them from what its own clients send.

docs.title: What the journal keeps
docs.text:
Among the refusals of the protocol, these are acts of the journal:

Refusal Act Whom the act names A client that fails to authenticate, invalid_client, or invalid_request when the authentication cannot be read client_authentication.failed Nobody The request_uri of a pushed request that grants nothing, invalid_request_uri pushed_request.refused Nobody An authorization code presented a second time, invalid_grant; the tokens issued from it are revoked authorization_code.replayed The person A rotated refresh token presented again, invalid_grant; its family is revoked refresh_token.reuse_detected The person and the client A refresh token of a session that has ended and that the end has not revoked yet, invalid_grant. Once revoked, it is refused as any revoked token is, and that writes nothing refresh_token.outlived_its_session The person and the client A budget spent, 429 load.budget_spent Nobody A logout token its client refused logout_token.given_up The person and the client

An act says which act it is, when it happened, the address and the user agent of the request with the place derived from the address, and the person and the client it names; it does not say which check failed. The other refusals of the protocol are answered, and leave nothing in the journal.

docs.title: Interactions
docs.text: An interaction is the part of an authorization request a person sees: signing in, proving one more factor, agreeing to what a client asks. The authorization endpoint signs nobody in. Once a request is read, it decides whether anything is missing, and when something is, it parks the request in an interaction and sends the browser to the page that asks for it. The page resumes the interaction once it has its answer, and the same rules are applied again, until a code is issued or the request is refused.

docs.title: The interaction
docs.text:
What Value Its identifier 256 random bits in base64url, in the query of the pages that serve it: /login?interaction=..., /consent?interaction=... What it holds The request as it was read, the language of its pages, and, once they are known, the session it goes on with and the consent it was given How long it waits Ten minutes from the request Who may resume it The browser that began it: the identifier is remembered in the HTTP session of that browser, which keeps the eight most recent ones, forgets the oldest first, and forgets one when it ends How it ends Once, with a code issued or a refusal, after which it cannot be resumed

A page that names an interaction this browser did not begin answers 400, saying no request is waiting for it, and tells nobody whether the interaction exists: an identifier read in a log or taken from another browser resumes nothing. The tabs of one browser share its session, so a person may finish an interaction in another tab of the same browser.

Every page of an interaction belongs to the interaction plane. A process started with BEFFROI_PLANE=protocol answers 404 to all of them, /authorize included, so a machine that serves only the protocol never shows a login form (routes and planes).

docs.title: What decides a login
docs.text:
With the request in hand and the session the browser holds, the questions are asked in this order, and the first that answers sends the browser to the login page:

The request The browser is sent to log in 1 Any When it holds no session of this tenant, or one that has ended or expired 2 id_token_hint When the sub of the hint is not the subject identifier of the account signed in 3 acr_values or claims asking for an acr When the session satisfies none of the classes asked for, and a credential of this person would: a step-up 4 prompt=login Always 5 prompt=select_account Always: there is no account chooser, so it is a login again 6 max_age When the authentication of the session is older than that many seconds

A login made during this interaction answers questions 3 to 6, whatever it proved, so a person is not sent round again for having signed in a moment ago. The login page says why it is shown: "Please sign in again to continue." for a reason other than the absence of a session, and, for a step-up, that the client requires a stronger sign-in than the one the person has, with the credentials they hold that would satisfy it, a passkey, the password, or the password followed by a code. A login of the person already signed in adds what it proved to the session the browser holds; a login of somebody else ends that session first.

The id_token_hint is compared with the subject identifier the account carries, which is the sub a client of the public kind holds. An id_token_hint carrying the sub of a pairwise client never names the account signed in, so a request carrying one is sent to the login page every time.

docs.title: The class asked for
docs.text:
acr_values asks for a class of authentication voluntarily. A claims request of acr in id_token, with values or value, asks for one too, and binds the provider when it says "essential": true (OIDC Core §5.5.1.1). The second wins when both are sent. The classes are the ones of the tenant, and the ID token carries in acr the first class asked for that the session satisfies, or the class of the session when none was asked for or none is satisfied.

  • An essential request the provider cannot meet at all, none of the classes asked for being one it can prove, a name the tenant does not declare or a class no login it is wired with produces, is refused before any page with unmet_authentication_requirements (OIDC Core §5.5.1.1).
  • An essential request this person cannot meet, the session satisfying none of the classes and none of their credentials able to, is refused the same way, with no step-up page.
  • An essential request still unmet after the login of the interaction is refused the same way.
  • A voluntary request is never refused: when nothing satisfies it, the token carries the class the session has.

docs.title: What decides a consent
docs.text: Once the login is settled, a client registered with requires_consent: false is answered at once. Any other client is sent to the consent page when the person has not agreed yet to every scope and every authorization detail of the request, or when the request says prompt=consent. A consent given during the interaction answers that, and the code is issued.

docs.title: prompt=none
docs.text: prompt=none asks for an answer without any page (OIDC Core §3.1.2.6). Where a login would have been shown, the client is answered login_required, and where a consent would have been, consent_required, both at its redirect URI. none combined with any other value of prompt is refused with invalid_request.

docs.title: The login page
docs.text:
The login page names the client asking, by the name it registered, and offers what the tenant admits: a password form, a passkey, or both, the floor of the logins of the tenant deciding (tenants). A refused login says one thing whatever the reason, "Sign-in failed. Check your username and your password, then try again.", so the page tells nobody which accounts exist.

A login_hint is read one way, the one the deployment chooses, and never searched for (OIDC Core §3.1.2.1). What it names fills the username field with the name that person signs in with, unless this browser has just typed another, and a hint that names nobody leaves the field empty, as a request without a hint would: the value the client sent appears nowhere on the login form. The step of the address, on a tenant that federates domains, below, is the exception: a hint that holds an @ fills its field as the client wrote it.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    interaction:
        login_hint: sub
Value What the hint is read as sub, the default The sub this provider issued to that client, read for that client, so a pairwise identifier names somebody only to a client of its sector username The name the person signs in with none Nothing of the bundle: a deployment that names its users some other way tags a UserHintInterface of its own beffroi.oidc.login_hint

backchannel_authentication.login_hint takes the same three names for the login_hint of the backchannel flow (backchannel authentication). Reading a sub costs what it costs: a client that holds one can learn the name its person signs in with by rendering the page itself, and none is the setting that does not pay it.

On a tenant that federates domains, the login of an interaction asks for the address first, and an address of a domain an upstream identity provider answers for is sent to that provider; a login_hint that is such an address sends the browser there without showing the page. What the client asked of the login, prompt=login, a max_age or a step-up, is asked of that provider in turn and checked against the instant the person authenticated there: signing in through an organisation says how.

docs.title: The language of the pages
docs.text: The language of an interaction is chosen at /authorize: the language of the record of a person already signed in, then the one this browser asked for, then ui_locales, then Accept-Language, then the default of the deployment, each read against the languages the deployment serves. It is kept on the interaction, so every page of the same journey is read in it, and it is never written in a URL. A visitor who picks another language with the control the pages carry changes the language of the interaction too, for the pages that follow (translations).

docs.title: What a client learns of an interaction that did not finish
docs.text:
What happened The client The person The person refused on the consent page access_denied at its redirect URI, with state and iss Is sent back to the client prompt=none, and a page was needed login_required or consent_required at its redirect URI Sees no page An essential acr could not be met unmet_authentication_requirements at its redirect URI Sees no page, or is sent back after the login The interaction waited more than ten minutes Nothing Reads a page, 400, saying the request took too long; once the expired interaction has been purged, which a timed step does every hour, saying no request is waiting for it The interaction had ended, a code issued or a refusal given Nothing Reads a page, 400, saying no request is waiting for it: the browser forgot the interaction when it ended. A request already on its way when another ended it reads that the request was already answered The page was reached from another browser, or without an interaction Nothing Reads a page, 400, saying no request is waiting for it The person left Nothing

A page that answers a person rather than the client asks them to start again from the application: nothing is sent to a redirect URI on behalf of somebody who is no longer there.

Consent and authorization request

docs.title: Introspection and revocation
docs.text: Introspection describes an access token to the client it was issued to and to nobody else, as JSON or as a signed JWT (RFC 7662, RFC 9701). Revocation lets a client give back a token it holds, and answers the same way whether the token existed or not (RFC 7009). Both are POST endpoints of the protocol plane, and both authenticate the client first, exactly as the token endpoint does.

docs.title: Introspection
docs.text:
POST /introspect, the introspection_endpoint of the discovery document, with the token in the token parameter of the form body. token_type_hint is accepted and ignored.

The caller is a confidential client. It authenticates with one of the methods announced in introspection_endpoint_auth_methods_supported, which are the wired methods that authenticate a client, every one but none. A public client is refused with invalid_client, status 401, since it has nothing to authenticate with.

A token is described to the client it was issued to, and to nobody else (RFC 7662 §2.2, §4). Everything else is answered {"active": false} and nothing more, whatever the reason:

  • a value the provider did not issue, or no longer holds;
  • a token issued to another client;
  • an expired token;
  • a token of a client no longer registered;
  • a refresh token, introspection describing access tokens only;
  • for a token somebody signed in for, and a token exchanged from one: a session that has ended, a grant that has been revoked, or a person the provider no longer serves, an account that is disabled among them.

The rules are the ones UserInfo applies, read in one place for both shapes of token, so that an at+jwt of a session ended at the end session endpoint is described as inactive from that moment, where a resource server that verifies it offline accepts it until it expires.

A token that descends from no sign-in is asked none of the last three questions. A token a client holds for itself names nobody. A token of the JWT bearer grant, and a token exchanged from one, names a person without descending from a sign-in of theirs: it is described as active until it expires, whatever became of that person's account in the meantime.

docs.title: What an active token is described with
docs.text:
active first, then the members of RFC 7662 §2.2 and those of RFC 9068 §2.2.1, whatever the shape of the token, at+jwt or opaque:

Member What it says active true, a JSON boolean scope The scopes of the token, space-separated client_id The client the token was issued to, which is the caller token_type DPoP for a token bound to a key, Bearer otherwise exp, iat When the token expires and when it was issued sub The subject identifier the token was written with. For a token somebody signed in for and a token of the JWT bearer grant, the one its client knows the person by, public or pairwise; for an exchanged token, the sub of the token presented at the exchange, as the client of that token knew it; for a token a client holds for itself, the client aud The client, or the resources the token was asked for (RFC 8707 §2): a string for one value, an array for several iss The issuer auth_time, acr, amr, sid The sign-in the token descends from. Absent from a token a client holds for itself, which descends from none (RFC 6749 §4.4) grant_id The grant the token descends from, a UUID act Who holds the token on behalf of its subject, the most recent actor outermost (RFC 8693 §4.1). Absent when nobody does authorization_details What the token is good for beyond its scopes (RFC 9396 §9). Absent when it carries none cnf What the token is bound to, jkt or x5t#S256 (RFC 7800 §3.1). Absent from a bearer token

A token bound to a certificate is described whatever certificate the caller presented: the client may introspect its token however it authenticates today, and the cnf is what a resource server needs to make its own check (RFC 8705 §3.2). Sender-constrained tokens says what to compare it with.

docs.title: A signed answer
docs.text:
A request whose Accept header names application/token-introspection+jwt is answered with a JWT of that type (RFC 9701 §4, §5), whatever the client registered:

Where Member Value Header typ token-introspection+jwt Header alg, kid The algorithm the provider signs with by default, RS256 in the bundle, and the key that signed Claims iss The issuer Claims aud The client that asked Claims iat When the request was received Claims token_introspection The members above, {"active": false} included

The answer is signed and not encrypted. A resource server verifies it against the JWK Set of the provider, whose URL it reads in the jwks_uri of the discovery document. The document announces the signing algorithms the provider is wired with in introspection_signing_alg_values_supported, and the answer is signed with the default one among them.

Either answer is served with Cache-Control: no-store and Pragma: no-cache, as application/json or as application/token-introspection+jwt.

docs.title: The journal
docs.text: An answer that hands a person over is an act of their journal. An introspection that describes an active token somebody signed in for, or a token exchanged from one, tells a third party who that token names, so it is written down, introspection.answered, naming the client that asked and the person. An answer {"active": false} writes nothing, since it describes nobody. The act is written for a token that descends from a sign-in and for no other: the description of a token a client holds for itself writes nothing, and neither does the description of a token of the JWT bearer grant or exchanged from one.

docs.title: Revocation
docs.text:
POST /revoke, the revocation_endpoint of the discovery document, with the token in the token parameter. token_type_hint is accepted and ignored: the provider recognises what it is given.

Every client may revoke its own tokens. It authenticates with the methods announced in revocation_endpoint_auth_methods_supported, which are the methods of the token endpoint, none included: a public client names itself in client_id and revokes what was issued to it.

The token What the provider does The answer An opaque access token issued to the caller Removes it: it is refused everywhere from then on 200 A refresh token issued to the caller Revokes it, and removes the opaque access tokens of its grant (RFC 7009 §2.1) 200 A refresh token already revoked Nothing 200 An at+jwt that verifies, whichever client it was issued to: signed by a published key of the tenant, not expired, issued to a client still registered, whatever became of its session, its grant or its person Nothing: a self-contained token cannot be taken back (RFC 7009 §2.2.1) 400, unsupported_token_type An at+jwt that does not verify: expired, or not issued by the provider Nothing 200 Any other token issued to another client, or a value the provider does not know Nothing (RFC 7009 §2.2) 200

A 200 has an empty body, with Cache-Control: no-store and Pragma: no-cache, so that the answer says nothing about whether the token existed.

What a revocation does not reach. An at+jwt issued under the grant of a refresh token that was revoked stays valid until it expires, at a resource server as at the endpoints of the provider: the provider keeps no list of the self-contained tokens it would refuse, and its lifetime is what bounds it, ten minutes unless tokens.access_token_ttl says otherwise. A client whose access tokens must be taken back at once is declared with access_token_format: opaque.

Every revocation is an act, token.revoked, in the journal of the person the token was issued for; the revocation of a token a client held for itself names nobody.

Revocation ends one token and what depends on it. What takes back everything issued under a session is the end of that session, at the end session endpoint or anywhere else, and what takes back the grants, the refresh tokens and the opaque access tokens a client holds for a person is that person taking back their consent, on the page of their account or with beffroi:user:revoke-consent. In both cases an at+jwt is refused by the provider from that moment, and accepted by a resource server that verifies it offline until it expires.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
Both endpoints answer with the errors of RFC 6749 §5.2, as JSON, with Cache-Control: no-store and Pragma: no-cache:

Error Status When invalid_client 401 The client does not authenticate, or is a public client at the introspection endpoint. A client that tried the Authorization header is answered WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="<issuer>" invalid_request 400 The token parameter is missing, a parameter is repeated, the request cannot be read as a client authentication, or it carries a client certificate in a header unsupported_token_type 400 At the revocation endpoint, an at+jwt that verifies

Introspection never answers an error for a token that is not active: that is {"active": false}. Every failed client authentication is an act, client_authentication.failed; errors says what the journal keeps of it.

docs.title: Logout
docs.text: Three specifications, and they are not interchangeable. RP-Initiated Logout 1.0 is a client asking for a session to end; Front-Channel Logout 1.0 tells the other clients of that session through the browser; and Back-Channel Logout 1.0 tells them server to server, with a signed logout token. A provider that implements only the first one has not logged anybody out of anywhere else. The provider implements the three, and announces them in its discovery document: end_session_endpoint, and frontchannel_logout_supported, frontchannel_logout_session_supported, backchannel_logout_supported and backchannel_logout_session_supported set to true.

docs.title: The end session endpoint
docs.text:
GET or POST at /logout, a page of the interaction plane (RP-Initiated Logout 1.0 §2). The parameters are read from the query of a GET and from the form body of a POST.

Parameter What the provider does with it id_token_hint An ID token the provider issued: signed by a key the tenant publishes, its iss the issuer, a sub, and a sid when it carries one. Its exp is not read, a hint describing a session that may be long past. It names the client, by the first of its audiences that is a client of the tenant client_id The client, when the request names it. With a hint, it must be one of the audiences of the hint post_logout_redirect_uri Where the browser goes once the logout is done: one of the post_logout_redirect_uris the client registered, compared byte for byte (§3). It needs a client, named by the hint or by client_id state Given back with the redirection, printable ASCII ui_locales The language of the pages the browser is shown logout_hint Read as text without control characters, and carried to the confirmation page. It decides nothing

What is refused is a page, never a redirection (§4): a hint that is not a signed compact JWT, or whose audiences name no client of the tenant, a client_id the tenant does not know or that is not an audience of the hint, a post_logout_redirect_uri the client did not register or that no client is named for, a parameter of the wrong shape. The browser is shown the error page of the provider, status 400, with the error invalid_request and its description; nothing reaches the client.

A hint the provider cannot verify is read as no hint. A hint signed by a key the tenant no longer publishes, or one that does not say what an ID token of the provider says, names no client: the person is asked, and a post_logout_redirect_uri that only that hint could have justified is dropped rather than refused (§6).

docs.title: What happens to the session
docs.text:
The session is the one the browser holds with the tenant.

  • No active session: there is nothing to end. The browser is sent to the post_logout_redirect_uri with its state, or shown the page that says it is signed out.
  • A hint that proves the session: its sub is the subject of the account signed in and its sid the session the browser holds. The session ends at once, without a question. The sub is compared as it is, with the subject the account carries, which is the sub a client of public identifiers receives: the hint of a client that receives pairwise identifiers proves no session, and its person is always asked.
  • Anything else: no hint, a hint that could not be verified, a hint of another person, a hint of another session or with no sid. The person is asked, on a page that names the client when one is named and the person signed in, with two buttons, Sign out and Stay signed in. The page posts the same parameters back with the answer and a form token; a form posted without a valid token is refused with a page, status 403. Stay signed in ends nothing and sends the browser nowhere: the page says the person is still signed in and that nothing was changed.

Once the session has ended, the browser goes, in this order, through the front-channel logout page when a client of the session registered a frontchannel_logout_uri, then through the SAML service providers that signed in under the session, as single logout describes, and lands at the post_logout_redirect_uri with its state and no iss, which RFC 9207 gives authorization responses only, or on the page that says the browser is signed out. When no client of the session registered a front-channel URI and no service provider signed in under it, the browser goes straight there, with a 302 to the post_logout_redirect_uri when there is one.

The confirmation page names, in its form-action, the origin of the post_logout_redirect_uri and of the single logout service of each SAML service provider the chain would go to: a browser checks that directive over every redirection of a submission.

A request posted from another site arrives without the session cookie, which is SameSite=Lax, and would find no session to end. The provider posts it again from its own origin first, so that the session it ends is the one the browser holds and the confirmation page is one the browser can answer. It reads where a post comes from in Sec-Fetch-Site, and serves a browser that does not send it as the request came.

docs.title: Front-channel logout
docs.text:
Once a browser has ended its session, it is given a page that loads one frame per client of that session that registered a frontchannel_logout_uri (Front-Channel Logout 1.0 §2, §3).

The clients of a session are the clients that exchanged an authorization code issued in it, each once, in the order of the first code each was issued; a client no longer registered is skipped. The back channel tells the same clients.

The URI of each frame is the one the client registered, with iss and sid added as query parameters when the client registered frontchannel_logout_session_required: true, and as it is otherwise, §2 making the two conditional.

The page loads nothing but those frames. Its Content-Security-Policy is default-src 'none', with the origins of the frames in frame-src, the one script of the page named by its hash in script-src, and form-action 'none', base-uri 'none' and frame-ancestors 'none'. It is served with Cache-Control: no-store. The script moves the browser on once every frame has loaded or failed, and after three seconds at the latest, since a logout has to end even when a client never answers; a browser that runs no script is moved on after the same three seconds. With nowhere to go, the page has no script and says the browser may be closed.

What it can promise is what it says. A frame of another origin reaches its client only if the browser sends that client its cookies, and a browser that blocks third-party cookies does not. The page says the provider asked the applications, those the browser let it reach were told, and the others sign the person out when they are next used: it does not say the person is signed out everywhere. The back channel is what does not depend on a browser.

docs.title: Back-channel logout
docs.text: Every session that ends is announced to each client of that session that registered a backchannel_logout_uri, with one logout token each (Back-Channel Logout 1.0 §2.6), whatever ended it: the announcement is made on the end of the session, never on the request that asked for it.

docs.title: The logout token
docs.text:
A JWT signed by the active key of the tenant, under the algorithm the client registered for its ID tokens, id_token_signed_response_alg, or the algorithm the provider signs with by default when it registered none, since that is the one the client knows how to verify (§2.6). Its header names typ: logout+jwt, alg and kid.

Claim Value iss The issuer sub The subject identifier the client knows the person by, public or pairwise, never the identifier of the account aud The client iat When the token was minted exp iat plus the budget of its delivery below, two hundred and thirty-five seconds by default jti A UUID drawn for this token events {"http://schemas.openid.net/event/backchannel-logout": {}} sid The session that ended, always, whether the client registered backchannel_logout_session_required or not

It carries no nonce, which is how a client tells it from an ID token (§2.4). The key that signed it stays in the JWK Set at least until that exp, so a client that receives the token late but in time can still verify it (discovery and JWKS).

docs.title: Its delivery
docs.text:
The token is minted on the lane of the events once the session has ended, and carried to the client on the lane of the notifications: a client that cannot be reached holds no logout back, and nothing a client does reaches the person, whose session is already closed.

One request per attempt: a POST of application/x-www-form-urlencoded whose only parameter is logout_token (§2.5), with no cookie and no authentication, read for its status code and nothing else. No redirect is followed: the URI a client registered is where the token goes, and nobody else moves it.

The client answers What the provider does A 2xx status Done 400 or 501, which §2.8 makes final Gives up at once A redirection Gives up at once: the same answer would come back every time, and the provider follows none. The client registers the URL it redirects to instead Any other status, or nothing within the timeout Sends it again later, waiting longer each time and never more than retry_max_delay seconds

A client that refuses the token is given up on, and that is said, never kept quiet: an act of the journal, logout_token.given_up, naming the client and the person, so that somebody can see that a client was left believing its user signed in.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    back_channel_logout:
        timeout: 5.0
        retries: 6
        retry_delay: 2
        retry_multiplier: 3
        retry_max_delay: 60
Option Default What it decides timeout 5.0 Seconds one attempt is given, connection included, 0.1 at least. A client that hangs holds no worker retries 6 How many retries the budget of a delivery counts retry_delay 2 Seconds before the first retry retry_multiplier 3 What each wait is multiplied by to give the next one retry_max_delay 60 Seconds a wait never exceeds

These numbers make the budget a logout token is written for. With the defaults, the waits before the first six retries are 2, 6, 18, 54, 60 and 60 seconds, and two hundred seconds of waiting plus five seconds for each of the seven attempts they count make two hundred and thirty-five seconds. That budget is the exp of the token, and the key that signed it stays in the JWK Set at least that long once it retires: changing one of these numbers moves both.

The budget bounds the token, not the sending. A client still out of reach when the budget has run out may be sent the token again, retry_max_delay seconds apart, and what it then receives is past its exp, which a client refuses as it would an expired ID token (§2.6). A client that answers within the budget receives a token it can act on; after it, it can only receive an expired one.

docs.title: What ends a session
docs.text:
A session ends:

  • at the end session endpoint, as above;
  • on the pages of the account, when its person ends it, ends every other session, or changes their password, which ends every other session;
  • with beffroi:user:revoke-session, at the console;
  • by a LogoutRequest of a SAML service provider, at the single logout service;
  • when another person signs in on the browser that held it.

Each end is an act, session.ended, and each one is announced on the back channel. Only the ones a browser ends itself, at the end session endpoint, on the page of the account for the session of that browser, and at the single logout service, go through the front-channel page and the SAML service providers.

A session that reaches its expiry is not ended. It is no longer active, so an authorization code issued under it and not exchanged yet is refused with invalid_grant. But nothing is announced to its clients, and the access tokens and the refresh tokens issued under it keep their own lifetimes.

docs.title: Every end of a session revokes what was issued under it
docs.text:
However a session ends, the refresh tokens issued under it are revoked, rotated ones included, and its opaque access tokens removed, on the lane of the events and dated by the end. The provider does not wait for that lane to refuse them: it reads the session itself, so from the moment the session ended, UserInfo and introspection refuse every access token of it, an at+jwt included by its sid, and the token endpoint refuses its refresh tokens and its codes not exchanged yet with invalid_grant. A refresh token of the session presented before the lane has revoked it is the act refresh_token.outlived_its_session, and so is a successor a refresh in flight saved after that revocation, which is revoked in turn. Once revoked, a refresh token is refused as any revoked token is, and that refusal writes nothing.

What the provider cannot reach is a self-contained access token in the hands of a resource server that verifies it offline (RFC 9068 §4): it is accepted there until it expires, ten minutes after it was issued unless tokens.access_token_ttl says otherwise. A resource server that has to know at once introspects, or its clients are declared with opaque access tokens.

A session is shared with SAML. The session a client signed in under is the one the SAML service providers of the browser signed in under too, which is why the end session endpoint goes through them before it reaches the post_logout_redirect_uri, and why a LogoutRequest of a service provider ends the session of the clients of OpenID Connect as well. Single logout says how that chain is played.

docs.title: What a client registers
docs.text:
Member What it is for post_logout_redirect_uris Where a logout may send the browser back to, compared byte for byte (RP-Initiated Logout 1.0 §3) frontchannel_logout_uri Loaded in a frame of the front-channel page when a session the client signed in under ends. HTTPS, or plain HTTP on a loopback host frontchannel_logout_session_required iss and sid added to that URI. It needs a frontchannel_logout_uri. Default false backchannel_logout_uri Where the logout token is posted. HTTPS, or plain HTTP on a loopback host backchannel_logout_session_required Whether the client reads the sid of the logout token, which is sent either way. It needs a backchannel_logout_uri. Default false config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    clients:
        portal:
            # ...
            post_logout_redirect_uris: ['https://portal.example.com/signed-out']
            frontchannel_logout_uri: 'https://portal.example.com/logout/frontchannel'
            frontchannel_logout_session_required: true
            backchannel_logout_uri: 'https://portal.example.com/logout/backchannel'

docs.title: What a logout can promise
docs.text:
• A session ended without its browser tells its clients only by the back channel. The console, the page of the account read on another browser, the other sessions closed or a password changed, a new person signing in: no frame is loaded and no SAML service provider is told, SOAP being out of scope.
  • The front channel reaches the clients the browser lets it reach, and says so.
  • A logout token is good for two hundred and thirty-five seconds by default: a client the provider cannot reach within that time is left believing its user signed in, and a client that refuses the token is written down as given up on.
  • A self-contained access token outlives the session at a resource server that verifies it offline, up to its expiry; the provider refuses it from the end of the session.
  • A session that expires is not a session that ends: nothing is announced for it.

docs.title: Pairwise subjects
docs.text: title: Pairwise subjects description: The same person under a different identifier per sector, OIDC Core §8.1: how a client chooses the kind, how the identifier is computed, what the sector is, and what keeps it stable.

docs.title: Pairwise subjects
docs.text: The sub a client receives for a person depends on the kind of subject identifier it registered (OIDC Core §8). With public, every client sees the identifier the account carries. With pairwise, each sector sees an identifier of its own, so that two clients of two sectors hold two different strings for one person and cannot find out they are looking at the same one by comparing them (OIDC Core §8.1).

docs.title: Choosing the kind
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    clients:
        billing:
            # ...
            subject_type: pairwise

subject_type is public or pairwise, the two kinds the bundle wires, which the discovery document lists in subject_types_supported in that order. A client that registers none takes the first, public. A client that registers itself may send the member too. A kind nothing wires is refused when the client is read, rather than served an identifier of another kind.

docs.title: The identifier
docs.text:
A pairwise identifier is the SHA-256 of three things, written in base64url:

BASE64URL(SHA256(sector || subject of the account || salt of the tenant))

It is computed and never drawn, so it is the same identifier after a restore of the database, after an import that keeps the subjects of the accounts, and in every worker at once. One person has one identifier per sector, and two clients of one sector see that person under the same one. It is the sub of every document written for the client: the ID token, the self-contained access token, the UserInfo answer, and the introspection of its tokens.

docs.title: The sector
docs.text:
The sector is a host, never a URL, read from what the client registered, the first of these that answers:

What the client registered Its sector A sector_identifier_uri The host of that URI Redirect URIs, all on one host That host No redirect URI, and a jwks_uri The host of the jwks_uri (CIBA Core §4), which is how a client of the backchannel flow, sending no browser anywhere, has a sector

A pairwise client whose redirect URIs are on several hosts and who registered no sector_identifier_uri names no sector, and neither does one that registered no redirect URI and no jwks_uri: both are refused when the client is read, rather than served an identifier computed from whichever value came first, because the sector decides which clients see a person under the same identifier.

Clients that must recognise the same people share a sector. Clients whose redirect URIs are all on one host are of that host's sector already. Clients on several hosts register one sector_identifier_uri on a host of their own, the same for all of them, behind which the document lists the redirect URIs of every one of them (OIDC Registration §5): they are then of that host's sector, and see a person under one identifier.

A sector is a claim a registered client proves. A client that registers itself with a sector_identifier_uri publishes behind it the JSON array of URIs of OIDC Registration §5, and the array lists every redirect URI the client registers, or its jwks_uri when it registers no redirect URI. The provider reads it once, when the registration or its replacement is written, with one GET that follows no redirect, within client_registration.sector_identifier_timeout, three seconds by default, and client_registration.sector_identifier_max_size, 65536 bytes by default. A document that cannot be read, that is not an array of strings, or that leaves one of those URIs out, refuses the registration with invalid_client_metadata. Without that proof, a client able to name any sector could put itself in another's and read its users under their identifiers. A client the deployment declares is not asked for the document: the deployment answers for what it declares, and the host of the URI is its sector.

docs.title: The salt
docs.text:
The salt is a secret of the tenant: 256 random bits, drawn the first time the tenant needs it and never again, sealed by the key management service of the tenant, and kept as a file beside its sealed keys, <keys.storage>/<tenant slug>/pairwise.salt. Two workers that draw at the same moment leave one salt, the one written first, and the other reads it back. The same salt computes the persistent NameID the SAML identity provider gives a service provider, from other inputs, so that no identifier of one is an identifier of the other, and whichever of the two is computed first draws it.

Back the salt up with the keys

A salt lost, or replaced by another, changes every pairwise identifier of the tenant: nothing leaks, but every client that attached an account to the identifiers it held stops recognising its users. Two deployments that share a salt give the same identifier to the same subject in the same sector.

docs.title: The way back
docs.text:
A hash goes one way, so a sub a client presents cannot be turned back into a person by computing anything. The first time an identifier is written for a sector, the provider records which person it names in that sector, in the beffroi_pairwise_subject table, and reads it back from there. A sub is always read for the client that presents it, in that client's sector and in no other:

  • a login_hint read as a sub (interactions) names somebody only when the client sending it was given that identifier, or a client of its sector was;
  • the hints of a backchannel authentication request are read the same way;
  • a self-contained access token somebody signed in for is found to be that person's by its sub, read for the client it was issued to. An opaque access token names its person in its record, and a self-contained one whose sub another client named carries its person sealed, so neither is looked up.

id_token_hint at the authorization endpoint

The authorization endpoint compares the sub of an id_token_hint with the subject identifier the account carries, which is what a public client holds. A pairwise client that sends an id_token_hint there is sent to the login page every time, and answered login_required when the request says prompt=none.

Clients and scopes and claims

docs.title: The ports of the protocol
docs.text:
beffroi/oidc knows no HTTP, no database and no container. What it needs of the outside it asks through a port: an interface of Beffroi\Oidc\Port, one capability each, with the few methods that capability needs and the exceptions an implementation may throw written in its contract. A use case is given the ports it calls and no other.

The bundle answers every port. An integration outside Symfony answers them itself, and starts from the implementations the package ships, below.

Besides its own, the package uses eighteen ports of the core, Beffroi\Core\Port: it calls sixteen and implements two. And it calls two interfaces of the PHP-FIG, the clock of PSR-20, which the use cases read the time from, and the event dispatcher of PSR-14, which every act leaves through.

Port of the core What the protocol does with it RandomnessInterface Draws every value it hands out and recognises later: codes, tokens, references, user codes UuidGeneratorInterface Names what it records, grants, consents and families of refresh tokens among them, and the jti of a logout token JwsSignerInterface Signs what the tenant issues: ID tokens, at+jwt, logout tokens, signed UserInfo, introspection and authorization responses JwsVerifierInterface Verifies what the tenant signed and is handed back: an at+jwt, an id_token_hint JweDecrypterInterface Opens a request object encrypted to the tenant PublicKeySetProviderInterface The JWK Set it publishes SignatureAlgorithmsInterface, KeyEncryptionAlgorithmsInterface, ContentEncryptionAlgorithmsInterface The algorithms it is wired with, which it signs, verifies and encrypts with and announces UserRepositoryInterface The person a public sub or a login hint names, and the person of a token AuthenticationSessionRepositoryInterface The session a token descends from CredentialRepositoryInterface What a person holds, when a request asks for more than the session proved LinkedIdentityRepositoryInterface The person the assertion of a trusted issuer is about (RFC 7523 §3) PasswordHasherInterface, PasswordAlgorithmsInterface The secrets of the clients, hashed when they are kept and read back by the algorithm they name SecretSealerInterface Seals what nobody but the provider may read: the person an at+jwt of a token exchange or of a JWT bearer grant is about, and the references a backchannel request keeps for the client it calls back KeyBoundArtifactInterface, implemented Six kinds of document bound to a key of the tenant, the ID token, the at+jwt, the logout token, the signed authorization response, the pushed request and the request object encrypted to it, each declaring how long a retiring key stays published for it ArchiveChapterInterface, implemented The two chapters the protocol adds to the archive of a person: the consents, and what each client was given

CanRevokeAccessTokensBySessionInterface, CanRevokeAccessTokensByConsentInterface What a store of opaque access tokens can take back: one token, the tokens of a grant, of a session, of a consent Doctrine, the same store ConsentRepositoryInterface, ActiveConsentsInterface, CanPageActiveConsentsInterface The consents, and the ones in force for the page of the account Doctrine InteractionRepositoryInterface An authorization request between the pages a person goes through Doctrine PushedAuthorizationRecordRepositoryInterface The pushed requests waiting for the authorization endpoint (RFC 9126 §2.2) Doctrine DeviceAuthorizationRecordRepositoryInterface The device authorization requests, by device code and by user code (RFC 8628 §3.2) Doctrine BackchannelAuthenticationRecordRepositoryInterface The backchannel requests waiting for their person and their client (CIBA Core §7) Doctrine RecordedGrantsInterface, CanRevokeGrantsByConsentInterface The grant a token descends from, whichever flow wrote its record, and the grants a person leaves to a client The module, over the three stores of records above InitialAccessTokenRepositoryInterface, IssuedInitialAccessTokensInterface The initial access tokens of a tenant, looked up by digest, and listed for whoever issued them (RFC 7591 §1.2) Doctrine PairwiseSubjectRepositoryInterface The person a pairwise identifier of a sector names (OIDC Core §8.1) Doctrine PairwiseSaltInterface The salt the pairwise identifiers of a tenant are computed with A file beside the sealed keys, sealed like them DisclosuresInterface, DisclosuresOfAPersonInterface What a client was given of a person, written and forgotten, and read for that person Doctrine
