docs.text: Port What it answers In the bundle ClientRepositoryInterface The client of a tenant that carries an identifier The module, over every source wired ClientSourceInterface One source of clients The clients the configuration declares, and the clients registered dynamically, in Doctrine ClientInventoryInterface Every client of a source, for whoever runs the deployment The module, over the same two sources ClientStoreInterface The rows of the clients registered dynamically (RFC 7591 §3.2.1, RFC 7592) Doctrine UnusedClientsInterface The clients a source may drop for lack of use Doctrine; the declared clients answer none, and are never dropped ClientRegistrationPolicyInterface Whether a tenant registers clients, and under which policy The configuration TrustedIssuersInterface The third parties whose assertions a tenant trusts (RFC 7523 §3) The configuration PushedAuthorizationRequirementInterface, RegisteredAccessTokenShapesInterface, RegisteredResourcesInterface, RegisteredScopesInterface, UnsignedRequestObjectsInterface What the clients of a tenant registered, read as a set: whether every one pushes its requests, which shapes of access token and which resources and scopes they take, whether one reads unsigned request objects The module, over the sources

docs.title: What the workers share
docs.text:
Each of these remembers something between two requests, and is meant to be shared by every worker of a deployment: a replay on another worker is a replay all the same, and a budget is the budget of the whole deployment.

Port What it remembers In the bundle ClientAssertionReplayGuardInterface The jti of a client assertion until it expires (RFC 7523 §3) The cache pool beffroi.client_assertions IssuerAssertionReplayGuardInterface The jti of an assertion a trusted issuer signed, until it expires beffroi.issuer_assertions RequestObjectReplayGuardInterface The jti of a request object until it expires (CIBA Core §7.1.1) beffroi.request_objects SoftwareStatementReplayGuardInterface The jti of a software statement until it expires (RFC 7591 §2.3) beffroi.software_statements DpopProofReplayGuardInterface The jti of a DPoP proof, per key, for as long as the proof stands (RFC 9449 §11.1) beffroi.dpop DpopNonceInterface Whether a proof must carry a nonce, and whether the one it carries is current (RFC 9449 §8) beffroi.dpop when nonces are required, nothing otherwise ClientJwksCacheInterface The keys read back from a jwks_uri, with when they were read beffroi.client_keys, and beffroi.issuer_keys for trusted issuers ClientLoadBudgetInterface What an authenticated client may still ask in the window A rate limiter on beffroi.load

The bundle declares each pool on cache.app, in a pool of its own, so that a deployment points one at a shared store without touching the rest of its cache.

docs.title: What the provider fetches
docs.text: Port What it reads In the bundle ClientJwksFetcherInterface The JWK Set behind a jwks_uri (RFC 7591 §2) Symfony's HTTP client, over HTTPS, no redirect followed, with a timeout and a bound on the size of the answer RequestObjectFetcherInterface The request object behind a request_uri the client registered (RFC 9101 §5.2) The same SectorIdentifierDocumentFetcherInterface The document behind a sector_identifier_uri (OIDC Registration §5) The same

docs.title: JOSE and X.509

docs.text: Port What it answers In the bundle EndpointLocatorInterface The URL of every endpoint of a tenant, under its issuer The router MutualTlsEndpointLocatorInterface The same endpoints on the host that asks for a client certificate, or none (RFC 8705 §5) The router, under mutual_tls.origin ClientConfigurationEndpointInterface The URL where one client reads, replaces and deletes itself (RFC 7592 §3) The router

It bounds the token and not the sending: a send that comes after it carries an expired token The waits of the retry policy of that lane and the timeout of the sender, from back_channel_logout

docs.title: What the wiring says
docs.text:
The rest are the ports through which the provider learns what it is wired with, which is what it serves and what it announces at once. Most of them are answered by the module itself, out of the classes the integration tags: a grant, a client authentication method, a shape of access token, a kind of subject identifier is a class and a line of wiring, and the port that lists them is never a list kept beside it.

answered The module ServedAuthorizationDetailTypesInterface, AuthorizationDetailsReaderInterface The types of authorization detail, and the reading of a request or a claim through them The module, over the tagged types, none in the bundle PresentedTokenTypesInterface The types of token a token exchange reads The module OfferedScopesInterface Every scope a tenant hands out tokens for The module ClaimsProviderInterface The claims of a person, by scope and by name, and what is served The module SubjectIdentifierResolverInterface, PresentedSubjectReaderInterface, AssignedSubjectTypesInterface, Discovery and JWKS says what the discovery document makes of them.

docs.title: What ships in the package
docs.text:
The package carries the implementations that need nothing but its own dependencies, under Beffroi\Oidc\Bridge:

Namespace What is in it Configuration The clients, the registration policy and the trusted issuers, read from what a deployment declares and validated when it starts JwtLibrary The reader of a compact JWT, the verifier of a client's signature, of a DPoP proof and of a client_secret_jwt MAC, and the JWE encrypter, on web-token/jwt-library Pki The reader of a client certificate, on spomky-labs/pki-framework Null NoDpopNonce, the provider that asks no nonce of a proof InMemory The stores, the replay guards, the cache of the keys of a client and a pairwise salt, for tests and examples: nothing in them survives the process

The stores that outlive a request, the router, the HTTP client and the lanes are the integration's, which is what the bundle provides.

docs.title: Pushed authorization requests
docs.text: title: Pushed authorization requests description: The authorization request sent server to server first, RFC 9126: the endpoint, the reference it answers with, how long it lives, and what a client may be held to.

docs.title: Pushed authorization requests
docs.text: The client pushes its authorization request to the provider, authenticating itself, and receives a request_uri the browser then carries to the authorization endpoint (RFC 9126). Nothing of the request travels in a URL the browser can read or change, and the request is read when it is pushed, by the two stages the authorization endpoint reads one with, before any browser is sent anywhere.

docs.title: Pushing a request
docs.text:
POST /par HTTP/1.1
Host: op.example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Authorization: Basic YmlsbGluZzpzM2NyM3Q...

response_type=code
&redirect_uri=https%3A%2F%2Fbilling.example.com%2Foidc%2Fcallback
&scope=openid%20profile
&state=af0ifjsldkj
&code_challenge=E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM
&code_challenge_method=S256

/par takes a POST and nothing else, its parameters in the form of the body. The client authenticates exactly as it does at the token endpoint, with the method it registered (client authentication); a public client names itself in client_id. The request is then read by the two stages the authorization endpoint reads one with (the order of the checks), the redirect URI included: what either stage refuses is refused here, by the same code. What the authorization endpoint asks of a request once it is read, the verification of an id_token_hint and whether an essential acr is one the provider can prove, is asked when the browser brings the reference there, and refused at the redirect URI.

  • The request names the client that authenticated and no other: a client_id of the body that names another is refused, and one left out is the authenticated client.
  • A request_uri in the body is refused with invalid_request. A request, a request object by value, is read here, against the client that has just authenticated, and is verified once, at this endpoint.
  • A request that carries a DPoP proof reserves its code for the key the proof proves, as a dpop_jkt would (RFC 9449 §10.1), and one that names a dpop_jkt and proves another key is refused with invalid_request (DPoP).

The answer is a 201:

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store
Pragma: no-cache

{"request_uri":"urn:ietf:params:oauth:request_uri:6esc_11ACC5bwc014ltc14eY22cQ2xpZW50UmVxdWVz","expires_in":60}

The reference is the URN of RFC 9126 §2.2 followed by 256 random bits in base64url. The provider keeps its SHA-256 and never its value, beside the parameters of the request as the client wrote them, or as the object it pushed carried them, without what authenticated it: client_secret, client_assertion and client_assertion_type authenticate the request that carried them and nothing else. The parameters are sealed where they are kept, since they carry the hints of the request word for word.

A refusal is never a redirection. Whatever the endpoint refuses, a parameter, the redirect URI or the client, is answered in the JSON of RFC 6749 §5.2 with the headers above, even when the request names a redirect URI the provider would otherwise have answered to: no browser has been sent anywhere yet. A client authentication that fails is invalid_client, a 401; one the request does not carry as it should, a client_id of the body that names another client included, is invalid_request, a 400, as every other refusal of the request is (client authentication). A request past a budget of load, the one of its address or the one of its client, is answered 429, with Retry-After, Cache-Control: no-store and an error_description but no error member.

docs.title: How long a reference lives
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    tokens:
        request_uri_ttl: 60
Option Default What it decides tokens.request_uri_ttl 60 Seconds a reference lives, at most 600 (RFC 9126 §2.2)

expires_in is the number of seconds the reference still has, never more than it has.

docs.title: Using the reference
docs.text:
GET /authorize?client_id=billing&request_uri=urn%3Aietf%3Aparams%3Aoauth%3Arequest_uri%3A6esc_11ACC5bwc014ltc14eY22cQ2xpZW50UmVxdWVz HTTP/1.1

client_id and request_uri are the whole of the request: the parameters are the ones that were pushed, and any other parameter of the query is dropped, so the query never contradicts what was pushed (RFC 9126 §4).

A reference is read by the client it was issued to, before it expires, and spent with the code it buys (FAPI 2.0 Security Profile §5.3.1). Until a code is issued, the reference may be read again: a person who reloads the page they were sent to is still holding a request nobody has answered. Two interactions begun on one reference cannot both finish: the reference is claimed when the code is issued, and the second to claim it is refused.

What the reference is Answered with Unknown, issued to another client, past its lifetime, or spent A page, 400, invalid_request_uri, the four the same answer. The audit trail keeps which it was, and both clients Spent by another interaction at the moment this one issues its code A page, 400, invalid_request_uri

A request_uri that is not a reference of this provider, not of the form of the URN above, is read as a request object by reference instead, and is fetched only from a URL the client registered.

docs.title: Requiring it
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    clients:
        billing:
            # ...
            require_pushed_authorization_requests: true

A client registered with require_pushed_authorization_requests starts an authorization request in no other way (RFC 9126 §6). An ordinary request of that client is refused on a page, with invalid_request, before its redirect URI is even read, so that nothing of the request goes back to the browser that carried it. It is a member of the client, and nothing of the deployment sets it for every client.

The discovery document announces pushed_authorization_request_endpoint, and require_pushed_authorization_requests (RFC 9126 §5) as true exactly when the tenant has clients and every one of them carries the requirement, whichever source holds them, and false as soon as one does not. When the deployment serves a host that asks for a certificate, the endpoint is announced under that host as well, in mtls_endpoint_aliases (mutual TLS).

Authorization request and request objects

docs.title: Request objects
docs.text: title: Request objects description: The authorization request as a JWT the client signed, RFC 9101: by value or by reference, the algorithms a client registers, what is checked, and what is refused.

docs.title: Request objects
docs.text: A request object is the authorization request as a JWT the client signed (RFC 9101, OIDC Core §6), so the provider reads what the client meant rather than what a browser passed along. The parameters are the claims of the object, and nothing of it is believed before its signature is verified, under the algorithm the client registered and against the keys it publishes. A client that registered nothing is never read an unsigned object.

docs.title: Two ways in
docs.text:
Parameter What it carries request The object itself, by value request_uri The URL the object is published at, read back by the provider (RFC 9101 §5.2)

The two together are no request at all, and are refused with invalid_request, unless the request_uri is a reference of the pushed authorization request endpoint: the request is then the one that was pushed, and a request beside the reference is dropped with every other parameter of the query. client_id is sent outside the object as well, because the provider has to know whose keys verify it before it reads anything of it (RFC 9101 §5).

The object is the request. Its parameters replace those of the query, which are dropped, client_id apart (OIDC Core §6.1): what the client signed and what the provider reads are one request, and the redirect URI is matched against the registration of the client byte for byte as it is everywhere else, so an object chooses how the answer travels and never where it goes. What the object asks is then judged exactly as an authorization request in the query would be.

Both ways are served at the authorization endpoint. The pushed authorization request endpoint takes the object by value, verifies it there, once, and keeps what it carried, so the authorization endpoint reads a pushed request as it reads any other.

docs.title: What a client registers
docs.text:
Member What it means for its objects request_object_signing_alg absent Signed under any algorithm the provider verifies: RS256, PS256, ES256 or EdDSA. Never unsigned request_object_signing_alg naming one of those Signed under that algorithm and no other. The client publishes its keys in jwks or behind a jwks_uri request_object_signing_alg: none Unsigned, and read all the same: the one exception, registered client by client, never a switch of the deployment request_uris The URLs its objects may be read back from, compared byte for byte, fragment included require_signed_request_object Its authorization requests are read from a request object and from nothing else, signed as its request_object_signing_alg says. A request without one is refused on a page, with invalid_request, before its redirect URI is read. Its backchannel authentication requests are read from an object it signed, and from nothing else

An object signed under an algorithm the client did not register is refused unread, whatever its signature is worth. The discovery document lists in request_object_signing_alg_values_supported the algorithms the provider verifies, and none beside them only when a client of the tenant registered it: the member says what a client of this tenant may register, not what any client is read under.

docs.title: What is checked
docs.text:
The key is one the client publishes, named by the kid of the header or, without one, tried among all of them; a key that names another alg, or a use other than sig, is not tried, and jwk, jku and x5c in the header are ignored (RFC 8725 §3.10). Keys behind a jwks_uri are read as they are for a client assertion. Once the signature verifies:

Claim What it has to say client_id When the object carries one, the client_id the request names outside it iss The client_id (RFC 9101 §4) aud The issuer of the tenant among its values, so an object made for another provider, or another tenant, is not replayed here (RFC 9101 §10.2) nbf Present, and not in the future exp Present, not past, and no more than the maximum lifetime after nbf

These are asked of every signed object, whatever the client. An unsigned object, from a client that registered none, is held to the client_id rule alone, OIDC Core §6.1 leaving the other claims optional for an object whoever wrote it could have written. The authorization endpoint and the pushed authorization request endpoint do not read iat and jti. The backchannel authentication endpoint asks both of a signed object, and remembers the jti until the exp of the object, so one signed backchannel request is made once (CIBA Core §7.1.1): an object without them, or with a jti already used, is refused there with invalid_request.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    request_objects:
        max_lifetime: 3600
        leeway: 30
        timeout: 3.0
        max_size: 65536
Option Default What it decides max_lifetime 3600 Seconds an object may stand, from its nbf to its exp leeway 30 Seconds allowed of the clock of the client, both ways timeout 3.0 Seconds one read of a request_uri is given, connection included max_size 65536 Bytes a request_uri may answer before the read stops

docs.title: What an object may carry
docs.text:
The claims of the object are the parameters of the request, each named as the parameter it stands for (RFC 6749 §8.2), except the ones RFC 7519 §4.1 reserves for what a token says about itself, iss, aud, exp, nbf, iat and jti, which are never parameters. A claim is a string, or what the query would have carried in its place (OIDC Core §6.1):

  • an integer, as max_age is sent in an object, is the parameter written in digits;
  • a list of strings is a parameter sent once per string, which is how resource travels in an object (RFC 8707 §2.1);
  • any other object or array is the parameter written as its JSON, which is how claims and authorization_details travel.

A boolean, a fraction or a null is no parameter of an authorization request, and is refused rather than converted, with a description that names the claim. An object carries no request and no request_uri of its own (RFC 9101 §4).

docs.title: By reference
docs.text:
A request_uri that is not a reference of the pushed authorization request endpoint is a URL the object is published at, and it is read back only when the client registered that very URL in request_uris, compared byte for byte, its fragment included. A URL the client did not register is refused before any request leaves the provider, which is what require_request_uri_registration: true announces.

The fragment, which OIDC Core §6.2 defines as the hash of the content, is not sent: the URL is read without it, with one GET that sends Accept: application/oauth-authz-req+jwt, application/jwt, follows no redirect, and refuses any status but 2xx, an answer longer than max_size and a read longer than timeout. What comes back is read as an object sent by value would be. The hash in the fragment is not compared with it.

docs.title: An encrypted object
docs.text:
A client may encrypt its object to a key the tenant publishes for encryption (RFC 9101 §6.1), the object signed first and then encrypted, which is what request and request_uri carry. The JWE names the key it was encrypted to in its kid, among the keys of the JWK Set of the tenant with use: enc, its alg is the algorithm of that key, and its alg and enc are among those the provider is wired with, which the discovery document announces in request_object_encryption_alg_values_supported, ECDH-ES+A256KW and RSA-OAEP-256, and request_object_encryption_enc_values_supported, A256GCM. A JWE that names no key, a key that signs or a key that has retired is refused.

What the JWE carries is the signed object, read and verified as one sent in clear: being encrypted says who may read the request, never who wrote it (OIDC Core §16.14). For a client that registered none, the JWE may carry the claims themselves, read as an unsigned object.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
A refused object is an object that was not read, so nothing of it names where an answer could go: every refusal is shown on a page at the authorization endpoint, with status 400, and answered in JSON at the pushed authorization request endpoint.

Error When invalid_request request and request_uri together; at the authorization endpoint, an unknown client or a client_id missing outside the object invalid_request_object An object that does not open or does not parse, an algorithm the client did not register, keys of the client that cannot be read, a signature no key of the client verifies, a claim refused as above, a claim whose value is no parameter invalid_request_uri A request_uri the client did not register, or one that cannot be read back

At the pushed authorization request endpoint the client authenticates before its object is read (client authentication): a client that is unknown there is refused with invalid_client, and the object is read against the client that authenticated, whose identifier stands for a client_id the body leaves out.

A description names the claim it refuses, and never repeats the alg of the object or a value it carries.

Pushed authorization requests and response modes

docs.title: Resources
docs.text: A client names, in resource, the resource server it intends to call, and its access token is issued for that audience rather than for everything the client might reach (RFC 8707 §2). A resource server that receives a token addressed elsewhere has what it needs to refuse it. A request made for a person that names no resource gets a token addressed to the client itself, which is the token UserInfo accepts.

docs.title: Registering resources
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    clients:
        billing:
            # ...
            resources:
                - 'https://api.example.com/'
                - 'urn:example:ledger'

resources is the closed list of what a client may ask a token for, with no pattern and no wildcard. Each value is an absolute URI (RFC 3986 §4.3) without a fragment. A query is allowed, RFC 8707 §2 recognising that it is sometimes what scopes the request, and a URN is a resource as an HTTPS URL is: a resource is an identifier, which the provider never fetches. What a request names is compared byte for byte with the list.

A client that registers no resource asks for none. Only a declaration writes the list: a client that registers itself and sends resources is refused with invalid_client_metadata, so it asks for none either.

docs.title: Asking for one
docs.text:
At the authorization endpoint and at the pushed authorization request endpoint, resource may be sent several times, once per resource, which no other parameter may:

GET /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=billing&...
    &resource=https%3A%2F%2Fapi.example.com%2F
    &resource=urn%3Aexample%3Aledger HTTP/1.1

In a request object, the same claim carries a list of strings. A value named twice counts once. A value that is not an absolute URI without a fragment, and a resource the client did not register, are both invalid_target, at the redirect URI of an authorization request and as JSON at the pushed request endpoint; the description names no resource, what a client registered being nothing an error teaches whoever sent the request. A request that names none asks for none, and nothing is filled in from the registration: a token valid at several resources is valid at each of them (RFC 8707 §3), so it is asked for and never assumed.

The resources named travel with the authorization: the code carries them, and the token endpoint may narrow them and never widen them.

docs.title: What the access token says
docs.text:
Resources asked for None asked for aud of the access token The resources, a string for one and a list for several (RFC 7519 §4.1.3) The client_id client_id of the access token The client, whatever the audience The client aud at the introspection endpoint The same as the token The same as the token UserInfo Refused, invalid_token with a 401: the token is addressed to a resource of its own and not to this provider Answered

The opaque shape of access token is described by the introspection endpoint with the same aud. When the provider reads a self-contained token of its own back, it accepts in aud only the client itself and the resources that client registered, so a value it would never have written is refused before anything else is believed.

docs.title: At the token endpoint
docs.text:
Grant A resource named None named authorization_code, refresh_token Narrows the access token of this response to those, among the ones the authorization carries. The refresh token stays bound to them all, so a later refresh may ask for another of them The resources of the authorization client_credentials Among the ones the client registered Refused with invalid_target: a token with nobody behind it is addressed to a resource, or it is not issued JWT bearer Among the ones the client registered Refused with invalid_target Token exchange Narrows to some of the resources the presented token is addressed to The resources of the presented token. One addressed to its client and to no resource has none to pass on, and is not exchanged

A resource outside what the line allows is invalid_target, in the JSON of the token endpoint. A token exchange is held to the registration of the client that asks as well: the resources its access token is addressed to, and the scopes it carries, are ones that client registered, so an exchange never reaches a resource or a scope its registration does not name. The device authorization endpoint and the backchannel authentication endpoint read resource when the flow starts, against the resources the client registered, answering invalid_target in their own JSON, and a request that names none there gets a token addressed to the client, a person being behind those flows.

docs.title: What the tenant announces
docs.text:
What a tenant announces as its protected resources is read from the clients that registered one, never from a list kept beside them, and it is the protected_resources member of RFC 9728 §4: the one member of the registry that says what the values of a resource parameter are, RFC 8707 registering none of its own. Every resource a client of the tenant registered is in it, each once. A tenant whose clients registered none announces nothing rather than an empty list, which a client would read as "no resource is acceptable here".

Access tokens and introspection and revocation

docs.title: Response modes
docs.text: title: Response modes description: How the answer of the authorization endpoint travels back to the client: in the query, in a form the browser posts, or as a JWT the tenant signs and may encrypt.

docs.title: Response modes
docs.text:
The response mode decides how the answer of the authorization endpoint reaches the redirect URI (OAuth 2.0 Multiple Response Type Encoding Practices §2.1): in the query, in a form the browser posts (form_post), or gathered in a JWT the tenant signs and may encrypt for the client (JARM §2.1). A refusal travels the way a code does. Whatever the mode, the one response type is code: response_types_supported is ["code"], and a request asking for anything else is refused with unsupported_response_type.

response_mode How the answer travels query In the query of the redirect URI, the browser sent there with a 302. The default for code (RFC 6749 §4.1.2) form_post In a page whose form the browser posts to the redirect URI (OAuth 2.0 Form Post Response Mode §2) query.jwt One response parameter in the query, a JWT the tenant signed (JARM §2.1) form_post.jwt One response field of the posted form, the same JWT jwt No delivery of its own: it names the signed mode of the response type, query.jwt for code

response_modes_supported lists the modes the provider is wired with, the four above in that order, and jwt after them because a signed mode is wired. What is wired is what a request may ask for and what the document announces: a mode is a class the bundle tags, and a deployment that wires fewer announces and serves fewer.

docs.title: Choosing one
docs.text:
A request names its mode in response_mode. The mode is read with the redirect URI, before anything else of the request is judged, because it says how anything reaches the client, a refusal as well as a code (OIDC Core §3.1.2.6). A mode the provider does not serve is refused with unsupported_response_mode, and that refusal travels in query, the mode the provider falls back on to say it. A request that names no mode is answered in query.

The mode inside a request object or a pushed request is the mode, as any other parameter of it is.

docs.title: The query
docs.text:
The parameters are added to the query the redirect URI already has, every value percent-encoded (RFC 3986 §2.1), and the browser is sent there:

HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://billing.example.com/oidc/callback?code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA0g2Wn7KcHtdUYvSYn4Ls8&state=af0ifjsldkj&iss=https%3A%2F%2Fop.example.com

docs.title: The form post
docs.text:
The answer is a page holding one form, whose hidden fields are the parameters, posted by the browser to the redirect URI, so that no parameter of the answer is written in a URL, an address bar, a history or an access log. One script submits the form as soon as the page loads. The page also says "Your browser is sending you back to the application. If nothing happens, use the button below." beside a Continue button, which is what a browser that runs no script shows.

The page carries a policy of its own, under which nothing loads and nothing frames it:

Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'sha256-8lDeP0UDwCO6/RhblgeH/ctdBzjVpJxrXizsnIk3cEQ='; form-action https://billing.example.com; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'

script-src names the one script by its hash and allows no other script, and form-action the origin of the redirect URI and nothing else. The page is form_post.html.twig, which an application overrides under templates/bundles/BeffroiBundle/: it extends no layout, since a stylesheet or a script a layout brings would be blocked by that policy, and the script stays exactly as the bundle gives it, its hash being the policy. Like every page of the interaction plane, it is answered with Cache-Control: no-store and Referrer-Policy: no-referrer.

The form reaches the redirect URI as a POST made from the provider's origin, and a browser does not send a cookie of the client set SameSite=Lax with a POST another site makes it send (RFC 6265bis); what the answer says travels in the posted fields, state among them. The provider meets the same rule the other way round, when a client posts a form to /authorize, and posts it again from its own origin (authorization request).

docs.title: A signed answer
docs.text:
query.jwt and form_post.jwt gather the answer in one document the tenant signs (JARM §2.1), so that a client can prove the answer came from this provider and was not rewritten on the way. The document is sent alone, as response; state and iss travel inside it and nowhere else.

Claim What it is The parameters of the answer code, state and iss, or error, error_description, state and iss, each one a claim iss The issuer of the tenant aud The client_id exp Five minutes after the answer: a response is read when the browser hands it over

A refusal is the same document with error among its claims (JARM §2.4): a client that asked for query.jwt, form_post.jwt or jwt never reads an unsigned answer, from the second stage of the request on. A signed mode the provider does not serve, fragment.jwt among them, is refused as any mode it does not serve is, with unsupported_response_mode in query, unsigned. A refusal of the first stage, before the redirect URI is known, is a page and reaches no client in any mode.

The document is signed with the active key of the tenant, in the algorithm the client registered in authorization_signed_response_alg, or in RS256, the first the provider is wired with, when it registered none (JARM §3); it carries no typ. A client that registered authorization_encrypted_response_alg and authorization_encrypted_response_enc receives it inside a JWE addressed to one of its keys, signed first and encrypted second (encryption).

The discovery document announces authorization_signing_alg_values_supported, the algorithms the provider signs with, authorization_encryption_alg_values_supported and authorization_encryption_enc_values_supported, the ones it encrypts to a client with, and the jwt alias, all of them only because a signed mode is wired.

Authorization request and request objects

docs.title: Scopes and claims
docs.text: A scope is a name for what a client may obtain, and a claim is one thing it learns about a person: a scope of OpenID Connect stands for a set of claims (OIDC Core §5.4), and the claims parameter asks for claims one by one (OIDC Core §5.5). What a client receives is what its request asked for and the provider holds a value of: the claims of the scopes the client registered and the person agreed to, and the claims it named in claims. A claim named in claims is served whichever scopes the client registered or the person agreed to, and the consent page lists scopes and authorization details, not the claims named this way.

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
Scope What it stands for openid That the request is an OpenID Connect authentication. Every authorization request carries it, or is refused with invalid_scope profile name, family_name, given_name, middle_name, nickname, preferred_username, profile, picture, website, gender, birthdate, zoneinfo, locale, updated_at email email, email_verified address address phone phone_number, phone_number_verified offline_access A refresh token (OIDC Core §11). Refresh tokens say when one is issued without it Any other Nothing the provider serves: a scope a client registered, which travels in the scope of the access token for the resource server that reads it

A client asks for what it registered. scope is a list of scope tokens separated by single spaces (RFC 6749 §3.3), each made of visible ASCII other than " and \, and a scope named twice counts once. The scope a client registered is the closed list of what it may ask for: scopes are compared byte for byte, and a request that names one outside the list is refused with invalid_scope.

The document says what the tenant hands out. scopes_supported lists openid first, then the scopes the wired claims providers stand for, then every scope a client of the tenant registered, then offline_access when a wired grant issues a refresh token and a wired grant spends one. A scope that stands for no claim exists because a client registered it, so a typing mistake in a registration shows in the document rather than being granted in silence. A client that registers itself is held to that list: a scope the tenant does not hand out is refused at its registration.

docs.title: Where a claim goes
docs.text:
Document What it carries about the person The ID token sub, the claims of the protocol (auth_time, acr, amr, sid and the others), and the claims the request asked for by name in claims.id_token. Nothing a scope stands for The UserInfo answer sub, the claims the scopes of the access token stand for, and the claims the request asked for by name in claims.userinfo, whatever their scope

So a client reads the claims of profile or email at UserInfo, and in its ID token only the ones it asked for by name. The names asked in claims.userinfo travel with the access token, in its private claim userinfo_claims for the self-contained shape, so UserInfo knows them when the token comes back. In the ID token, the claims of the protocol win over a claim of the same name a provider of claims returns; in the UserInfo answer, sub does.

docs.title: The claims parameter
docs.text:
{
    "id_token": {
        "email": null,
        "acr": { "essential": true, "values": ["phr", "2"] }
    },
    "userinfo": {
        "phone_number": null
    }
}

claims is a JSON object, URL-encoded in the request, whose members id_token and userinfo each map a claim name to null or to an object with essential, a JSON boolean, value, a string, a number or a boolean, and values, a non-empty array of those (OIDC Core §5.5.1). A member other than the two is ignored. A name made of digits, a member of another shape, a document nested deeper than a request needs or anything that is not JSON is refused with invalid_request at the redirect URI. claims_parameter_supported is true.

What is asked for is served by name, with or without its scope, when the person has a value for it. essential, value and values say nothing to the provider of claims; the one claim they decide is acr, whose values name the classes of authentication a client accepts and whose essential makes the request binding (interactions).

docs.title: Where a claim is read from
docs.text:
The claims of OIDC Core §5.1 are read from the account of the person in the core (users):

Claim Read from name, given_name, family_name, middle_name, nickname, preferred_username, profile, picture, website, gender, birthdate, zoneinfo, locale The profile of the account, one field each email, email_verified The address of the account, and whether it was verified phone_number, phone_number_verified The phone number of the account, and whether it was verified address The postal address of the account, as an object of the members it holds among formatted, street_address, locality, region, postal_code and country (OIDC Core §5.1.1) updated_at When the account last changed, in seconds since the epoch

A claim the account holds no value for is left out, its verification flag with it; a flag beside a value is a JSON boolean, true or false, never a string. sub is not among them: it comes from the kind of subject the client registered (pairwise subjects). claims_supported lists sub and every claim above.

docs.title: Claims of your own
docs.text:
A deployment that serves claims the core does not hold, and the scope that stands for them, adds a class beside the one that serves the claims of §5.1, implementing Beffroi\Oidc\Port\ClaimsProviderInterface and tagged beffroi.oidc.claims_provider:

src/Claims/EmployeeClaims.php
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

namespace App\Claims;

use Beffroi\Core\Domain\Identity\User;
use Beffroi\Oidc\Domain\Scope\Scope;
use Beffroi\Oidc\Domain\Scope\Scopes;
use Beffroi\Oidc\Port\ClaimsProviderInterface;
use Symfony\Component\DependencyInjection\Attribute\AutoconfigureTag;

#[AutoconfigureTag('beffroi.oidc.claims_provider')]
final readonly class EmployeeClaims implements ClaimsProviderInterface
{
    /**
     * @param EmployeeDirectory $directory where this deployment keeps its employee numbers
     */
    public function __construct(
        private EmployeeDirectory $directory,
    ) {
    }

    public function claims(User $user, ?Scopes $scopes, array $requested): array
    {
        $due = isset($requested['employee_number']) || ($scopes?->has(new Scope('employee')) ?? false);
        $number = $due ? $this->directory->numberOf($user->subject->value) : null;

        return $number === null ? [] : ['employee_number' => $number];
    }

    public function supportedScopes(): array
    {
        return [new Scope('employee')];
    }

    public function supportedClaims(): array
    {
        return ['employee_number'];
    }
}

$scopes is null when the document is an ID token, which carries what was asked for by name and nothing a scope stands for, and $requested holds the names asked for by the request, for the document being written. A claim without a value is left out of what the method returns. What the class serves is announced in scopes_supported and claims_supported, and a client registers the scope as it registers any other. Two providers that both return a value for one claim are refused when they meet; two that stand for the same scope are not, a scope being a name for a set of claims.

UserInfo and ID tokens

docs.title: UserInfo
docs.text: UserInfo answers the claims an access token allows, about the person the token was issued for, to the client it was issued to (OIDC Core §5.3). It is the one endpoint where the answer depends on the token and on the consent behind it rather than on the request, and the protected resource of the provider itself: the rules a resource server applies to an access token, the provider applies here.

docs.title: The request
docs.text:
GET or POST at /userinfo, the userinfo_endpoint of the discovery document. The access token travels in one of two places, never both, and never in the query string (RFC 6750 §2.3, RFC 9700 §4.3.2):

  • the Authorization header, under Bearer or DPoP, the scheme read without regard to case; a header of a scheme the provider does not serve is left alone, as if the request carried none. A token bound to a key is honoured under DPoP only, with its proof in the DPoP header (RFC 9449 §7.1), and a token bound to a certificate under Bearer only; a token bound to nothing is served under either;
  • the access_token parameter of a POST form body (RFC 6750 §2.2), which carries a bearer token and nothing else.

The token must be one the provider honours today. Issued by the provider and not expired, issued to a client still registered, descending from a session that has not ended and from a grant that has not been revoked, naming a person the provider still serves, an account that is disabled being one it does not. An at+jwt is held to the same rules as an opaque token here, by the sid and the grant_id it carries: a token of a session ended at the end session endpoint is refused at once, where a resource server that verifies it offline accepts it until it expires.

It must be bound as it was issued. A token bound to a key is honoured when the request presents it under DPoP with a valid proof of that key; a token bound to a certificate, when the connection presents the same certificate, which is what the userinfo_endpoint of the mutual TLS aliases is for.

It must have been asked for no resource. A token asked for a resource (RFC 8707 §2) is addressed to that resource and not to its client, and is refused here with invalid_token, however valid it is there: a client that comes for the claims of its user asks for a token that names no resource. The client credentials and JWT bearer grants are always asked for a resource, and a token exchange always issues a token addressed to resources, so their tokens, a token a client holds for itself among them, are refused this way.

It must carry openid. A token somebody signed in for whose scopes leave openid out, which a device authorization request may do and a refresh may narrow them to, is refused with insufficient_scope (OIDC Core §5.3.1).

docs.title: The answer
docs.text:
The claims of the person, as the token entitles its client to them:

  • sub first, the subject identifier this client knows the person by, public or pairwise as the client registered (OIDC Core §8), never the identifier of the account;
  • the claims the scopes of the token stand for (OIDC Core §5.4);
  • the claims the authorization request asked for by name in the userinfo member of its claims parameter (OIDC Core §5.5), by their names: the essential, value and values such a request may carry decide nothing here.

A claim the provider holds no value of is left out rather than sent empty, and a name it does not know is no error. Scopes and claims says which claims each scope stands for.

JSON unless the client registered otherwise, with Content-Type: application/json, Cache-Control: no-store and Pragma: no-cache. A client that registered a signature, an encryption or both receives a JWT instead (OIDC Core §5.3.2), served as application/jwt with the same two caching headers:

Member of the registration What it does to the answer userinfo_signed_response_alg The claims are signed by the active key of the tenant under that algorithm, the header naming alg and kid, and iss and aud, the issuer and the client, are added beside them userinfo_encrypted_response_alg, userinfo_encrypted_response_enc The answer is encrypted to a key the client publishes in jwks or behind jwks_uri, the header naming the two algorithms and the kid of that key when it has one. The two come together, never one alone

Signed then encrypted, never the other way round: with both, the payload of the JWE is the JWS, and its header says "cty": "JWT" (RFC 7519 §5.2). Encrypted without a signature, the payload is the JSON of the claims, iss and aud included. Each algorithm is one the provider is wired with, which the discovery document announces in userinfo_signing_alg_values_supported, userinfo_encryption_alg_values_supported and userinfo_encryption_enc_values_supported; a registration naming another is refused. Encryption says what the provider encrypts with.

Every answer the endpoint writes carries x-fapi-interaction-id, served or refused: the value the request sent in that header when it sent one UUID, a UUID drawn for the exchange otherwise (FAPI 1.0 Advanced Final §6.2.1), so that the client and the provider find the same exchange in their logs.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
Every refusal is a challenge of RFC 6750 §3: a WWW-Authenticate header naming the scheme that would have worked and, unless the request carried no token at all, the error and its error_description, repeated as a JSON body. The same two caching headers come with each.

The request Status WWW-Authenticate Carries no access token 401 Bearer, DPoP, with no error and an empty body Sends the token in the header and in the body, or in a header or a parameter of the wrong shape 400 Bearer error="invalid_request" Carries a client certificate in a header, or reaches PHP with a certificate that cannot be read 400 Bearer error="invalid_request" Carries a DPoP proof that does not verify, or names another request or another token 401 DPoP error="invalid_dpop_proof" Carries a proof without the nonce the provider asks for 401 DPoP error="use_dpop_nonce", and a fresh nonce in DPoP-Nonce Presents a token the provider does not honour, or one addressed to a resource, which every token a client holds for itself is 401 Bearer error="invalid_token" Does not prove what the token is bound to, or presents it under the wrong scheme 401 error="invalid_token", under DPoP for a token bound to a key and Bearer for one bound to a certificate Presents a token somebody signed in for, without openid 403 Bearer error="insufficient_scope", with scope="openid"

The descriptions say which rule refused and nothing more: a token refused because it was not issued here reads the same whatever gave it away. DPoP gives the rules of a proof.

docs.title: The journal
docs.text: Every answer is an act, userinfo.answered, in the journal of the person whose claims were served, naming the client they were served to: it is one of the two reads that hand a personal datum to a third party, introspection being the other. It is written once the answer exists, so a request that was refused writes nothing, nothing of anybody having left. The act says that the read happened, who asked and about whom, and not which claims were served.

docs.title: Grants
docs.text:
A grant is a way of obtaining tokens at the token endpoint, POST /token (RFC 6749 §3.2). The provider serves seven, and a client uses the ones it registered in grant_types and no other.

grant_type What the client presents Who the tokens are about Page authorization_code The code a browser brought back to it The person who signed in and agreed Authorization code refresh_token A refresh token it was issued The person of the authorization it renews Refresh token client_credentials Its own authentication, and nothing else Nobody: the client itself Client credentials urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code The device code it is polling with The person who confirmed the code on another device Device code urn:openid:params:grant-type:ciba The auth_req_id of a backchannel request The person who approved it on a page of the provider Backchannel authentication urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange An access token of this provider Whoever that token is about Token exchange urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer An assertion signed by an issuer the tenant trusts The person the assertion names JWT bearer

No class serves the resource owner password credentials grant, and the authorization endpoint answers with a code and nothing else, so there is no implicit flow either: a grant_type of password is answered unsupported_grant_type, as every name the provider does not serve is. Secure by default says why neither exists.

docs.title: What the token endpoint does
docs.text:
The endpoint takes a POST of form parameters and answers in JSON, a success as an error, with Cache-Control: no-store and Pragma: no-cache. It reads a request in this order and stops at the first refusal:

  1. The client. It authenticates with the one method it registered (client authentication). A request whose authentication is malformed is invalid_request: credentials that cannot be read, two authentication mechanisms in one request, or a client_id that is not the one the credentials name. A client that does not prove who it is, or proves it with another method than the one it registered, is invalid_client.

  2. What the request binds its tokens to (RFC 8705 §3, RFC 9449 §5):

    • the key of the DPoP proof the request carries;
    • the certificate of the TLS connection, for a client that authenticates with tls_client_auth or self_signed_tls_client_auth, or that registered tls_client_certificate_bound_access_tokens. A client that authenticates with a secret or an assertion and registered no such binding gets bearer tokens, whatever certificate its connection presented;
    • and nothing else: a request that would bind both a certificate and a key is refused with invalid_dpop_proof.

    A client registered with require_sender_constrained_tokens whose request binds nothing, and a client registered with tls_client_certificate_bound_access_tokens whose request presents no certificate, are refused with invalid_request before anything the request came to spend is read.

  3. The grant type. grant_type is looked up among the grants the provider is wired with, and a name none of them gives itself is unsupported_grant_type.

  4. The registration. A client that did not register that grant is unauthorized_client.

  5. The grant, whose refusals are the errors of RFC 6749 §5.2 and of the specification it implements.

Of those errors, invalid_client is answered 401 and every other one 400. A request refused because a load budget is spent, that of the address it comes from or that of the client once it has authenticated, is answered 429 with a Retry-After header and an error_description, and no error member. Sender-constrained tokens says what a binding changes for the client that holds the tokens.

docs.title: The answer
docs.text: Member When it is there access_token Always token_type Always: DPoP for a token bound to a key, Bearer otherwise, a token bound to a certificate included (RFC 8705 §3) expires_in Always, the seconds the access token lives issued_token_type In the answer of a token exchange (RFC 8693 §2.2.1), and of no other grant refresh_token When the grant issued one id_token When openid is among the scopes of the answer and a person who signed in at this provider is behind it scope Always, the scopes the access token carries authorization_details When the authorization carries details beyond its scopes (RFC 9396 §7)

docs.title: What each grant answers with
docs.text:
Grant ID token Refresh token A public client Authorization code With openid When one is due Served Refresh token With openid Its successor, when the token rotates Served Client credentials Never, openid being refused Never Refused at registration Device code With openid When one is due Served Backchannel authentication Always, openid being required When one is due Served Token exchange Never Never Its request fails: no token is issued JWT bearer Never, openid being refused Never Its request fails: no token is issued

A refresh token is due when the client is registered for refresh_token and either offline_access is among the scopes or the client is confidential. Refresh token says what spending one does.

docs.title: What a registration carries
docs.text:
A client declared in the configuration that names no grant_types is registered for authorization_code and refresh_token; a client that registers itself and names none is registered for authorization_code alone, which is what RFC 7591 §2 gives it. What a client names is read against the grants the provider is wired with, and against what each of them does:

  • A name no wired grant gives itself is refused.
  • refresh_token needs, beside it, a grant that issues refresh tokens: authorization_code, the device code grant or backchannel authentication.
  • authorization_code needs at least one redirect URI. A client registered for no grant that sends a browser back to it registers no redirect URI and no response_types: a redirect URI nothing would ever use is refused.
  • client_credentials needs an authentication method that proves something, so none is refused, and a client_id that can be a sub: one to 255 visible ASCII characters, and no space.
  • Token exchange needs a token_exchange declaration, and a token_exchange declaration needs the grant. The client_id is held to the same rule as for client_credentials.

A declared client that breaks one of these rules is an error of the configuration, raised with the name of the client as soon as the clients are read. A registration request that breaks one is answered invalid_redirect_uri for the two rules on redirect URIs and invalid_client_metadata for the others.

One more condition is read at the endpoint and not at registration: a client of backchannel authentication is served only once it registered a backchannel_token_delivery_mode, a member with no default. A client registered for the grant without one is accepted, and refused at the backchannel authentication endpoint with unauthorized_client. Clients has every other member of a registration.

docs.title: What is announced
docs.text: grant_types_supported, in the discovery document, is the list of the wired grants in the order they are wired, which is the order of the table at the top of this page. The members that go with a grant follow it: the backchannel authentication endpoint and its metadata are announced only while a grant of that flow is wired, and offline_access is offered only while a wired grant issues refresh tokens and another spends them.

docs.title: Adding a grant
docs.text:
A grant is a class implementing Beffroi\Oidc\Application\Token\GrantInterface, tagged beffroi.oidc.grant. It names its grant_type, and turns an authenticated client and the parameters of a request into tokens or into an error of RFC 6749 §5.2. The token endpoint, the reading of a registration and the discovery document read the one tagged list, so a grant added to the wiring is served, registrable and announced, and a grant removed from it is none of the three. Two grants that give themselves the same name are refused, and so is a token endpoint wired with none.

What a grant does beyond that is declared by the interfaces it implements beside GrantInterface, in the same namespace, and never by a rule written about its name:

Interface What the grant declares What it changes IssuesRefreshTokensInterface Its answer may carry a refresh token The rule on refresh_token, and the offer of offline_access SpendsRefreshTokensInterface It spends a refresh token Whether a refresh token is due, the rule on refresh_token, and the offer of offline_access SendsTheUserToTheClientInterface Its flow sends a browser back to the client The rule on redirect URIs and response types ActsForTheClientItselfInterface Nobody is signed in behind it The rule on public clients and on the client_id AsksTheUserOnAnotherDeviceInterface Its flow starts at the device authorization endpoint That endpoint, which refuses a client of no such grant AsksTheUserThroughABackchannelInterface Its flow starts at the backchannel authentication endpoint That endpoint, its metadata, and the audiences a client assertion may name ExchangesATokenInterface It takes a token and gives one back The rule on token_exchange

docs.title: Authorization code
docs.text: The authorization code grant ends every flow that goes through a browser. The authorization request brings the person to the provider, the provider signs them in and asks for their consent where one is needed, and the browser carries a code back to a redirect URI of the client. The client then spends that code at the token endpoint (RFC 6749 §4.1.3), with the PKCE verifier that only it holds.

docs.title: The code
docs.text:
Lifetime 60 seconds, tokens.authorization_code_ttl, at most 600 (RFC 6749 §4.1.2) Value 256 random bits in base64url, 43 characters What the provider keeps Its SHA-256, never the value Bound to The client, the redirect URI of the request, the PKCE challenge, the DPoP key the request reserved it for when it reserved it for one (RFC 9449 §10), and the session it was issued in What it carries The scopes, the resources, the authorization details, the nonce and the claims of the request, and what the session had proven at that instant: auth_time, acr and amr

What the session had proven is frozen on the code: a step-up or a new login afterwards changes the session, and never a code already issued nor a token that descends from one.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    tokens:
        authorization_code_ttl: 60

docs.title: The request
docs.text:
Parameter grant_type authorization_code code Required redirect_uri Required: the one the authorization request carried, as it carried it code_verifier Required when the authorization request carried a code_challenge (RFC 7636 §4.5), refused when it carried none resource Optional and repeatable: narrows what the access token is addressed to, among the resources of the authorization (RFC 8707 §2.2) authorization_details Optional: narrows the details the access token carries, among those of the authorization (RFC 9396 §7)

The client authenticates beside them with the method it registered, which for a public client is its client_id and nothing else (client authentication).

docs.title: What is checked
docs.text:
A code is spent by its first presentation, whatever comes of it. It is looked up by its digest and consumed atomically before anything else is compared: of any number of requests presenting the same code at once, exactly one is the first, and a presentation that fails a check below has spent the code all the same. Every refusal of this list is invalid_grant with the one description The authorization code is invalid., so that a client guessing learns nothing of which check it failed.

  1. The code is one this provider issued, and it was not presented before.
  2. It was issued to the client that authenticated.
  3. It has not expired.
  4. redirect_uri is the redirect URI of the authorization request, compared as a string (RFC 6749 §4.1.3).
  5. PKCE holds (RFC 7636 §4.6): the code_verifier, transformed with S256, is the code_challenge of the request. A code issued without a challenge, which only a confidential client registered with requires_pkce: false obtains, is refused when a code_verifier comes with it (RFC 9700 §4.8.2).
  6. A code the request reserved for a key, with dpop_jkt or by the DPoP proof of its pushed request, is spent by a request whose DPoP proof is signed by that key (RFC 9449 §10), and by no other.
  7. The session the code was issued in is still active: it has not ended, and it has not expired.

A missing code or redirect_uri is invalid_request, answered before the code is read, which leaves it unspent. A code_verifier that is not 43 to 128 unreserved characters (RFC 7636 §4.1) is refused. Other refusals come after every check has passed, and the code is spent: a resource the authorization does not carry is invalid_target, and an authorization_details it does not carry is invalid_authorization_details.

docs.title: What the answer carries
docs.text:
• An access token, in the shape the client registered (access tokens). It is addressed to the resources the token request named, or to all those of the authorization when it named none, or to the client itself when the authorization carries none. It is bound to what this request binds it to, the key of its DPoP proof or the certificate of its connection, as grants says, and is a bearer token otherwise.
  • An ID token when openid is among the scopes, carrying the nonce of the authorization request (ID tokens).
  • A refresh token when one is due: the client is registered for refresh_token, and either offline_access was granted or the client is confidential. It starts a family whose absolute lifetime is tokens.refresh_token_absolute_ttl, ninety days by default, and it carries the whole authorization, whatever subset of its resources and details the access token beside it was narrowed to (refresh tokens).

The act tokens.issued is written in the journal of the person, with what the client was given.

docs.title: A code presented twice
docs.text:
A code presented a second time is refused with invalid_grant, and the authorization it stood for is taken back (RFC 6749 §4.1.2): one of the two presentations may have been an attacker's, and the provider cannot tell which.

What descends from the code What happens to it The grant itself Revoked: the provider's own endpoints and its introspection refuse every access token of that grant from then on Every refresh token descending from the code Revoked, the rotated ones included The opaque access tokens of the grant Removed, so that wherever they are presented they are unknown A self-contained access token of the grant Accepted until it expires by a resource server that verifies it offline against the JWK Set, which nothing the provider does can reach. It lives tokens.access_token_ttl, ten minutes by default

The act authorization_code.replayed is written in the journal of the person, naming the client the code was issued to, the client that presented it again, and the refresh tokens it revoked.

docs.title: Backchannel authentication
docs.text:
In Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication (CIBA Core 1.0) the client has no browser anywhere in the flow, and the device that asks is not the one that answers. The client names the person it wants authenticated, the provider lets that person know, the person approves on a page of the provider they already know, and the client collects the tokens at the token endpoint, by polling or once the provider has pinged it.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant P as Beffroi
    participant U as The person
    C->>P: POST /backchannel_authentication, naming the person
    P->>C: auth_req_id, expires_in, interval
    P-->>U: A notification, on the channels the deployment wired
    U->>P: /account/approvals, signed in: Allow
    P-->>C: A ping, in ping mode
    C->>P: POST /token with the auth_req_id
    P->>C: Access token, ID token, refresh token

docs.title: Registering a client
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    clients:
        branch-terminal:
            client_name: 'Branch terminal'
            token_endpoint_auth_method: private_key_jwt
            jwks_uri: 'https://terminal.example.com/jwks.json'
            grant_types: ['urn:openid:params:grant-type:ciba', refresh_token]
            scope: 'openid profile'
            backchannel_token_delivery_mode: ping
            backchannel_client_notification_endpoint: 'https://terminal.example.com/ciba/notify'
Member What it decides grant_types urn:openid:params:grant-type:ciba, with refresh_token beside it for a client that renews backchannel_token_delivery_mode poll or ping (CIBA Core §4), the two modes the provider is wired with. It has no default: a client that registered none is refused at the backchannel authentication endpoint with unauthorized_client, so that a client of another flow never becomes a client of this one by accident backchannel_client_notification_endpoint Where the provider pings the client (CIBA Core §10.2): required with ping and refused without it. HTTPS, or plain HTTP on a loopback host require_signed_request_object Every request of this client is a request object it signed, as FAPI-CIBA §5.2.2 asks: an unsigned one is invalid_request

A client of this flow registers no redirect URI, nothing of it sending a browser to the client, and one is refused unless the client is also registered for authorization_code. Push mode, where the tokens themselves are sent to the client (CIBA Core §10.3), is not served: the token endpoint is the one place this provider hands out a token.

Two rules follow from registering the grant. A client that authenticates with an assertion, private_key_jwt or client_secret_jwt, may name in its aud the issuer, the URL of the token endpoint or the URL of the backchannel authentication endpoint, the three CIBA Core §7.1 lets it choose from, and those URLs on the host that asks for a certificate when the deployment serves one; a client of no backchannel grant names the issuer alone. And a client that takes pairwise subjects, registers no redirect URI and no sector_identifier_uri is of the sector of the host of its jwks_uri (CIBA Core §4).

docs.title: The request
docs.text:
POST /backchannel_authentication (CIBA Core §7.1). The client authenticates exactly as at the token endpoint, then:

Parameter scope Required, openid among the scopes, every one of them registered. There is no default: what the person is shown is what the request named login_hint, id_token_hint, login_hint_token Exactly one of the three, naming the person: below binding_message Optional: shown to the person beside the name of the client, at most 64 characters of letters and their marks, digits, spaces, currency signs and the punctuation . , : ; ! ? ( ) [ ] @ # % + * / = _ - acr_values Optional: the classes the client would like the authentication to reach, in its order of preference requested_expiry Optional: a positive number of seconds the request should live. More than the ceiling is served the ceiling, not refused client_notification_token Required of a ping client and refused from a poll one: what the provider presents when it pings, a bearer token (RFC 6750 §2.1) of 22 to 1024 characters resource Optional and repeatable, among the resources the client registered (RFC 8707 §2) user_code Refused: the provider takes none, and says so in backchannel_user_code_parameter_supported request or request_uri The request as a signed request object (CIBA Core §7.1.1), whose parameters are then the request

A signed request object is read and verified as at the authorization endpoint (request objects), and it carries an iat and a jti besides: the jti is remembered until the exp of the object, so that one signed request is made once.

Refusal Error The client is not registered for the grant, or registered no delivery mode unauthorized_client No scope invalid_request No openid in it, a scope the client did not register, or a scope that is not a list of scope tokens invalid_scope A resource the client did not register, or one that is not an absolute URI without a fragment invalid_target A binding_message the person could not be shown as it was sent invalid_binding_message No hint or several, a hint the provider does not read, an acr_values that is not a space-separated list of classes, a user_code, a requested_expiry that is not a positive number of seconds invalid_request A client_notification_token missing from a ping client, sent by a poll one, or not a bearer token of 22 to 1024 characters invalid_request A request and a request_uri together, a request object that cannot be read or verified, an unsigned one from a client that requires a signed one, a signed one without iat or jti, or one whose jti was used already invalid_request A request_uri the client did not register, or whose object cannot be read back invalid_request_uri

A request object this endpoint will not read is invalid_request, and not the invalid_request_object of the authorization endpoint: CIBA Core §13 does not name that error.

docs.title: The answer
docs.text:
{
    "auth_req_id": "1bMVbP0yKpXLzwWWE8VgXGDxeQOCX3Bz6DkWnAAgiKM",
    "expires_in": 300,
    "interval": 5
}

200, never cached (Cache-Control: no-store, CIBA Core §7.3). The auth_req_id is 256 random bits in base64url, 43 characters, of which the provider keeps the SHA-256 and, for a ping client only, the value itself sealed by the key management service of the tenant, together with the client_notification_token, since it has to present both when it pings.

Option Default At most What it is tokens.backchannel_authentication_ttl 300 seconds 3600 How long a request lives when it asks for no requested_expiry, never longer than the option below tokens.backchannel_authentication_max_requested_expiry 1800 seconds 3600 The longest a request lives, whatever it asks for tokens.backchannel_authentication_interval 5 seconds 30 How long the client waits between two polls

docs.title: Naming the person
docs.text:
Hint How it is read login_hint As backchannel_authentication.login_hint says, below id_token_hint An ID token this provider issued to this very client, whose sub names the person; its exp is not looked at, a hint describing a past sign-in being the ordinary case. A token of another issuer, or issued to another client, is invalid_request login_hint_token Read by nothing the bundle wires, so invalid_request login_hint What the hint is sub, the default The subject this provider gives the person for this client, public or pairwise username The name the person signs in with none Nothing the bundle reads: the deployment tags a reader of its own, and without one a login_hint is invalid_request config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    backchannel_authentication:
        login_hint: sub

CIBA Core §15 asks for an identifier that says nothing outside this provider, which the subject is and a username is not, hence the default. A reader of its own is a class implementing Beffroi\Oidc\Application\Hint\UserHintInterface, tagged beffroi.oidc.ciba_user_hint; two readers of the same parameter are refused, a parameter being read one way. The login_hint of an authorization request, read on the login page, is set apart with interaction.login_hint, which takes the same three values.

Nobody is told whether the person exists. A hint that names nobody is answered with an auth_req_id like any other, and the request then goes the way of every request nobody answers, to expired_token. CIBA Core §13 defines unknown_user_id for that case, and the provider never answers it: a client that names a stranger learns exactly what a client that names somebody who never answers learns. The hints are read last, after every other parameter, so that a request refused for anything else has looked nobody up.

docs.title: Reaching the person
docs.text:
When the hint named somebody, the provider puts the word on the notifications lane and answers the client without waiting for it. What travels is the name of the provider, the name of the client, the binding message when there is one, the expiry, and the address of the page where requests are answered. It carries no identifier of the request and no link that answers one, so that nothing reaching the person from outside can carry them to an approval.

What carries it to the person is a channel the deployment wires: a class implementing Beffroi\Bundle\Ciba\PendingApprovalChannelInterface, tagged beffroi.pending_approval_channel. The bundle ships one, web push to the browsers the person subscribed on the notifications page of their account, wired when web_push.subject is set. A deployment that wires no channel still serves this flow: the person finds the request on the page where requests are answered, which is where any channel sends them anyway.

docs.title: Answering: /account/approvals
docs.text:
The page is "Requests waiting for you", the first card of the account pages. The person signs in first, then sees the requests made for them that are still waiting, oldest first, and nothing else: there is no code to type and no link that carries a request, the requests being found by who is signed in. Each one shows the provider that is asking, the client, its binding message, where the request came from, by its address and what its user agent says, every scope of the request, and a warning that whoever did not start it refuses it.

  • Allow and Refuse are a POST with the form token of the page, naming the request by a handle of that very list. A request that was answered, has expired or was never this person's is not answerable, and the page says that nothing is waiting there any more, answered 400.
  • A class the client asked for with acr_values that the session proves none of, when a credential of the person would, sends them to the login of the provider for one more proof, and back to the page to answer. A class nothing of theirs could ever reach is asked of nobody: the request is approved with the class the session has, and the acr of the tokens says it.
  • Allowing records a consent to those scopes for that client, as the consent page of a browser flow does, and freezes on the request the session and what it had proven. The acr of every token of the request is the first class the client asked for that the session satisfies, or the class the session has.
  • Refusing ends the request, and the client learns access_denied.

docs.title: The ping
docs.text:
In ping mode, once the person has answered either way, the provider tells the client so at its backchannel_client_notification_endpoint (CIBA Core §10.2):

POST /ciba/notify HTTP/1.1
Host: terminal.example.com
Authorization: Bearer <the client_notification_token of the request>
Content-Type: application/json

{"auth_req_id": "1bMVbP0yKpXLzwWWE8VgXGDxeQOCX3Bz6DkWnAAgiKM"}
  • No token travels there. The ping says there is something to collect, and the client collects it at the token endpoint.
  • It leaves on the notifications lane, never in the request of the person, with no cookie and no redirect followed. Each call is given backchannel_authentication.client_notification_timeout seconds, 3.0 by default, connection included.
  • A 2xx is done. A redirection and a 400, 401, 403, 404, 405 or 501 are given up at once, the same answer coming back at every try. Any other answer, or none, is tried again under the retry policy of the lane.
  • A client that cannot be reached holds nothing up: it finds the same answer by polling.
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    backchannel_authentication:
        client_notification_timeout: 3.0

docs.title: Collecting the tokens
docs.text:
The client sends POST /token with grant_type=urn:openid:params:grant-type:ciba and the auth_req_id (CIBA Core §10.1), in either mode. The answers come in the order the client can act on them (CIBA Core §11):

Answer When invalid_grant The auth_req_id is unknown, or was issued to another client expired_token The request is past its lifetime: the client starts a new one access_denied The person refused slow_down Nobody has answered yet, and the client polled sooner than its interval allows: the interval grows by five seconds, for this request and for every poll after it authorization_pending Nobody has answered yet invalid_grant The person allowed, and the auth_req_id was spent already, or the session they allowed with has ended or is past its expiry The tokens The person allowed

Every poll is recorded, the refused ones included, and a request that has an answer is answered however soon it is asked, which is what a ping client needs, the ping coming sooner than its interval. The auth_req_id is spent once, atomically.

The tokens are those of an ordinary authorization, descending from the session the person approved with: an access token addressed to the resources of the request, or to the client itself when it named none; an ID token, always, openid being required of the request, without a nonce; and a refresh token when one is due. They are bound to what the token request binds them to (grants), never to anything the browser that approved proved.

docs.title: What is announced
docs.text:
While a grant of this flow is wired, the discovery document carries:

Member Value backchannel_authentication_endpoint /backchannel_authentication under the issuer backchannel_token_delivery_modes_supported poll and ping backchannel_authentication_request_signing_alg_values_supported The algorithms the provider verifies a signature with backchannel_user_code_parameter_supported false

docs.title: Client credentials
docs.text: In the client credentials grant (RFC 6749 §4.4) there is nobody behind the request: a confidential client asks for an access token for itself, to call a resource it names. Nobody is asked, so there is no consent; nobody signed in, so there is no ID token; and the answer carries no refresh token (§4.4.3), the client asking again when it needs a new one.

docs.title: Registering a service
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    clients:
        billing-service:
            client_name: 'Billing service'
            secret: '%env(BILLING_SERVICE_SECRET)%'
            token_endpoint_auth_method: client_secret_basic
            grant_types: [client_credentials]
            scope: 'invoices.read invoices.write'
            resources: ['https://invoices.example.com']
Member What it decides here token_endpoint_auth_method Any method that proves something. none is refused for a client registered for this grant The client_id The sub of every token this grant issues the client, so it is one to 255 visible ASCII characters, and no space grant_types client_credentials. A client registered for no grant that sends a browser back to it registers no redirect URI scope The scopes it may ask for. openid is refused whatever the registration says, this grant having nobody to authenticate resources The resources it may ask a token for. A client that registered none can obtain nothing with this grant, a request having to name one

docs.title: The request
