docs.text: Parameter grant_type client_credentials scope Required here, although RFC 6749 §4.4.2 makes it optional: a request that named nothing would otherwise be answered with everything the client is registered for resource Required and repeatable, among the resources the client registered (RFC 8707 §2): a token addressed to the client that asked for it is a token no resource server is meant to accept, and it is the one thing this grant does not hand out Refusal Error No scope invalid_request openid among the scopes (OIDC Core §2) invalid_scope A scope the client did not register, or a scope that is not a list of scope tokens invalid_scope No resource invalid_target A resource the client did not register, or one that is not an absolute URI without a fragment invalid_target

docs.title: What the token says
docs.text:
Claim Value sub The client_id (RFC 9068 §2.2) client_id The client_id aud The resources the request named scope The scopes the request named grant_id An identifier drawn for this answer cnf What the token is bound to, when the request binds one (grants) may_act Who may act for the subject of a token of this client, in the self-contained shape, when it registered may_act

There is no sid, auth_time, acr or amr, nobody having signed in, and no person, the token being about nobody. The answer is the access token, its token_type, expires_in and scope, and nothing else. Access tokens has every claim of either shape.

docs.title: What a resource server reads
docs.text:
• A self-contained token is verified offline, as every at+jwt is: its sub is the client, and nothing in it describes a person.
  • An opaque token is introspected by the client it was issued to, the introspection endpoint describing a token to that client and to nobody else (RFC 7662 §2.2). The answer renders the same members, and the same absence of the members of a sign-in.
  • No end of a session and no consent taken back reach it: it descends from neither. The client takes an opaque one back at the revocation endpoint, and a self-contained one lives tokens.access_token_ttl, ten minutes by default.
  • The UserInfo endpoint does not answer it: the token names nobody, and it is addressed to a resource rather than to the provider.

docs.title: Device code
docs.text:
The device authorization grant (RFC 8628) signs a person in on something that has no browser or no keyboard to sign them in with. The device asks the provider for two codes, shows one of them to the person, and polls the token endpoint with the other while the person confirms the code in a browser somewhere else.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant D as Device
    participant P as Beffroi
    participant B as Browser of the person
    D->>P: POST /device_authorization
    P->>D: device_code, user_code, verification_uri
    D-->>B: The user code and where to type it
    B->>P: GET /device, sign in, type the code
    B->>P: Allow
    loop Every interval
        D->>P: POST /token with the device_code
        P->>D: authorization_pending, then the tokens
    end

docs.title: Registering a device
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    clients:
        living-room-tv:
            client_name: 'Living room TV'
            token_endpoint_auth_method: none
            grant_types: ['urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code', refresh_token]
            scope: 'openid profile offline_access'

A device that cannot keep a secret is a public client, token_endpoint_auth_method: none; a confidential client is served the same way. It registers no redirect URI: nothing of this flow sends a browser back to the client, so a redirect URI is refused unless the client is also registered for authorization_code. A public client gets a refresh token only by asking for offline_access (refresh token).

docs.title: Starting: the device authorization endpoint
docs.text:
POST /device_authorization (RFC 8628 §3.1) authenticates the client exactly as the token endpoint does, then reads what it asks for. Its errors are the JSON of RFC 6749 §5.2, never a redirection and never a page.

Parameter scope Required, among the scopes the client registered. RFC 8628 §3.1 makes it optional; here it is what the person is shown, and a request naming nothing would ask them to agree to everything the client ever registered resource Optional and repeatable, among the resources the client registered (RFC 8707 §2) Refusal Error The client is not registered for the device code grant unauthorized_client No scope invalid_request A scope the client did not register, or a scope that is not a list of scope tokens invalid_scope A resource the client did not register, or one that is not an absolute URI without a fragment invalid_target

The answer is 200, never cached (Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, RFC 8628 §3.2):

{
    "device_code": "GmRhmhcxhwAzkoEqiMEg_DnyEysNkuNhszIySk9eS0k",
    "user_code": "WDJB-MJHT",
    "verification_uri": "https://op.example.com/device",
    "verification_uri_complete": "https://op.example.com/device?user_code=WDJB-MJHT",
    "expires_in": 600,
    "interval": 5
}

The device code is 256 random bits in base64url, 43 characters, which only the device holds.

The user code is eight characters out of twenty consonants, BCDFGHJKLMNPQRSTVWXZ, shown in two groups of four. With no vowel it spells no word, and no character of it is read for another (RFC 8628 §6.1). Eight characters out of twenty are a little over 34 bits, which is worth something only because guessing it is slow (§5.1): the page below counts the codes that are refused. No two requests alive at once hold the same user code.

The provider keeps the SHA-256 of both codes, never the codes, beside the client, the scopes, the resources and where the device asked from.

Option Default At most What it is tokens.device_code_ttl 600 seconds 1800 How long both codes live tokens.device_code_interval 5 seconds 30 How long the device waits between two polls

docs.title: Confirming: the page at /device
docs.text:
verification_uri is /device under the issuer, a page of the interaction plane (beffroi_interaction_device), and verification_uri_complete is the same page with the code already in it, for a device that can show a link or a QR code.

  1. The person signs in first, at the login of the provider, and comes back to the page with the code it carried. No code is read before somebody is signed in.
  2. They type the code, in upper or lower case, with or without the dash, with or without spaces.
  3. The page shows what they are about to allow: the name of the provider, the account they are signed in as, the name of the client and the code, where the request came from, by its address and what its user agent says, every scope of the request, and a warning that whoever did not start this on a device of their own refuses it.
  4. They allow or refuse, with a POST that carries the form token of the page. Nothing is approved on a GET, so a link followed from a screen, or fetched ahead of time by a browser, approves nothing.

Allowing records a consent to those scopes for that client, as the consent page of a browser flow does, and freezes on the request the session and what that session had proven. Refusing ends the request: the device learns access_denied at its next poll, and nobody is asked twice about the same code.

A code that names no request waiting for an answer, because it was never issued, expired, was answered already or belongs to another tenant, gets one refusal whatever the reason, answered 400. Only those refusals are counted, against the person signed in: after five of them in a sliding minute, the page answers 429 to every code until the window has room again. The count is the one the codes of a second factor are counted on.

docs.title: Polling: the token endpoint
docs.text:
The device polls POST /token with grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code and its device_code (RFC 8628 §3.4), authenticated as it was at the device authorization endpoint. The answers come in the order the device can act on them (RFC 8628 §3.5):

Answer When invalid_grant The device code is unknown, or was issued to another client expired_token The request is past its lifetime: the device starts a new one access_denied The person refused slow_down Nobody has answered yet, and the device polled sooner than its interval allows: the interval grows by five seconds, for this request and for every poll after it authorization_pending Nobody has answered yet invalid_grant The person allowed, and the code was spent already, or the session they allowed with has ended or is past its expiry The tokens The person allowed

Every poll is recorded, the refused ones included, so asking again buys no faster answer; a request that has an answer is answered however soon it is asked. The device code is spent once, atomically, by the first poll after the approval: of several polls at once, exactly one is served.

The tokens are those of an ordinary authorization, descending from the session the person approved with: an access token addressed to the resources the device named at the device authorization endpoint, or to the client itself when it named none; an ID token when openid was among the scopes, without a nonce; and a refresh token when one is due, starting a family with the absolute lifetime of every other. They are bound to what the polling request binds them to (grants), never to anything the browser that approved proved.

docs.title: JWT bearer
docs.text:
A client presents an assertion, a JWT signed by an issuer the tenant trusts, and receives an access token for the person that assertion is about (RFC 7523 §2.1). The person signed in somewhere else, so this provider authenticates nobody here: it issues no ID token, takes no openid, and creates nobody. The assertion names somebody the tenant already knows, through an identity an operator linked, or it is refused.

Whoever holds the signing key of a trusted issuer can name a person of the tenant and be answered with an access token, so everything about that issuer is declared in advance and nothing about it is inferred.

docs.title: Declaring the issuer
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    trusted_issuers:
        'https://issuer.example.com':
            jwks_uri: 'https://issuer.example.com/jwks.json'
            signing_algorithms: ['ES256']
            clients: ['gateway']
            identity_provider: example-issuer
            trusted_scopes: ['invoices.read']
Option What it decides The key The iss the issuer signs with, an absolute URI without a fragment, compared byte for byte. An issuer nobody declared is unknown jwks or jwks_uri Its keys, written down or read back from a URL, one or the other and never both, nor neither. A URL is HTTPS, or plain HTTP on a loopback host, and is read with one GET, no redirect followed. The keys read are kept in a pool the workers share, and read again at most once per cooldown when an assertion names a kid the kept set does not hold, which is how an issuer that rotates its keys is followed. These keys are the only ones an assertion is verified against, whatever its header names (RFC 8725 §3.10) signing_algorithms The algorithms an assertion of the issuer may be signed with, at least one, among those the provider is wired with: RS256, PS256, ES256, EdDSA clients The clients that may present its assertions, at least one. An issuer trusted for a gateway is not thereby trusted for every client of the tenant identity_provider The source of the linked identities its subjects name: a sub is a person of the tenant only when a linked identity of that source says so trusted_scopes What the issuer is trusted for, at least one scope. openid among them buys nothing, the grant refusing it

A declaration that breaks one of these rules, or carries an option this table does not name, is an error of the configuration. A tenant that declares no issuer accepts no assertion.

What one read of a jwks_uri costs is set in client_authentication, for the issuers as for the clients: jwks_ttl, how long the keys read are kept, a day by default; jwks_refetch_cooldown, 300 seconds; jwks_timeout, 3 seconds for one read, connection included; and jwks_max_size, 65536 bytes. The pool of the issuers is not the pool of the clients, so a client is never verified against a set read for an issuer.

docs.title: Linking the people
docs.text:
The sub of an assertion names a person of the tenant through a linked identity of the source the issuer declares, and through nothing else. An operator writes that link before the issuer can name the person:

bin/console beffroi:user:link alice example-issuer 248289761001

The arguments are the username of the person, the source as identity_provider names it, and the subject that source gives them, compared byte for byte. Running the command again refreshes the link. A subject no link resolves, or that resolves to a disabled account, is refused like an assertion of an unknown issuer.

docs.title: Registering the client
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    clients:
        gateway:
            client_name: 'API gateway'
            secret: '%env(GATEWAY_SECRET)%'
            token_endpoint_auth_method: client_secret_basic
            grant_types: ['urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer']
            scope: 'invoices.read'
            resources: ['https://invoices.example.com']

The client is named in the clients of the issuer, registered for the grant, and registered with the resources its tokens may be addressed to: a request names at least one, and a client that registered none obtains nothing. The request of a public client fails, and no token is issued: a token of this grant is issued only to a client that authenticates itself.

The assertion is the authorization, not the authentication of the client (RFC 7523 §2.1): the client authenticates beside it with the method it registered, as for every other grant. The two readings of an assertion share no registration, no validator and no record of the assertions already seen, so an assertion accepted as one is never thereby accepted as the other.

docs.title: The request
docs.text: Parameter grant_type urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer assertion Required: the assertion, a compact JWS scope Required: a request that named nothing would otherwise be answered with everything the registration of the client and the declaration of the issuer have in common resource Required and repeatable, among the resources the client registered (RFC 8707 §2)

docs.title: What is checked of the assertion
docs.text:
Every refusal is the same refusal: invalid_grant, with the one description The assertion is not one this provider accepts as an authorization (RFC 7523 section 3). Whoever presents an assertion learns that it was not accepted and nothing else: not whether the issuer is known, not whether the client may present its assertions, not whether the subject resolves.

  1. It is a compact JWS.
  2. Its iss is an issuer the tenant declares, and the client is among the clients of that issuer. Nothing of the assertion is verified before that: which keys would verify it is the declaration's answer, never the assertion's.
  3. Its signature verifies against the keys of that issuer, under one of its signing_algorithms, the kid of the header choosing among those keys only. Keys behind a jwks_uri that cannot be read are this same refusal.
  4. Its aud is one value, the issuer identifier of the tenant.
  5. It has an exp, which is still in the future and no further ahead than client_authentication.assertion_max_lifetime, 300 seconds by default, both allowing client_authentication.assertion_leeway, 30 seconds, of the clock of the issuer.
  6. It has an iat, no further in the future than the leeway.
  7. It has a jti this provider has not seen from that issuer before: the jti is remembered until the exp, so that an assertion is spent once.
  8. It has a sub, which a linked identity of the source of the issuer resolves to a person whose account is enabled.

Then what it may obtain:

Refusal Error No resource, or one the client did not register invalid_target No scope invalid_request openid among the scopes (OIDC Core §2) invalid_scope A scope the client did not register, or the issuer is not trusted for, or a scope that is not a list of scope tokens invalid_scope

docs.title: What the token says
docs.text:
The answer is an access token, with its token_type, expires_in and scope, and nothing else: no ID token and no refresh token.

Claim Value sub The subject this provider gives the person for this client, public or pairwise, never the subject of the issuer client_id The client aud The resources the request named scope The scopes the request named, within what the client registered and what the issuer is trusted for grant_id An identifier drawn for this answer person In the self-contained shape, the person, sealed by the key management service of the tenant, which only the provider can open; the record of an opaque token keeps the person beside it may_act In the self-contained shape, when the client registered one cnf What the token is bound to, when the request binds one (grants)

There is no sid, auth_time, acr or amr: the person was authenticated somewhere else, and how is not this provider's to claim. The act tokens.issued is written in the journal of that person, and not under the subject the client reads.

docs.title: Refresh token
docs.text: A refresh token renews an access token while the person is elsewhere (RFC 6749 §6). The client spends it at the token endpoint with grant_type=refresh_token, and it is the only client that can: a refresh token is issued to one client and refused to every other. What a refresh token is, how long it lives and everything that ends one are on refresh tokens; this page is the request.

docs.title: When a client gets one
docs.text:
Three grants issue refresh tokens: authorization code, device code and backchannel authentication. Their answer carries one when the client is registered for refresh_token, and either:

  • offline_access is among the scopes of the authorization (OIDC Core §11), or
  • the client is confidential, whether it asked for offline_access or not.

So a public client gets one only by asking for offline_access, and a client registered for no refresh_token gets none, whatever it asks for. The provider offers offline_access only while it is wired with a grant that issues refresh tokens and a grant that spends them, and a client asks for it as for any other scope, among the ones it registered.

docs.title: The request
docs.text:
Parameter grant_type refresh_token refresh_token Required scope Optional: a subset of the scopes of the refresh token, for this answer only (RFC 6749 §6) resource Optional and repeatable: a subset of the resources of the authorization, for this access token only (RFC 8707 §2.2) authorization_details Optional: a subset of the details of the authorization, for this access token only (RFC 9396 §7)

The client authenticates beside them with the method it registered.

docs.title: What is checked
docs.text:
In this order. The first five refusals are invalid_grant, all with the one description The refresh token is invalid.:

  1. The token is one this provider issued, to the client that authenticated, and it has not been revoked.
  2. It has not been replaced. A token that was rotated and is presented again is a reuse (RFC 9700 §4.13.2): its whole family is revoked, the successor the client holds included, and the act refresh_token.reuse_detected is written in the journal of the person.
  3. The session it descends from has not ended. A session that merely expired does not stop a refresh, renewing while the person is away being what the token is for; a session that ended does, however it ended, and the act refresh_token.outlived_its_session is written.
  4. It has not expired. Its own lifetime never reaches past the absolute lifetime of its family.
  5. A token bound to a key or to a certificate is refreshed by a request that proves that key or presents that certificate again (RFC 9449 §5, RFC 8705 §4).
  6. scope names nothing the token does not carry: invalid_scope otherwise. A scope that is not a list of scope tokens is invalid_scope too, before the token is even looked up.
  7. resource and authorization_details narrow and never widen: invalid_target and invalid_authorization_details otherwise.

docs.title: Rotation
docs.text:
A refresh token is replaced where nothing else tells it from a copy of itself (RFC 9700 §4.13.2). Three things can: the authentication of a confidential client, the key or the certificate the token is bound to, and rotation. One is enough, so the provider rotates exactly where the other two are missing:

The client Its refresh token Confidential Stands. The answer carries no refresh_token, and the client keeps the one it holds until it expires Public, the token bound to a DPoP key or to a certificate Stands, for the same reason Public, the token bound to nothing Rotates. The token presented is marked replaced, and the answer carries its successor

A successor belongs to the same family. It carries the whole authorization, whatever this request narrowed for its access token, and what the session had proven when the authorization was granted. Its own lifetime, tokens.refresh_token_ttl, starts at the rotation and never reaches past the end of the family. The act refresh_token.rotated is written in the journal of the person.

docs.title: What the answer carries
docs.text:
• An access token, bound to what this request binds it to and not to what bound the request that obtained the refresh token (grants): a confidential client whose tokens are bound to its certificate, and whose certificate was renewed, gets tokens bound to the new one.
  • An ID token when openid is among the scopes of the answer. It describes the same authentication as the first one, the same auth_time, acr and amr, and it carries no nonce, the refresh having none to carry (OIDC Core §12.2).
  • A refresh token when the token rotated, and only then.

A client takes a refresh token back itself at the revocation endpoint (RFC 7009 §2.1), which revokes that token and removes the opaque access tokens of its grant. Introspection and revocation describes the endpoint.

docs.title: Token exchange
docs.text:
A client presents an access token this provider issued and receives another one, about the same subject, addressed to resources the first one was already addressed to, and good for no scope the first one did not carry (RFC 8693 §2.1). It is how a gateway that received a person's token calls the service behind it with a token of its own, narrowed to that service, and how a service tells the resource it calls that it acts for somebody else.

The presented token may have been issued to any client of the tenant: holding it is what the request is about. What the client may do with it is registered in advance and never asked for, and the answer is an access token and nothing else.

docs.title: Registering a client for it
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    clients:
        gateway:
            client_name: 'API gateway'
            secret: '%env(GATEWAY_SECRET)%'
            token_endpoint_auth_method: client_secret_basic
            grant_types: ['urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange', client_credentials]
            scope: 'invoices.read'
            resources: ['https://invoices.example.com']
            token_exchange:
                subject_token_types: ['urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token']
                may_act_for_a_user: true
Member What it decides token_exchange.subject_token_types The types of token the client may present as a subject_token or as an actor_token (RFC 8693 §3), at least one. The provider reads one type, urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token, an access token of this provider in either shape; a name it does not read is refused token_exchange.may_act_for_a_user Whether the client may present a token issued on a sign-in at this provider. false by default: a service that only ever exchanges tokens clients hold for themselves is not the same party as a gateway carrying a person's token, and the registration says which of the two it is. A token that carries no sign-in, one a client holds for itself or one of a JWT bearer assertion, is presented without it resources The resources the new token may be addressed to. Every resource of the new token is one of these as well as one of the presented token scope The scopes the new token may carry. Every scope of the new token is one of these as well as one of the presented token may_act Registered on the client the presented token was issued to, not on this one: below

A client registered for the grant declares token_exchange, and a token_exchange without the grant is refused. The client_id of a client registered for the grant is one a sub can be, one to 255 visible ASCII characters and no space, since it is named where a subject is expected. client_credentials is beside the grant in the example for the delegation, whose actor token is a token the client holds for itself.

The new token never holds more than the registration of the client that asks. A request that names no scope asks for every scope of the presented token, and one that names no resource for every resource it is addressed to; when that is more than the client registered, the request fails and no token is issued. A client that may be presented a token holding more than it registered names, in scope and resource, what it registered. The request of a public client fails the same way: an exchanged token is issued only to a client that authenticates itself.

docs.title: The request
docs.text: Parameter grant_type urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange subject_token Required: the token the new one is about subject_token_type Required, a type the provider reads and the client registered actor_token Optional: the token of whoever acts, which makes the exchange a delegation actor_token_type Required with an actor_token, refused without one requested_token_type Optional, and urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token when present: it is the one type the provider issues scope Optional: a subset of the scopes of the presented token, each one registered by the client. Absent, the request asks for all of the presented token's resource Optional and repeatable: a subset of the resources the presented token is addressed to, each one registered by the client. Absent, the request asks for all of the presented token's audience Refused: what a token of this provider is addressed to is named by resource (RFC 8707 §2), and a logical name beside it would be a second way of saying it with nothing registered behind it

docs.title: What is checked
docs.text:
Refusal Error The client did not register token_exchange unauthorized_client A requested_token_type other than the access token type invalid_request An audience parameter invalid_target A token type the provider does not read, or the client did not register, or a type missing beside its token, or present without one invalid_request A presented token this provider does not honour, below invalid_request A subject token somebody signed in for, presented by a client not registered with may_act_for_a_user invalid_request An actor token issued to another client than the one presenting it invalid_request A party may_act does not name invalid_request A scope the presented token does not carry, or a scope that is not a list of scope tokens invalid_scope A resource the presented token is not addressed to, or a presented token addressed to its own client and to no resource invalid_target

A scope or a resource of the new token that the client did not register, and a public client, make the request fail with no token issued, as said above.

A presented token is read the way the provider's own endpoints read one. It is an access token of this provider, in either shape, that has not expired; and a token issued on a sign-in at this provider is one whose session has not ended, whose grant has not been revoked, and which names a person the provider still serves, so that a session somebody ended cannot be turned into a fresh token by a service that kept an old one. What the client is told is that the token is not good, and not which of those questions it failed (RFC 8693 §2.2.2).

A token addressed to its own client is not exchangeable. It was asked for no resource, so there is nothing to narrow, and the new token could only be addressed outside what the old one covered.

docs.title: Delegation and impersonation
docs.text:
The two cases of RFC 8693 §1.3 are told apart by the request and by nothing else: no flag, scope or registration member turns one into the other.

Delegation, with an actor tokenImpersonation, without one

The new token names who acts for the subject in an act claim (RFC 8693 §4.1), whose sub is the subject of the actor token. The actor token is a token issued to the client that presents it, typically one it holds for itself, whose sub is its client_id: a token is held by whoever holds it, so a client that could present somebody else's would write that somebody into the act of a token they never asked for.

When the presented token already carried an act, the new actor is added around it, the most recent actor outermost, so a chain of exchanges nests and is never flattened:

"act": {
    "sub": "invoices-worker",
    "act": {
        "sub": "gateway"
    }
}

The new token says nothing of anybody acting beyond what the presented token already said: it is the subject, and the act the presented token carried, if any, is carried unchanged.

docs.title: Who may act
docs.text:
may_act is the word of the subject's side on the matter (RFC 8693 §4.4). Registered on a client, it names the one party that may act for the subject of a token issued to that client: it is written on every self-contained token that client receives, and an exchange of one of its tokens is refused with invalid_request for anybody else, whatever the registration of the client that asks says. The party compared is the one about to hold the new token: the outermost actor the new token would name or, when it would name none, the client that asked, whose client_id stands for it. A client that registered no may_act leaves the decision to the registration of whoever asks.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    clients:
        frontend:
            # ...
            may_act: gateway

docs.title: What the issued token says
docs.text:
Claim Value sub The sub of the presented token, unchanged, as it was written for the client that token was issued to (RFC 8693 §2.2.1) client_id The client that asked for the exchange aud The resources the request named, or every resource the presented token is addressed to scope The scopes the request named, or every scope of the presented token act Who acts for the subject, on a delegation, and on an impersonation of a token that already said sid, auth_time, acr, amr The sign-in of the presented token, unchanged, when it had one grant_id The grant of the presented token person The person the token is about, sealed, when the presented token was issued on a sign-in: below may_act In the self-contained shape, when the client that asked registered one cnf What the new token is bound to: what the exchange request binds it to (grants), whatever the presented token was bound to

The answer carries the access token, issued_token_type set to urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token (RFC 8693 §2.2.1), its token_type, expires_in and scope, and no refresh token and no ID token. The new token lives tokens.access_token_ttl, in the shape the client that asked registered.

The new token descends from the grant the presented one descended from. Taking that grant back takes both, and the end of the session the presented token named refuses both, at the provider's own endpoints and at its introspection.

The issued token knows the person it is about, when the presented token was issued on a sign-in. Its sub was written for another client, and may be a pairwise subject the client that asked cannot read. So the provider keeps the person the presented token named beside it: on the record of an opaque token, and, in a self-contained one, as the private claim person, sealed by the key management service of the tenant, which only the provider can open and which tells the holder nothing it did not know. That is what lets the provider's own endpoints and introspection read an exchanged token, and what puts the acts it gives rise to, the tokens issued and the introspections that describe it, in the journal of that person.

A presented token that carries no sign-in names no person to the exchange: a token a client holds for itself, and a token of a JWT bearer assertion alike. The token issued for it then carries no person claim, its record names nobody, and its tokens.issued act is written in no journal.

docs.title: Sender-constrained tokens
docs.text: A bearer token opens what it opens for whoever presents it. A sender-constrained token is bound to something its client proves again every time it presents the token: a key it signs a proof with, DPoP (RFC 9449), or the certificate of its TLS connection, mutual TLS (RFC 8705). Whoever takes the token without what it is bound to holds a token that UserInfo refuses, and so does every resource server that checks the binding.

docs.title: The two bindings
docs.text:
DPoP Mutual TLS What the client proves A key, with a proof it signs for each request and sends in the DPoP header The certificate it presented at the TLS handshake Which clients are bound Every client whose token request carries a proof A client that authenticates with its certificate, and a client that registered tls_client_certificate_bound_access_tokens What the token names in cnf (RFC 7800 §3.1) jkt, the JWK SHA-256 thumbprint of the public key (RFC 7638 §3) x5t#S256, the SHA-256 thumbprint of the DER encoding of the certificate (RFC 8705 §3.1) token_type of the token response and of introspection DPoP Bearer How the token is presented Authorization: DPoP <token>, with a new proof that names the token in ath Authorization: Bearer <token>, on a connection that presents the same certificate

The binding is made at the token endpoint, by every grant. The access token of an authorization code, a refresh token, client credentials, a device code, a backchannel authentication, a token exchange and a JWT bearer grant is bound to what the token request proved. An ID token carries no binding.

Both shapes of access token carry it. An at+jwt carries cnf among its claims, and an opaque token keeps the same member in its record, which introspection returns. A resource server that verifies an at+jwt offline reads the binding in the token; one that introspects reads it in the answer.

A token is bound to one thing. A token request that proves a certificate the tokens would be bound to, and a DPoP key as well, is refused with invalid_dpop_proof, status 400, rather than arbitrated: a token names one thing in its cnf, and the provider does not choose for the client. A certificate presented only because the listener asked for one binds nothing (see mutual TLS), so a client that authenticates another way may send a DPoP proof over that connection.

docs.title: Refresh tokens
docs.text:
The refresh token of a public client is bound to what the token request proved, key or certificate, and it is refreshed only by a request that proves the same thing again: any other request is answered invalid_grant. Such a token is not rotated when it is used, the binding being what tells it from a copy. A public client that binds nothing has its refresh token rotated at every use instead.

The refresh token of a confidential client is bound to nothing, since the client authenticates every time it refreshes. The access token a refresh issues is bound to what that refresh request proves, which may be a key the earlier tokens were not bound to.

Refresh tokens

docs.title: A client that must bind
docs.text:
Two members of a registration refuse a token request rather than answer it with bearer tokens. Both are read at the token endpoint, after the client has authenticated and before the grant is read, and both refuse with invalid_request, status 400.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    clients:
        payments-app:
            # ...
            require_sender_constrained_tokens: true
Member What a token request of that client must prove Who sets it require_sender_constrained_tokens A certificate its tokens are bound to, or a DPoP key, whichever (FAPI 2.0 Security Profile §5.3.1) The deployment, in the declaration of the client. A client that registers itself and sends it is refused with invalid_client_metadata tls_client_certificate_bound_access_tokens The certificate of its connection, whatever way it authenticates (RFC 8705 §3.4) The declaration of the client, or the client itself when it registers, RFC 8705 §3.4 making it a member of a registration

Both default to false, and neither is a setting of the deployment as a whole.

docs.title: Where the binding is checked
docs.text:
At a resource of the provider, which is UserInfo: a bound token is honoured only when the request proves again what it is bound to, and refused with invalid_token, status 401, otherwise. A resource server of your own makes the same check against the cnf it reads, as RFC 9449 §7.1 and RFC 8705 §3.2 describe; DPoP and mutual TLS say what each one compares.

What the provider announces. The discovery document always carries dpop_signing_alg_values_supported, the signature algorithms the provider is wired with. It carries tls_client_certificate_bound_access_tokens set to true because a client authentication method that proves a certificate is wired, which the bundle does. The bare challenge of UserInfo, answered to a request that carries no token at all, is what is read from the bindings themselves, both wired in the bundle: WWW-Authenticate: Bearer, DPoP.

docs.title: DPoP
docs.text:
The client holds a key pair and signs a proof with it for every request it makes, the provider binds the tokens it issues to the thumbprint of the public key, and a resource that checks the binding refuses a token so bound to whoever cannot sign a proof with that key. The key belongs to the client and nobody vouches for it, so a public client, which holds no secret, binds its tokens as well as a confidential one.

DPoP is always on. A client that sends no proof is not concerned, and gets bearer tokens unless its registration requires bound ones.

docs.title: The proof
docs.text:
A proof is a JWT in the DPoP header of the request (RFC 9449 §4.1), one per request: a request that carries two DPoP headers is refused with invalid_dpop_proof, since which of them was read would decide which key the tokens are bound to.

Where Member What the provider requires Header typ dpop+jwt (RFC 9449 §4.2) Header alg One of dpop_signing_alg_values_supported: the signature algorithms the provider is wired with, RS256, PS256, ES256 and EdDSA in the bundle. No MAC algorithm is among them Header jwk The public key the proof is signed with. A key that carries a private member (d, p, q, dp, dq, qi, or the k of a symmetric key) is refused. kid, jku and x5c are not read, and nothing is looked up anywhere Claims jti A non-empty string, accepted once for that key Claims htm The method of the request, compared exactly: POST is not post Claims htu The URL of the endpoint, as below Claims iat An integer, inside the window below Claims ath Present exactly when the request presents an access token: the base64url SHA-256 of that token (RFC 9449 §4.2, §7.1) Claims nonce When present, a non-empty string. It is compared with the nonces the provider issued only when the provider asks for one

The signature is verified against the key the proof carries, and what comes out is that key, named by its JWK SHA-256 thumbprint (RFC 7638 §3): the 43 characters of base64url a token bound to it names in cnf.jkt.

htu names the endpoint the provider publishes, never what a header of the request says. The URL is the one under the issuer that the discovery document announces in token_endpoint, pushed_authorization_request_endpoint or userinfo_endpoint, including for a request that reached the host of the mutual TLS aliases. The two are compared as URLs and not as bytes (RFC 9449 §4.3, RFC 3986 §6.2.2 and §6.2.3): the query and the fragment are dropped, the scheme and the host compared without regard to case, and a port that is the default of its scheme is the same URL as no port, so HTTPS://OP.EXAMPLE.COM:443/token names https://op.example.com/token. The path is compared as it is, RFC 3986 making it case sensitive.

A proof stands for the time a request spends on the wire. It is refused when its iat is more than leeway seconds ahead of the clock of the provider, and when the request arrives proof_max_age plus leeway seconds or more after its iat: 30 seconds ahead and 90 seconds behind, by default.

A proof is used once. Its jti is remembered with the thumbprint of the key until the proof stops being accepted, so that two clients choosing the same jti do not collide, and a proof presented again inside its window is refused (RFC 9449 §11.1).

docs.title: Where a proof is read
docs.text:
Three endpoints read the DPoP header, and every other endpoint ignores it.

Endpoint htm ath What the proof does there /token POST Absent Binds the tokens of the response to its key, and proves the key a code or a refresh token was bound to /par POST Absent Reserves the authorization code of the pushed request for its key /userinfo The method of the request, GET or POST Required Proves the key the access token is bound to

At the token endpoint the proof is verified once the client has authenticated, and before anything of the grant is read.

docs.title: Tokens bound to the key
docs.text:
A token request that carries a valid proof is answered with tokens bound to its key, whatever the grant:

  • the token response says "token_type": "DPoP" (RFC 9449 §5), and the client presents the access token as Authorization: DPoP <token> from then on, with a proof beside it;
  • an at+jwt carries "cnf": {"jkt": "<thumbprint>"} (RFC 9449 §6.1), and an opaque token keeps the same member in its record;
  • introspection describes the token with "token_type": "DPoP" and the same cnf;
  • the refresh token of a public client is bound to the key too, refreshed only by a request that proves it again and not rotated; the refresh token of a confidential client is bound to nothing.

A request that proves a certificate its tokens would be bound to and carries a proof as well is refused with invalid_dpop_proof: a token is bound to one thing.

docs.title: A code reserved for a key
docs.text:
An authorization request may name the key that will come and exchange its code, in dpop_jkt (RFC 9449 §10): a JWK SHA-256 thumbprint, 43 characters of base64url, or the request is refused with invalid_request, sent back to the redirect URI at the authorization endpoint and answered as JSON at /par.

A request pushed to /par with a proof is reserved for the key of that proof (RFC 9449 §10.1): the provider writes the thumbprint into the request as the dpop_jkt the client could have written itself. A pushed request that names a dpop_jkt of another key than the proof that carried it is refused with invalid_request, rather than arbitrated.

A reserved code is exchanged only by a request that proves that key. The token endpoint answers any other exchange with invalid_grant, and the attempt spends the code all the same: a code intercepted on its way back through the browser is worth nothing to whoever does not hold the key. A code reserved for no key is exchanged by whichever request the rest of the grant accepts.

docs.title: The nonce
docs.text:
The provider may ask that every proof carry a value it handed out (RFC 9449 §8), which says when the proof was made in terms the provider knows rather than in the iat its client wrote. It is off by default.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    dpop:
        nonce:
            required: true

With required: true, a proof that carries no nonce, or one the provider did not issue in the last ttl seconds, is refused with use_dpop_nonce and a fresh nonce in the DPoP-Nonce header of the answer. The client makes its proof again with that nonce and sends the request again. A nonce stands for its whole lifetime and is not spent by the first proof that carries it, what makes a proof single-use being its jti; the provider hands out a new one only with a refusal, so a client keeps the last nonce it was given until the next refusal.

With required: false, the nonce claim of a proof is compared with nothing, and no answer carries DPoP-Nonce.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    dpop:
        proof_max_age: 60
        leeway: 30
        nonce:
            required: false
            ttl: 300
Option Default What it decides proof_max_age 60 Seconds a proof stands from its iat, before the leeway is added, one at least. Every second beyond what a request spends on the wire is a second a proof taken off that wire may be sent again in leeway 30 Seconds allowed of the clock of a client, added on both sides of the window: a proof is taken up to leeway seconds ahead of the provider, and until proof_max_age plus leeway seconds after its iat nonce.required false Whether every proof carries a nonce the provider issued nonce.ttl 300 Seconds a nonce is accepted once issued, one at least

What a proof may be signed with is not an option: it is the list of signature algorithms the provider is wired with, which the discovery document announces in dpop_signing_alg_values_supported.

The proofs already seen and the nonces live in a cache pool

Both are kept in the pool beffroi.dpop, which the bundle declares on cache.app. A deployment that runs on several machines points that pool at a store they all reach: otherwise a proof replayed on another machine is not recognised as a replay there, and a nonce one machine issued is refused by the next. The pool tells a hit from a miss and not an insertion from a replacement, so two presentations of one proof arriving in the same instant may both be taken; what a replay needs is a wider window than that.

docs.title: What a resource server checks
docs.text:
UserInfo, the resource of the provider, honours a token bound to a key only when the request presents it under the DPoP scheme with a valid proof of that key, and refuses it with a 401 whose challenge names the scheme that would have worked. The proof is verified before the token is read, and the binding once the token is known to be valid:

The request Status WWW-Authenticate Presents the bound token as Bearer 401 DPoP error="invalid_token" Presents it as DPoP with no proof, or with a proof of another key 401 DPoP error="invalid_token" Carries a proof that does not verify, or that names another request or another token 401 DPoP error="invalid_dpop_proof" Carries no nonce, or a stale one, while the provider asks for one 401 DPoP error="use_dpop_nonce", and the fresh nonce in DPoP-Nonce

The body of each refusal carries the same error and its error_description as JSON. UserInfo gives the rest of its refusals.

A resource server of your own reads the thumbprint the token is bound to in the cnf.jkt of the at+jwt, or in the cnf of the introspection answer, verifies the proof as RFC 9449 §4.3 describes, its ath included, and compares the thumbprint of the key of the proof with that member (RFC 9449 §7.1). A token introspected as "token_type": "DPoP" is one to refuse when it arrives under the Bearer scheme.

The same refusals at the endpoints that issue tokens are answers of RFC 6749 §5.2 rather than challenges: invalid_dpop_proof and use_dpop_nonce are a 400 with the JSON body, and the second one carries the DPoP-Nonce header (RFC 9449 §8).

A client running in a page

The standalone application lets a script of any origin send the DPoP header to /token, /par and /userinfo, and read DPoP-Nonce and WWW-Authenticate in their answers, without credentials. Behind the bundle alone, that CORS policy is the application's to write.

docs.title: Mutual TLS
docs.text: RFC 8705 has two halves, and the provider serves both. A client authenticates with the certificate it presents at the TLS handshake (§2), and the tokens it receives are bound to that certificate (§3), so that a token presented over a connection without it is refused wherever the binding is checked. The certificate is the one the TLS listener of the deployment received, handed to PHP by that listener and never read from a header of the request.

docs.title: Authenticating with a certificate
docs.text:
Two methods recognise a client by its certificate, and both are wired in the bundle. Either way the request names the client in client_id and presents the certificate at the handshake: a request without a certificate presents neither method.

token_endpoint_auth_method The certificate What makes it the client's tls_client_auth (RFC 8705 §2.1) Issued by a certificate authority the TLS listener trusts The one value the client registered, read out of the certificate and compared self_signed_tls_client_auth (RFC 8705 §2.2) Any, self-signed included The client publishes it in its JWK Set, jwks or jwks_uri: the first certificate of the x5c of one of its keys (RFC 7517 §4.7), or the x5t#S256 of one of them (§4.9)

A tls_client_auth client registers exactly one of the five values of RFC 8705 §2.1.2, and a client registered for any other method registers none of them: a declaration that does not hold is refused at boot, and a registration that does not is refused.

Member Compared with the certificate tls_client_auth_subject_dn The subject distinguished name, in the string form of RFC 4514. The registered value is written again, when the registration is read, the way the provider writes the name it reads out of a certificate, so a name as openssl x509 -noout -subject -nameopt RFC2253 prints it is registered as it is tls_client_auth_san_dns A dNSName entry of the subject alternative name, without regard to case (RFC 4343 §1). A wildcard entry is text like any other and is never expanded tls_client_auth_san_uri A uniformResourceIdentifier entry, as the text it is, with no normalisation tls_client_auth_san_ip An iPAddress entry, as the octets it stands for, so the registered text may be written in any form RFC 4291 §2.2 allows tls_client_auth_san_email An rfc822Name entry, as the text it is, nothing folded config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    clients:
        payments-app:
            token_endpoint_auth_method: tls_client_auth
            tls_client_auth_subject_dn: 'CN=payments-app,O=Example,C=FR'
            redirect_uris: ['https://payments.example.com/callback']

The provider judges no chain. Only the leaf certificate reaches PHP, so what makes a certificate trustworthy, its chain, its validity period and its revocation, is judged by the TLS listener during the handshake, against the authorities the deployment configures there. A self-signed certificate is trusted for what the client published and for nothing else, as the keys of private_key_jwt are; a client that renews its certificate publishes the new one before it presents it.

A certificate beside another credential does not make two methods. A client reaching the host that asks for a certificate presents one because it was asked: the credential its request carries, a secret or an assertion, authenticates it, and the certificate authenticates only a client registered for one of the two methods above.

A request that names a client and does not prove it is refused with invalid_client, status 401, and the same description whatever the cause: a certificate that is not the registered one, a certificate the client does not publish, a certificate that cannot be read, no certificate from a client registered for one. Each refusal is an act of the journal, client_authentication.failed.

docs.title: Tokens bound to the certificate
docs.text:
Two clients get tokens bound to the certificate of their connection:

  • a client that authenticated with tls_client_auth or self_signed_tls_client_auth, bound to the very certificate that authenticated it (RFC 8705 §3);
  • a client that registered tls_client_certificate_bound_access_tokens: true, whatever way it authenticates (RFC 8705 §3.4). A token request of such a client that presents no certificate is refused with invalid_request, status 400, before anything of what it came to spend is read.

Any other client that presents a certificate, because the listener asked for one, is not bound to it: binding a client that never asked for it would break the resource servers it calls.

What a bound token says. An at+jwt carries "cnf": {"x5t#S256": "<thumbprint>"}, the base64url SHA-256 of the DER encoding of the certificate (RFC 8705 §3.1), and an opaque token keeps the same member in its record. The token response says "token_type": "Bearer": the client changes nothing in the way it presents the token, the transport proving the holder at every request. The refresh token of a public client is bound to the certificate as well; the one of a confidential client is bound to nothing, since the client authenticates when it refreshes. A token request that proves the certificate and carries a DPoP proof as well is refused with invalid_dpop_proof, a token being bound to one thing.

UserInfo honours a bound token only over a connection that presents the same certificate, and refuses it otherwise with invalid_token, status 401, WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token". A client therefore reads UserInfo at the userinfo_endpoint of the aliases below: the ordinary host asks for no certificate, and a request that reaches it proves none.

Introspection describes a bound token whatever certificate the caller presented, since the client it was issued to may introspect it however it authenticates today, and its answer carries the cnf a resource server needs to make its own check. A resource server of your own compares that thumbprint with the SHA-256 of the certificate its own TLS connection received (RFC 8705 §3.2).

docs.title: The endpoint aliases
docs.text:
A deployment may serve the endpoints that read a certificate on a host of their own, whose listener asks for one, and leave the ordinary host of the issuer asking for nothing, so that a browser is never asked for a certificate at the authorization endpoint or on a page. The configuration names that host:

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    mutual_tls:
        origin: 'https://mtls.op.example.com'
Option Default What it decides origin none The scheme and the authority of the host whose listener asks for a certificate, without a path. The discovery document announces the aliases under it. Left out or empty, it announces none, and a client authenticating with a certificate reaches the ordinary endpoints, which is what a deployment serving one host does

With an origin, the discovery document carries mtls_endpoint_aliases (RFC 8705 §5): the same paths, on the other origin, for six endpoints.

{
    "mtls_endpoint_aliases": {
        "token_endpoint": "https://mtls.op.example.com/token",
        "userinfo_endpoint": "https://mtls.op.example.com/userinfo",
        "introspection_endpoint": "https://mtls.op.example.com/introspect",
        "revocation_endpoint": "https://mtls.op.example.com/revoke",
        "pushed_authorization_request_endpoint": "https://mtls.op.example.com/par",
        "device_authorization_endpoint": "https://mtls.op.example.com/device_authorization"
    }
}

The issuer does not change, and neither does anything else the document says: an alias is another way to the same provider. The backchannel authentication endpoint reads a certificate as well, and is not among the aliases. Independently of the origin, the document announces tls_client_certificate_bound_access_tokens as true whenever a method that authenticates by certificate is wired, which the bundle does.

docs.title: How the certificate reaches the application
docs.text:
The bundle reads the certificate in one place, the server variable SSL_CLIENT_CERT, named after the one mod_ssl sets: the leaf certificate in its PEM envelope, set by the TLS listener from the handshake it carried out. An empty envelope, or no variable, is a request made without a certificate. A client controls every header of its request and no variable of the process that serves it, so no header is ever read in its place.

A certificate in a header is refused. A request that carries Ssl-Client-Cert, X-Ssl-Client-Cert, X-Client-Cert or X-Forwarded-Client-Cert is somebody trying, and is refused rather than served without its certificate, so that a deployment placed behind a proxy that forwards one learns it on its first request. The refusal is invalid_request, status 400, at the seven endpoints that read a certificate: /token, /par, /introspect, /revoke, /userinfo, /device_authorization and /backchannel_authentication. So is a variable that does not hold a PEM certificate, the listener being misconfigured then.

In the standalone applicationIn a Symfony application

The image carries a second site block, /etc/frankenphp/mtls.Caddyfile, for the host whose listener asks for a certificate. A deployment turns it on with three variables, and the host of SERVER_NAME keeps asking for nothing.

Variable Read by Value MTLS_SERVER_NAME Caddy The name of the host that asks for a certificate CADDY_EXTRA_CONFIG Caddy import mtls.Caddyfile, which adds that site block BEFFROI_MTLS_ORIGIN The application The origin of that host, which becomes mutual_tls.origin

The .env of the application names the host of its development stack, https://mtls.op.localhost, so a deployment sets BEFFROI_MTLS_ORIGIN to its own host, or to nothing when it serves no such host and announces no alias.

The site block asks for a certificate without requiring one (client_auth in mode request), so a client that authenticates another way completes its handshake on that host too. A certificate is only accepted with the signature of the handshake that proves its holder has the private key (RFC 8446 §4.4.3), and the leaf is handed to PHP as SSL_CLIENT_CERT, empty when the client presented none.

The block verifies no chain, so it accepts a certificate whatever authority issued it, which is what self_signed_tls_client_auth needs. A deployment that authenticates clients with tls_client_auth has that block verify a presented certificate against the authorities it accepts: that is where the chain is judged, and nowhere else.

The web server that terminates TLS sets SSL_CLIENT_CERT to the PEM of the leaf certificate it verified, and leaves it empty when the client presented none. It asks for a certificate on the host the aliases point at, and judges there the chain of a certificate that tls_client_auth will rely on.

A deployment whose edge hands the certificate over some other way implements Beffroi\Bundle\Http\Tls\ClientCertificateResolverInterface, which returns the certificate of a request or none, and aliases it in place of the resolver of the bundle, rather than teaching the bundle a header to trust.

docs.title: Tokens
docs.text:
Three kinds of token leave this provider, all of them at the token endpoint, and a client never has to guess which one it is holding:

Token Who it is for Its shape How long it lives Page Access token A resource server A JWT of type at+jwt or an opaque reference, as the client registered tokens.access_token_ttl, 600 seconds Access tokens ID token The client, about the person who signed in A JWT signed by the tenant, encrypted when the client asked for it tokens.id_token_ttl, 600 seconds ID tokens Refresh token The token endpoint, to ask again An opaque reference tokens.refresh_token_ttl, 30 days, within tokens.refresh_token_absolute_ttl, 90 days Refresh tokens

The authorization endpoint answers with a code and never with a token, and the grants say which of the three each way of asking issues. Encryption says what the provider encrypts, and for whom.

A reference is worth nothing outside the provider, and nothing inside a copy of its database. An opaque access token, a refresh token, an authorization code, a device code and an auth_req_id are each 256 random bits in base64url, 43 characters, and the provider keeps the SHA-256 of each, never the value. The user code a device shows is the one value made to be typed by a person, eight characters out of twenty consonants, and it is kept as its SHA-256 too (device code).

docs.title: Lifetimes
docs.text:
Every lifetime is a number of seconds, at least one, set under tokens; some have a ceiling, which a configuration past it fails to load with.

Option Default At most What it is authorization_code_ttl 60 600 An authorization code, RFC 6749 §4.1.2 recommending ten minutes at most access_token_ttl 600 Both shapes of access token id_token_ttl 600 An ID token refresh_token_ttl 2592000 refresh_token_absolute_ttl One refresh token, from the moment it was issued refresh_token_absolute_ttl 7776000 A family of refresh tokens, from the authorization that started it request_uri_ttl 60 600 The reference a pushed authorization request is answered with (RFC 9126 §2.2) device_code_ttl 600 1800 A device code and the user code beside it device_code_interval 5 30 How long a device waits between two polls backchannel_authentication_ttl 300 3600 A backchannel request that asked for no requested_expiry backchannel_authentication_max_requested_expiry 1800 3600 The longest a backchannel request lives, whatever it asks for backchannel_authentication_interval 5 30 How long a client waits between two polls of a backchannel request config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    tokens:
        authorization_code_ttl: 60
        access_token_ttl: 600
        id_token_ttl: 600
        refresh_token_ttl: 2592000
        refresh_token_absolute_ttl: 7776000

The standalone application reads access_token_ttl and id_token_ttl from the environment variables BEFFROI_ACCESS_TOKEN_TTL and BEFFROI_ID_TOKEN_TTL, both 600 in its .env.

A lifetime is also how long a retired signing key is kept. The rotation of a signing key dates its retirement from the longest lifetime among what the tenant signs with it, the ID token and the self-contained access token among them, so that a token signed just before a rotation verifies until it expires. Lengthening one of these lifetimes delays every retirement by as much. Keys describes the rotation.

docs.title: Access tokens
docs.text:
An access token is what a client presents to a resource server. Each client receives its access tokens in one shape, the one it registered, so a resource server knows from that registration what it is validating:

Shape access_token_format What it is How a resource server reads it At the revocation endpoint Self-contained jwt A JWT signed by the tenant, of type at+jwt (RFC 9068) Offline, against the JWK Set of the issuer Refused: it expires on its own (RFC 7009 §2.2.1) Reference opaque 256 random bits in base64url, 43 characters, which mean something to this provider alone At the introspection endpoint (RFC 7662) Taken back at once

A client that registers no shape takes jwt, the first one the provider is wired with. A name no wired shape answers to is refused: a declared client is an error of the configuration, and a registration request is answered invalid_client_metadata. Both shapes live tokens.access_token_ttl seconds, ten minutes by default: the self-contained one cannot be taken back, so its lifetime is what bounds it, and the opaque one gets the same, a revocation being a facility and not a reason to live longer.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    tokens:
        access_token_ttl: 600
    clients:
        reporting:
            # ...
            access_token_format: opaque

No access token is ever encrypted.

docs.title: What it says
docs.text:
Both shapes carry the same facts: the self-contained one in its claims, the reference in the record the provider keeps under its SHA-256, which introspection renders under the same names.

Claim What it holds iss The issuer of the tenant sub Who the token is about: for a person who signed in, the subject this provider gives them for this client, public or pairwise; for a client acting for itself, its client_id; for a token of a token exchange or of a JWT bearer assertion, the subject the grant named client_id The client the token was issued to (RFC 9068 §2.2) aud The resources it is addressed to (RFC 8707 §2), named by the request or carried by what the grant spends, as the page of each grant says: a token exchange that names none is addressed to every resource of the presented token, and a token of an authorization that carries no resource is addressed to the client_id. One value is written as a string, several as a list exp, iat When it expires, and when it was issued scope The scopes it carries, space-delimited auth_time, acr, amr, sid What the session had proven when the authorization was granted, and that session (RFC 9068 §2.2.1). Absent from a token nobody signed in for grant_id The grant the token descends from, which the provider asks, of a token somebody signed in for, whether it is still alive authorization_details What the person agreed to beyond the scopes (RFC 9396 §7), when there is any act Who acts for the subject (RFC 8693 §4.1), on a token of a token exchange cnf What the token is bound to: jkt, the thumbprint of a DPoP key (RFC 9449 §6.1), or x5t#S256, the thumbprint of a certificate (RFC 8705 §3.1)

The self-contained shape carries four claims more, which introspection does not render: jti, a random UUID; userinfo_claims, the claims the client asked for by name for the UserInfo endpoint (OIDC Core §5.5); may_act, who may act for the subject of a token of this client (RFC 8693 §4.4), when it registered one; and person, below.

docs.title: The header
docs.text: typ is at+jwt (RFC 9068 §2.1), kid names the key of the JWK Set that signed it, and alg is the algorithm the provider signs with by default, the first one it is wired with, RS256. It is never the algorithm the client registered for its ID tokens: an access token is read by resource servers, not by the client.

docs.title: The person a token is about
docs.text: A token whose sub was written for another client says who it is about, sealed. A token issued by a token exchange of a token issued on a sign-in keeps the sub of that token, written for the client it was issued to, which may be a pairwise subject the client now holding it cannot read; a token of a JWT bearer assertion names a person nobody signed in for here. For both, the provider keeps the person beside the token: on the record of a reference, and in a self-contained token as the private claim person (RFC 7519 §4.3), sealed by the key management service of the tenant. Only the provider opens it, and a resource server reads it as it reads any claim it was given no meaning for. A token a client holds for itself is about nobody and carries none, and so does a token of a token exchange whose presented token carried no sign-in.

docs.title: What the provider asks of a token it is presented
docs.text:
The provider's own endpoints that take an access token, UserInfo, introspection and the token exchange, read both shapes the same way and ask more of a token than its signature:

  1. it was issued by this tenant, and it has not expired, with no leeway, the clock being the provider's own;
  2. the session it descends from has not ended;
  3. the grant it descends from has not been revoked;
  4. the person it is about is still served.

A token nobody signed in for at this provider descends from no session, and only the first question is asked of it. A resource server that holds the token and the JWK Set and nothing else cannot ask the other three, which is what verifying offline means: a self-contained token outlives the end of its session, the consent taken back and the revocation of its grant wherever it is verified offline, until it expires. Introspection answers "active": false for it from the instant any of those happened.

The UserInfo endpoint takes only a token addressed to the client itself, the one a request that names no resource gets: a token addressed to a resource is refused there with invalid_token, whatever it is good for elsewhere.

docs.title: Choosing a shape
docs.text:
jwtopaque

For a resource server that verifies tokens itself, with no call to the provider per request. The token cannot be taken back: the revocation endpoint answers unsupported_token_type for one, and the end of a session, a consent taken back or a replayed code reach it only at the provider's own endpoints and at introspection. Its lifetime is therefore the window in which a stolen one is worth something.

For a resource server that asks the provider about every token. The revocation endpoint takes one back at once, and the end of a session or a consent taken back removes the ones a person signed in for. The resource server introspects as the client the token was issued to: introspection describes a token to that client and to nobody else (RFC 7662 §2.2), and only to a client that authenticates.

A token is a bearer token unless the request that obtained it binds it: to the key of its DPoP proof, or to the certificate of its connection for a client that authenticates with that certificate (tls_client_auth, self_signed_tls_client_auth) or registered tls_client_certificate_bound_access_tokens (grants). The token_type of the answer then says DPoP for a key and Bearer for a certificate. Sender-constrained tokens says what a resource server then asks of the caller.

docs.title: Adding a shape
docs.text: A shape is two classes answering to one name, which is what a client registers in access_token_format: an issuer implementing Beffroi\Oidc\Port\AccessTokenShapeIssuerInterface, tagged beffroi.oidc.access_token_issuer, and a verifier implementing Beffroi\Oidc\Port\AccessTokenVerifierInterface, tagged beffroi.oidc.access_token_verifier. The first tagged issuer is the shape a client that registers none takes. A shape written with no verifier, read with no issuer, or written by two issuers is refused, a token the provider writes and cannot read back being a token nobody can spend.

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text:
A client may ask for three of the documents the provider hands it to be encrypted to a key of its own: its ID token, its UserInfo answer, and its signed authorization responses. The provider encrypts for the client that registered it and for nobody else, and a client that registered nothing receives its documents unencrypted.

Document The pair a client registers Signed before it is encrypted ID token (OIDC Core §3.1.3.7) id_token_encrypted_response_alg, id_token_encrypted_response_enc Always UserInfo answer (OIDC Core §5.3.2) userinfo_encrypted_response_alg, userinfo_encrypted_response_enc When the client also registered userinfo_signed_response_alg; otherwise what is encrypted is the plain JSON of the claims Signed authorization response (JARM §3) authorization_encrypted_response_alg, authorization_encrypted_response_enc Always

Access tokens, refresh tokens and logout tokens are never encrypted. A logout token is signed with the algorithm the client registered for its ID tokens, and travels in clear.

Signed, then encrypted, never the other way round (OIDC Core §16.14). The signature says who wrote the document and travels inside what hides it, so that a client that opens the JWE finds something to verify rather than something to trust. A signed document inside a JWE is a nested JWT, and the header of the JWE says so with cty JWT (RFC 7519 §5.2).

docs.title: Registering it
docs.text:
config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    clients:
        my-application:
            # ...
            jwks_uri: 'https://app.example.com/jwks.json'
            id_token_encrypted_response_alg: RSA-OAEP-256
            id_token_encrypted_response_enc: A256GCM
            userinfo_signed_response_alg: ES256
            userinfo_encrypted_response_alg: RSA-OAEP-256
            userinfo_encrypted_response_enc: A256GCM
  • The two members of a pair come together. OIDC Registration §2 lets the enc be left out and defaults it to A128CBC-HS256, which this provider is not wired with, so it takes no default: one member without the other is refused.
  • Each name is one the provider is wired with, below, and any other is refused.
  • The client publishes its keys, in jwks or behind a jwks_uri, and a client that registers an encryption and publishes neither is refused. A jwks written down is read at registration and has to hold a key the registered algorithm can be addressed to; a set behind a URL is read when a document is minted.

A declared client that breaks one of these rules is an error of the configuration, and a registration request that breaks one is answered invalid_client_metadata.

docs.title: The algorithms
docs.text:
Wired Announced in the discovery document as Key management, the alg ECDH-ES+A256KW, to an EC key, and RSA-OAEP-256, to an RSA key id_token_encryption_alg_values_supported, userinfo_encryption_alg_values_supported, authorization_encryption_alg_values_supported Content encryption, the enc A256GCM id_token_encryption_enc_values_supported, userinfo_encryption_enc_values_supported, authorization_encryption_enc_values_supported

The document announces what is wired and nothing else. The two authorization_ members are announced only while the provider serves a response mode that signs its answer, and a provider wired with no algorithm of one of the two lists announces none of these members at all, since it can encrypt nothing. The same two lists are what a client may encrypt a request object to the tenant with, in the other direction.

docs.title: The key it is encrypted to
docs.text:
The provider encrypts to a key the client publishes, chosen by what the keys say of themselves (RFC 7517 §4.2, §4.4):

  1. Only a key of the type the algorithm takes is a candidate: EC for ECDH-ES+A256KW, RSA for RSA-OAEP-256.
  2. A key whose use is anything but enc is never one.
  3. A key that names an alg is a candidate for that algorithm and no other.
  4. Among the candidates, a key that names the algorithm wins over one whose use is enc, which wins over one that says neither, and inside each of the three the first one published wins.

A client that publishes several keys therefore chooses the one it is encrypted to by saying more about it.

A set behind a jwks_uri is read with one GET, over HTTPS or in plain HTTP on a loopback host, no redirect followed. What is read is kept for client_authentication.jwks_ttl seconds, a day by default, in a pool the workers share, under the URL it was read from. Encrypting a document never reads it again before that, a document addressed to a client naming no kid the provider could find missing. The kept set serves every use of the keys of the client, though, and a signature of the client whose header names a kid the set does not hold, the assertion of private_key_jwt or a request object, reads it again, at most once per client_authentication.jwks_refetch_cooldown, 300 seconds by default. A client that replaces its encryption key publishes the new one and keeps the private half of the old one for jwks_ttl after that.

docs.title: When the key cannot be read
docs.text:
No document leaves in clear. When the set behind the jwks_uri cannot be read, or holds no key the registered algorithm can be addressed to, the provider writes nothing for that client, and the request that was to carry the document fails: the token request that was to carry the ID token, once the code, the device code or the auth_req_id it presented has been spent, the UserInfo request, or the authorization response.

A read is given client_authentication.jwks_timeout seconds, 3 by default, and client_authentication.jwks_max_size bytes, 65536 by default, before it counts as a set that cannot be read.

docs.title: ID tokens
docs.text: An ID token is a statement about an authentication, addressed to one client (OIDC Core §2): who the person is to that client, when they proved it, how, and in which session. It is signed by the tenant, encrypted when the client asked for it, and it leaves the provider at the token endpoint and nowhere else, the authorization endpoint answering with a code alone. It is never a credential for an API.

docs.title: When one is issued
docs.text:
When openid is among the scopes of the answer and a person who signed in at this provider is behind it:

Grant ID token Authorization code With openid, carrying the nonce of the authorization request when it had one Refresh token With openid among the scopes of the refresh, describing the same authentication and carrying no nonce (OIDC Core §12.2) Device code With openid among the scopes the device asked for Backchannel authentication Always, openid being required of the request Client credentials, token exchange, JWT bearer Never: nobody signed in at this provider

docs.title: The claims
docs.text:
Claim What it holds iss The issuer of the tenant sub The subject this provider gives the person for this client, public or pairwise (OIDC Core §8) aud The client_id, as a string exp tokens.id_token_ttl seconds after iat, ten minutes by default iat When it was issued auth_time When the session last proved something, as it stood when the authorization was granted nonce The nonce of the authorization request, when it carried one acr Always. The first class the request asked for that the session satisfies, or, when it asked for none the session satisfies, the first class of the policy of the tenant the session satisfies amr The methods the session proved (RFC 8176 §2), and mfa beside them when two factors of different kinds were proven azp The client_id at_hash The left half of the digest of the access token of the same answer, under the hash of the signing algorithm, in base64url (OIDC Core §3.1.3.6) sid The session, in every ID token and for every client (Front-Channel Logout 1.0 §3, Back-Channel Logout 1.0 §2.1)

What the session had proven is the one frozen when the authorization was granted: a step-up or a new login afterwards moves the session, and never the auth_time, acr or amr of a token that descends from that authorization, those of the ID tokens a refresh issues included.

Beside these, an ID token carries the claims the authorization request asked for by name in claims.id_token (OIDC Core §5.5), when the person has a value for them and a wired claims provider serves them; one of them never replaces a claim of the table. The claims the scopes stand for, those of profile or email, are not in the ID token: the client reads them at the UserInfo endpoint.

The header carries alg and kid, and no typ: a resource server that requires at+jwt refuses an ID token presented to it as an access token, which is the point.

docs.title: Signing
docs.text:
The client chooses the algorithm in id_token_signed_response_alg (OIDC Registration §2), among those the provider is wired with: RS256, PS256, ES256 and EdDSA. A client that registers none gets the first of them, RS256, which OIDC Core §15.1 makes mandatory. A name nothing signs under, none among them, is refused: a declared client is an error of the configuration, and a registration request is answered invalid_client_metadata.

config/packages/beffroi.yaml
beffroi:
    tokens:
        id_token_ttl: 600
    clients:
        my-application:
            # ...
